identification: Anonymous prose tract "De regiminibus tractantes", after about 1245; a source or sibling of Gutolf of Heiligenkreuz, Summa grammatica ch. XVI; not identified
note: The front pastedown is an opened bifolium whose right page begins the work: "De regiminibus tractantes. Notandum quod differt regere et exigere ... Regimen est determinati casus collatio", reworking Jordanus, Notulae super Priscianum minorem (ed. Sirridge, snippets). The accusative section runs rule by rule parallel to Gutolf ch. XVI as read in Munich Clm 18796 ff. 81v-82r (page images): same conditions, one shared sentence, the mnemonic "Flagito posco peto", with Sor where Gutolf has Petrus; wording otherwise differs, so not Gutolf's text. Back pastedown: supines, then "Ultimo videamus de constructione inpersonalium". Negative: Kneepkens I-IV, Petrus Helias, Gosvin, Sponcius, Thurot, Bursill-Hall (snippets or OCR); and Johannes Balbus, Catholicon pars IV, compared by a research reader (Claude) on page images of Autun, BM, S 47 (41) (Catholicon per ARCA): its regimen chapter (f. 47v b, 'De regimine amodo videamus. Dicas quod regere est conferre dictioni ut ponatur in tali vel in certo casu') and accusative section (f. 49v b) share the doctrine (passive verbs keeping an accusative, 'doceor grammaticam'; 'ardet' with accusative) and the verse 'Flagito posco peto doceo rogo calceo celo', but continue 'Induo succingo moneo simul exuo cingo(?)' where the fragment (front pastedown, left column, checked on the image) has 'moneo doceo rogo celo ... interrogo calceo cingo, accusativos geminos hec verba requirunt'; no 'regiminibus', 'regere et exigere', Coridon/Alexis or 'tu fis a me miles' in the Catholicon text (CoMMA machine text searched, the two chapters read on the images). The incipit was not found in manuscripta.at, Handschriftenportal or Bursill-Hall, and no Gutolf manuscript is described as carrying the tract; In Principio not searched. Readings are a research subagent's; coordinator did not recheck.

content.remarks: Written after about 1245; reworks Jordanus, Notulae super Priscianum minorem. The section on the accusative runs rule by rule parallel to Gutolf of Heiligenkreuz, Summa grammatica, cap. XVI (Munich, Clm 18796, ff. 81v-82r), in different wording, so it is a source or sibling of Gutolf's text, not that text. Not the Catholicon of Johannes Balbus. Not identified.

catalogue_title: Alexander of Hales, Summa Theologica; unidentified theological text
identification: Paper pastedowns: Summa Halensis III (as catalogued) and an unidentified text on giving out of pietas. The parchment cover (a gradual) and the Juvencus sheets in the same images are the separate records F-dd8g and F-q01a
note: Front strip: six consecutive lines match Summa Halensis III, exposition of the Nicene Creed, Quaracchi IV p. 1133 (snippets). The sideways Juvencus sheets are F-q01a and the neumed parchment cover is F-dd8g (catalogued as an eleventh-century gradual with chants for Passion Sunday); both appear in these images but are not this record. For F-dd8g, a reading of the visible pieces checked in Cantus Index (tools/cantus.py) gives Tuesday of Lent IV (Of Exspectans exspectavi g01210, Cm Laetabimur g00788, then FER IIII) and Saturday of Lent IV to Passion Sunday (GrV Ut quid Domine g00796a, Of Factus est Dominus g00798, Cm Dominus regit me g00799, In Judica me g00800 with V. Emitte lucem, Gr Eripe me g00801 with V. Liberator meus, Tc Saepe expugnaverunt g00803, Cm Hoc corpus g00808, then FER II). The order is the common Roman one: 123 of the 220 inventories in the Cantus Index network that have any of the nine chants have all nine (cantus.py seq), so the run gives no basis for a use or region. Back strip unidentified after three passes: a preaching text on pietas shown in giving, with numbered divisions, Luke 11:42 and Valerius Maximus V.1.9 and V.1.8 in the form Cessolis gives them ("capiti reponi iussit"), which suggests a date after about 1300. Not the Summa Halensis (its index cites Valerius once, elsewhere), not Cessolis, John of Wales, Peraldus, Servasanctus's Antidotarius or the sermons printed under Bonaventure's name (searched inside; few page images). Untested: Stephen of Bourbon, distinction collections, Servasanctus's unprinted works.

identification: Peter of Reims OP (Petrus de Remis, d. 1247; attributed), Sermones de tempore (Sunday sermons on the epistles and gospels), Schneyer IV nos. 85 (Alter alterius onera portate, Gal 6:2; front pastedown) and 93-94 (Renovamini spiritu mentis vestrae, Eph 4:23, and the opening of Surge tolle grabatum; flyleaf and back pastedown)
note: Lead from a CoMMA manuscript-text search (tools/comma.py), checked on page images. A research reader (Claude) read all four text images of the fragment at reading size and collated them on page images of Troyes, Médiathèque du Grand Troyes, Ms. 303 (rubric fol. 135v 'Incipiunt capitula magistri Petri provincialis super epistolas et evangelia', image-checked; sermon lxxxv on fol. 183r col. b, sermon xciii on fol. 187v col. a, its end and sermon xciiii on fol. 188r col. a) and Amiens, BM, Ms. 268 (IIIF canvases 346 and 351). The front pastedown (22 lines on bearing burdensome people: Mt 17, Jer 23, Num 11, Hos 11, Eccli 22, Prov 21, Acts 13) and the flyleaf recto (22 lines on renewal by baptism and the stag) agree with both witnesses in wording and sequence; the flyleaf verso (the phoenix, the explicit 'tanto resurgent gloriosius quanto hic vixerunt humilius', then 'Surge tolle grabatum tuum et ambula') and the back pastedown (Judas Maccabeus cleansing the sanctuary, lines 1-12) were not used in discovery and also agree. The fragment shares several variants with Amiens 268 against Troyes 303 (honus, illorum excipias, vel tedio, portans eos, quam hominem imprudentem, desidia; reformavit, homo without peccator, veneno prave persuasionis) and has a few readings of its own (humoribus? for in moribus; a shorter text on the back pastedown). Attribution: Schneyer, Repertorium IV, Petrus de Remis, Sermones de tempore, no. 85 incipit 'Sunt onera culpae, poenae, morum incompositorum', no. 93 incipit 'Bene dicit apostolus spiritu non carne' and explicit 'quanto hic vixerunt humilius', followed by no. 94 Surge tolle grabatum (archive.org full-text search, snippets only; page images not seen); Schneyer's list of further manuscripts of this series names Amiens 268, Lille 88 and Troyes 303, and his vol. I notes that Peter of Reims is often called only 'provincialis'. The Clairvaux catalogue (Rothschild and Heid 2021, P 71) gives Troyes 303 fol. 135v-216v as Petrus Provincialis Remensis, Sermones in epistolis, in evangeliis, citing Kaeppeli, Scriptores I 3326, and an edition printed under the name of Antony of Padua (Pedeponti 1739); Kaeppeli and that print were not consulted. Lille 88 was compared only in machine HTR. Leaf order, the codicological relation of the four pieces, dating and recension are not established. Transcription is source-assisted and not human-reviewed.

identification: Abbreviated sermon book drawing on Berthold of Regensburg (Rusticanus de Dominicis, 14th Sunday after Pentecost; Rusticanus de Sanctis 3), Philip the Chancellor's Summa (Sermones) super Psalterium on Ps 19:4, and Conrad of Saxony; the compilation is not identified
note: Leaves 88r-86v carry Berthold's sermon on threefold fidelity and the opening of his sermon on the three crosses, both abridged and reworded; a research reader matched the first on page images of Freiburg UB Hs. 152 f. 111v (full text) and Munich Clm 8739 ff. 205v-206r (another abridgement), and the second on a page image of Leipzig UB Ms 498 f. 5v plus snippets of Hoetzl's 1882 edition. In place of Berthold's ending of the first sermon (88v 14 to 86v 12) the fragment has an instruction for laypeople who do not say the hours to meditate on the Passion hour by hour. Its source is Philip the Chancellor's Summa super Psalterium, in the treatment of Ps 19:4 'Memor sit omnis sacrificii tui', just before Ps 20:4. Found by a CoMMA HTR search. A research reader (Claude) then compared the fragment images of 88v 14-25, 86r 1-7 and 86v 1-9 with page images of Paris BnF lat. 14594 f. 29r col. a (catalogued as Philip's Sermones super Psalterium) and Soissons BM 65 f. 41r col. b (ARCA: 'Psalterium magistri Philippi, cancellarii Parisiensis'). The same frame and order recur in both: 'valde necessarium ... maxime laicis qui horas non cantant ... diligenter attendant', the hour-by-hour list from capture at Matins to burial at Compline, 'Qui hoc cogitat', and the close 'Attende ... vide ne polluas ... Eccli. conserva tempus et declina a malo. Alioquin fiet tibi ... Thren. vocavit adversum me tempus'. Most wording agrees (ad columpnam ligatus, virgis cesus, colaphizatus, crucem ferre coactus, clavis confixus, felle et aceto potatus, cum clamore expiravit, sindone involutus, a iudeis custoditus). The fragment's 'virgis cesus' agrees with BnF lat. 14594 and Auxerre against Soissons 'flagellis cesus'. Auxerre BM 4 f. 38v, seen on its page image and catalogued as Odo of Chateauroux's Distinctiones super Psalterium, has a shorter form of the passage without the 'Attende ... Thren.' close. The fragment shares that close with the Philip witnesses. Valenciennes BM 18 (catalogued as Philip) was read only in HTR. The fragment rewrites the passage freely and adds to it: Christ's bloody sweat and betrayal, the apostles' flight, the resurrection and the appearance to Mary Magdalene at Prime, the Spirit given at Terce, the Ascension meal at Sext, the Seven Words, and a note on blood shed between flesh and skin. So Philip is a source here, as Berthold is, and not the work these leaves come from. Attribution: BnF catalogue and ARCA records; RBMA IV (1989) p. 430 lists BnF lat. 14594, Soissons 65 and Valenciennes 18 under Philippus Cancellarius on the Psalms; Lacombe (1927) p. 121 cites the 14594 explicit 'Expliciunt sermones cancellarii Parisiensis super psalterium' (not seen on the image). Leaves 87r-89v carry an All Souls sermon built on the ps.-Bonaventure / Conrad of Saxony De mortuis III (1596 print, OCR) with large additions; its containing work is not identified. The abridged collection is not located, and it is not the one in Clm 8739. Recorded as partial because the sermons are reworked and the book they come from is unknown. The coordinator compared 88r lines 1-7 with the Freiburg page image. The printed Philip editions (Paris 1523, Brescia 1600) were not consulted. Catalogue date and origin not reassessed.

identification: Student notes of a scholastic philosophy course (physics running into natural theology, with some logic), by a Dutch-speaking writer; not identified
note: Not metaphysics in the narrow sense. One hand throughout 37 leaves: questions on whole and parts, the definition of nature, nature and art (with a passage on alchemy naming Raymond Lull), the four causes, creation as a 'modus substantialis', God's concurrence with secondary causes and a section 'De Praedeterminatione' arguing against physical predetermination; then, after blank pages, logic notes and a second run headed 'De Physica' (prime matter, substantial form, 'De unione'), breaking off at a catchword. A three-line entry on fol. 13r mixes Latin and Dutch. No title, date, place, owner or professor's name was read; fol. 21r opens with two names after 'illustrissimus ... vir doctissimus' that could not be made out. The doctrine and vocabulary look later than the catalogue's 1551-1600, which was not assessed further. Helper readers covered the top half of each page only. The record's manifest serves the first three images again in place of canvases 9-13, 24-28 and 34-37; the right images were fetched by correcting the file number. Compton Carleton and Cornaeus were searched without a match; Arriaga, Hurtado, Oviedo, the Conimbricenses and the Louvain and Douai dictated courses are untested.

identification: Exposition of Peter of Spain, Tractatus V (De locis), on the topics from opposites; not a musical treatise; the exposition is not identified
note: No musical term occurs on the leaf or its three sibling leaves (F-hwsh, F-21br, F-jfv6, same hand). The leaf works through the topics from relative, contrary, privative and contradictory opposites in the order of Peter of Spain's Tractatus V, chapters 27-31 ('Contraria mediata sunt inter que aliquid est medium ut album et nigrum ... immediata ut sanum et egrum'; 'si una fuerit vera altera erit falsa'), paraphrasing and adding matter Peter lacks (a topic 'a disparatis', the proviso of 'constantia subiecti'). F-21br has the topics from the greater and the lesser, and F-hwsh ends 'Et sic est finis quinti tractatus'. Peter's text was compared only through archive.org search snippets of two lending-restricted editions. No printed commentary was matched; about half the lines rest on the first reading. Probably classroom notes.

note: The leaf lists ten pieces of one bound volume. The catalogue already recognises a composite volume with prints and links entries 2 (Beissel, Rosacea corona, Antwerp, Bac) and 6 (Tabulare de Carmelo, Alost, Martens) to incunables. Added here: entry 3 is Wimpfeling and Gaguin, Epistole et carmina, Cologne, Renchen, after 20 February 1492 (title-page image of the Munich copy), which dates the list; entry 9 is the Life of Gerard of Brogne; entry 8 matches a sermon printed under Gerson's name by title only; entries 4, 5, 7 and 10 are unmatched. Candidates for surviving pieces, not established: Den Haag, KB, KW 169 G 7 (Gregory, Dialogi, Louvain, Westfalia, with the priory's ownership note, which is its standard formula and occurs in other books) and Brussels, KBR, ms. II 734 (a Life of Gerard with the leaf's title and nearly its format). Both were bought at the 1884 Vergauwen sale, which also had a Beissel and a Tabulare, but shared ownership, similar size, one sale and matching nineteenth-century bindings do not show that these copies were bound in this volume, and the edition of entry 1 rests on that link. Known only from MEI, the Brussels catalogue (OCR) and the sale catalogue; neither book was seen. Comparing paper, edges, sewing holes and offsets of those two books with the leaf would settle it.

content.title: Table of contents of a composite volume of the canons of St Leonard, Liège
content.description: Ten entries. Entry 3: Wimpfeling and Gaguin, Epistole et carmina (Cologne, Renchen, after 20 February 1492). Entry 8: a sermon printed under Gerson's name. Entry 9: Life of Gerard of Brogne.
content.remarks: Entry 3 dates the list after 1492. Entry 8 is matched by title only; entries 4, 5, 7 and 10 are not identified. Den Haag, KB, KW 169 G 7 and Brussels, KBR, ms. II 734 may be surviving pieces of the volume; not established.

identification: Breviary strip: hymn Martyris Christi colimus triumphum (Cantus 008347, as catalogued) and a second, unidentified hymn for St Lawrence at Matins
note: The first hymn is confirmed against Daniel, Thesaurus hymnologicus IV p. 140 (OCR), as the catalogue already names it; it is widespread (Cantus 008347: 25 sources in Bohemia, Slovakia, Austria, south Germany, Hungary and Italy, 11th-16th c., mostly at Vespers), so it does not place the book. After the rubric "In primo No[cturno]" a second Lawrence hymn in four-line iambic strophes follows ("... Laurentius dignus sac... qui vicit ignium ... Hic unus est e... columnis lucidis ... simulque fecit opifex"); about twenty letters are lost at the left of every line, so its incipit is unknown. None of the Lawrence hymns in Cantus Index or the Cantus Database has its strophes, including the Matins hymns of the manuscripts that also have 008347; its one shared half-strophe, "Quid furis hostis impie", belongs to Devota mente socii (AH 14 no. 103), which Benevento 20 appears to sing at Lawrence Matins (doxology only) and which the Rheinau hymnaries also carry. The Tübingen UB sister fragments (Mm IV 1, Mm V 28, Gb 55 a.4), not digitised, remain the best chance of the full text.

content.title: Hymn Martyris Christi colimus triumphum
content.remarks: Cantus 008347.

content.remarks: Not among the Lawrence hymns in Cantus Index or the Cantus Database. Shares one half-strophe, 'Quid furis hostis impie', with Devota mente socii (AH 14, no. 103).

identification: Literal commentary on Jeremiah 32:35-41 and 36:2-9 built on Hugh of St Cher's Postilla; the work is not identified
note: The glosses and their order follow Hugh of St Cher (Gloss-e text): 'ut initiarent id est dedicarent', 'idolum Ammonitarum', 'sic construe ... propter ista scilicet mala', and at chapter 36 'Composuit Salomon ... veritate plenos' followed by 'verbum Dei non est alligatum'. It is not Hugh's own literal layer: it adds a division of the text at 32:36 that Hugh lacks and omits his 'Triplici ratione' at 36:4. Thomas Aquinas, Nicholas of Lyra and the Glossa ordinaria were compared and excluded. The later postills built on Hugh (William of Luxi, William of Alton, Nicholas Gorran) are unedited or not online and were not tested; Luxi is the first to check. Script is tiny and many readings are uncertain.

content.title: Literal commentary on Jeremiah, based on Hugh of St Cher, Postilla
content.remarks: The glosses follow Hugh of St Cher's Postilla in wording and order, but the text adds a division at 32:36 and omits Hugh's 'Triplici ratione' at 36:4. Not Thomas Aquinas, Nicholas of Lyra or the Glossa ordinaria. The work is not identified.

catalogue_title: Neumed Easter dialogue and canonistic miscellany
identification: Florilegium of short extracts (gloss on Wisdom 1:7, Peter Damian against clerical marriage, the five reasons for St Peter's tonsure); the compilation is not identified. The neumed Easter dialogue in leonine hexameters on the other leaf is not identified.
note: The prose column strings together three extracts. The tonsure passage has the reworked form with both closing sentences that Munich Clm 4654 f. 62v has (compared on the page image) and that Fournier reports for Collectio XII partium III.277. A research reader (Claude) compared strip B's nine prose lines on the fragment image with Reims, Bibliothèque Carnegie, Ms. 683 f. 145v col. b (page image; ARCA describes the volume as Rufinus, Summa decreti extracts, an anonymous commentary on Gratian and other texts, 13th century), where the canon 'Petrus .v. ex causis tonsuram accepit' stands among conciliar canons near the end of the volume. Reims has the same sequence and both closing sentences ('In cuius capite cesaries ab aure ad aurem tonsa est in anteriore parte ...'; 'In cuius capite arula ab aure ad aurem ducta per frontem tonsurando pendebat ...'), and shares the odd 'gan(n)ituram/gannaturam'. Differences: the fragment has no room for Reims's 'et ut in habitu sic operibus discernerentur' after the second cause, and reads 'ab sub aure', 'in sola fronte' and 'c(ir)cu(m) habebant' where Reims has 'ab aure', 'sola in fronte' and 'cirram haberent'. Troyes, Médiathèque, Ms. 246 (a canon collection, c. cclxi 'De exordio tonsure') has only the second closing sentence in CoMMA's machine-read text, not checked on images. In CoMMA's machine-read text neither Reims 683 nor Troyes 246 has the Peter Damian sentences or the Wisdom 1:7 gloss, so neither is the fragment's compilation; this is a no-hit in HTR, not a page-by-page check. Two sentences headed 'Petrus Damiani ... in uxores clericorum' match his letter against clerical marriage as quoted in MGH Libelli de lite I p. 354. The gloss on Wisdom 1:7 has no source found, and no manuscript or work with the three together was found. The neumed Easter dialogue ('... medicamina demus. Cur estis tristes, quid queritis hic, mulieres? Querimus hic Iesum quem novimus esse sepultum. Si surrexisset, dic nobis ...'; the angel's '... uacuus ... positus ... uos preuenit in galileam') is in none of these: Cantus Index standard texts or Cantus Database manuscript readings (October 2026; the drama items there include Einsiedeln, Prague, Vic and Wilton Visitationes); Lange 1887, Milchsack, Coussemaker, Analecta Hymnica 19-21, 46-49 and 52-55 in full text; Lipphardt's Lateinische Osterfeiern und Osterspiele III-VI and Young I-II by Google Books in-volume search; and CoMMA (no hit). Lipphardt I-II could not be searched, so it may still be edited there.

content.remarks: The tonsure passage in the form of Munich, BSB, Clm 4654, f. 62v, and Reims, Bibliothèque Carnegie, Ms. 683, f. 145v (Petrus .v. ex causis tonsuram accepit), as Fournier reports for the Collectio XII partium III.277. The Peter Damian sentences as quoted in MGH Libelli de lite I, p. 354. The gloss on Wisdom 1:7 and the compilation are not identified.

catalogue_title: Latin commentary on an unidentified theological treatise
identification: Late scholastic logic course: questions on Aristotle's Categories and a lemma exposition of Posterior Analytics I; not identified
note: Not theology, as catalogued. The strips have chapter-numbered questions on the whole Categories ('Circa quintum capitulum. Queritur primo utrum qualitas bene diffinitur', 'utrum habitus et dispositio sint prima species qualitatis') closing with a fixed 'Conclusio responsalis ... est a philosopho bene assignata ... Sed oportet dicere ad rationes', and an exposition of Posterior Analytics I with 'Istud est N capitulum huius tractatus in quo philosophus'. The format is the Paris school type: Petrus Tartaretus (snippets) and Johannes de Magistris (Heidelberg 1488, page images) are the nearest and are not the text; Versor, the Cologne Copulata, Harderwijck, Parreut, Friesner, Bricot and Nicholas of Amsterdam were also rejected. About twelve of 76 faces were read closely, the rest surveyed by headings. Usingen, Trutfetter and Hundt untested; it may be an unprinted course.

content.title: Questions on Aristotle, Categories
content.description: Questions by chapter, e.g. 'Circa quintum capitulum. Queritur primo utrum qualitas bene diffinitur', each closing with a 'Conclusio responsalis'.

content.description: Lemma exposition, with chapters opened 'Istud est N capitulum huius tractatus in quo philosophus'.
content.remarks: Close in form to Petrus Tartaretus and Johannes de Magistris, but not their text. The course is not identified.

institution: Leuven, Archief van de Abdij van Park
identification: Preaching text on preparing the heart, akin to Nicolaus de Byard's distinctio "Preparare"; not identified
note: Both faces were read in full: a run of "Item debemus preparare corda nostra sicut ..." comparisons (a host readying his lodging for a great guest, Esther dressing for the king, a vessel washed by confession, Judith). The same scheme and proof-texts (Ps 9:38, Sir 2:20, Jer 4:14, 1 Reg 7:3) stand in compressed form in Nicolaus de Byard's Distinctiones under "Preparare" (Yale, Beinecke MS 746, ff. 170v-171r, page images) and in his Summa de abstinentia, chapter "De preparatione" (1518 print, OCR), but the wording and order differ and several of the fragment's passages are absent, so this is kinship, not the work. Byard's sermon on 1 Reg 7:3 (incipit "Dicitur vulgariter"), the likeliest fuller version, was not reachable: Angers BM 251, listed under his name, proved on its page images to be a different collection, and BnF lat. 12419, Avranches 133 and Laon have no images online. Google Books, Corpus Corporum, archive.org and the Munich full-text search found no sentence of the fragment.

content.title: Preaching text on preparing the heart
content.description: A series of comparisons, Item debemus preparare corda nostra sicut ...: a host readying his lodging for a great guest, Esther dressing for the king, a vessel washed by confession, Judith.
content.remarks: The same scheme and proof-texts (Ps 9:38, Sir 2:20, Jer 4:14, 1 Reg 7:3) stand in shorter form, with different wording and order, in Nicolaus de Byard, Distinctiones, s.v. Preparare (New Haven, Beinecke MS 746, ff. 170v-171r), and in his Summa de abstinentia, cap. De preparatione. Not identified.

identification: Not identified
note: The catalogued item is the narrow strip stuck upside down along the rear pastedown; about 19 line-ends of five to nine letters are legible (credo, [h]abemus, ministerio, celi et ter[re], inquit), too little to match. The computus leaf beneath it, read by the first reader, is a separate item (apparently record F-xr53): an anonymous Carolingian text on lunar regulars and epacts that also stands in Munich Clm 22307 f. 193r.

identification: Johannes Matthaeus, Concionum dispositiones (Wittenberg, 1581; 2nd ed. 1590), end of the outline "De templorum dedicatione" (handwritten copy of pp. 865-868)
note: Four paper pieces are a pen copy of the last four pages of a printed book, with its running titles, page numbers 865-868 and signatures Kkk and Kkk2. A research reader compared six passages from all four pages with page images of the 1581 Wittenberg edition (part 2, pp. 408-412), where the text agrees closely, including the Epilogus, the Greek doxology and the print's slip "1. Pet. 3"; the coordinator compared the Epilogus and doxology on the fragment image with the 1581 page image of p. 412. Differences: page and line division, and a few words (significabat for significat, purgarit for purgaverit, ita for ibi facere). The page numbers fit the catalogued collation of the 1590 edition (VD16 E 4591: 8 leaves, 868 pages, 2 leaves), which was not seen, so the edition copied is inferred and the variants are unassigned. Aretius, De encaeniis, and Legenda aurea c. 182 are Matthaeus's sources, not the work copied.

identification: Notes on the dialectical topic of etymology following Melanchthon's Erotemata dialectices IV; not found in print
note: One unfinished page says that the 'autor', after definition and its parts, 'statim subiungit Etymologiam' and then 'coniugata et casus', which is the order of topics in Melanchthon's Erotemata dialectices book IV. This is agreement of structure only: no sentence was found in print through Google Books or the Munich full-text search, and a textbook derived from Melanchthon would give the same order. The parchment cover in the record's later images belongs to record F-x06a, already catalogued as Cicero, De natura deorum II; the manifests of this record and F-v0qx both carry those images.

identification: Abridged or adapted text built on Guido de Monte Rocherii, Manipulus curatorum, pars I, tract. V, cap. 3-4; containing text not established
note: Both columns of the verso follow the Manipulus in order, collated by a research reader against page images of the Cologne 1476 print. The leaf departs in substance: the preamble of cap. 4 is cut to about three lines, the author's "reputo verius" judgements are absent, and the chapter closes with a list of the nine orders and "Et hec ... sufficiant", where the Cologne 1476, Rome 1481 and Blaubeuren 1474 prints agree with one another and pass to cap. 5. The abraded recto was not read. Manuscript catalogues were not searched for an abbreviated Manipulus with this ending.

The verso holds pen trials: the "staves" are three freehand lines with a few note-like marks, not readable notation. The wording matches none of the printed commentaries compared for F-21br. The lower two thirds of the recto rest mainly on the first reading.

identification: Exposition of Peter of Spain, Tractatus V (De locis), loci a maiori, a minori, a coniugatis, a casibus; not a musical treatise; commentary unidentified
note: Recto: topics a maiori and a minori with the stock example of king and knight taking a castle ("attribuendo duobus subiectis duo predicata"); verso: loci medii, a coniugatis and a casibus ("duo concreta, vnum nominale et alterum aduerbiale"). A research reader compared page images of Dorp 1499 and the Cologne Copulata 1494 and machine-read text of Versor, Georgius Bruxellensis, Tartaretus and Johannes de Magistris: the doctrine, order and examples agree, the sentences never do. The reading is at clause level; unprinted expositions were not searched. Same hand and work as F-7smu and F-hwsh.

identification: Not identified
note: Only one face is available: the catalogue links the same image to both canvases. The leaf is in the hand of the Tractatus V exposition on F-7smu, F-21br and F-hwsh but has other matter, a question with numbered conclusions on what is "scibile siue considerabile" in a science and on unity by aggregation. It is not a musical treatise. No complete sentence was secured and phrase searches found nothing. Questions on the Posterior Analytics or a Physics proem of the Buridan school are an untested lead.

identification: Charter: letter of institution to a benefice (issuer, place and date unread); not a literary text
note: A single-sheet fifteenth-century Latin letter of institution and investiture to a benefice at a place ending in "-kirchen", vacant by the death of one Andreas, on the presentation of a patron "dominus Henricus de [...]dorff", with a mandate to induct and a sealing clause. The issuer in line 1 is lost and the surname, place and date could not be read securely; a reading "Kranichberg / Prellenkirchen" was tested and rejected on the letter forms. Read by a research reader on the images; the verso shows only show-through. Better imaging of lines 3-9 and 24-25 would probably settle the names.

identification: Not identified
note: The spine strips carry numbered first-person questions on confession: whether all sins must be confessed, whether a priest may ever reveal a sin, whether one can confess through another, argued from profession and marriage. The order resembles the clauses of Omnis utriusque sexus. Phrase searches in Google Books, Internet Archive, Corpus Corporum, the Munich full text and the German manuscript catalogues found no text with this wording. What could be read on the 45 Da 6 head lining does not mention confession, so its belonging to the same text is not confirmed. Stopped for want of a candidate.

identification: Johannes Faventinus, Summa super Decretum Gratiani, pars I, D. 86 (comment on c. 8 Qui venatoribus to c. 24 Tanta nequitia)
note: Four passages on the spine strips (hunting in the arena, the Elisha narrative, the publicans with Misericordia plenitudo virtutum and Morte luitur, and the scheme of dispensation at Tanta nequitia) agree in wording and order with two manuscripts of the unprinted Summa, BAV Borgh. lat. 71 f. 57ra-57va and Reims BM 684 (openings f. 35v-36 and 36v-37), read on page images by a research reader; the coordinating model checked the publican passage against the Vatican page and the dispensation passage against the Reims page. The hunting passage is Stephen of Tournai's and the publican passage is Rufinus's in wording Stephen does not share, joined in one text and followed by a dispensation scheme that neither edition has at D. 86; the Elisha story is in both sources and separates nothing. Most of the fragment's differences from the Vatican copy recur in the Reims copy; two readings (exigunt ... sectantur with autem; movet for adducit) are matched in neither. The Summa Lipsiensis copies the dispensation scheme but differs in the hunting and publican passages; Simon of Bisignano, Sicardus, Tractaturus magister and Huguccio were not tested. Two panels are unread, and the script looks earlier than the catalogue's fourteenth century, recorded without redating.

identification: Justinian, Digestum vetus with the Accursian Glossa ordinaria, Digest 4.8.42-49 and 4.8.52-4.9.3 pr. (five of six strips placed, in one leaf)
note: Five of the six strips are placed in one two-column leaf (strip 3 is unplaced): line ends and beginnings on strips 2, 4, 5 and 6 agree in wording and sequence with Digest 4.8.45-49 on one page and 4.8.52, the rubric of 4.9 and 4.9.1-3 pr. on the other, with red initials at the inscriptions of Ulpian, Paulus and Julian. Five marginal glosses to D. 4.9.1 agree in wording and order with the Accursian ordinary gloss, and one is signed 'ac.' in the manuscript. A research reader compared the images with a transcription of Mommsen-Krueger for the text and with page images of the Paris 1566 glossed edition for the gloss; the coordinator read strip 2 'verso' and strip 6 'recto' against D. 4.9.1.1-2 and 1.7. Differences are slight: an apparent 'et' in the rubric, a probable omission supplied under one line, and two small variants in the gloss. Strip 3 and one face of strip 1 are unplaced, one column is abraded and barely read, the gloss was compared in one sixteenth-century print only, and Ms. 1033 was not examined.

identification: Guards from at least two manuscripts; one is a lemmatic commentary on Justinian, Institutes 4.6.35-38; commentary unidentified
note: Guards 17/18 and 5/6 join edge to edge into one column whose underlined lemmata follow Inst. 4.6.35-38 in order ("testamento in[tenderit]", "quam persequimur", "facultates / retentione / ipso iure / dotem", "cum parente"). Each lemma is short and several are uncertain, so the locus rests on the sequence; no whole gloss was read and the apparatus was compared only with poor machine-read text of the Accursian gloss in a 1607 print. A second hand on six guards and guard 113/114 were not read. The scans are about 640 pixels wide. The library's catalogue description was not consulted.

identification: Jacobus de Voragine, Legenda aurea, Southern Middle Dutch translation of c. 1357 attributed to Petrus Naghel (Gulden legende), chapter on the dedication of a church (Vander wiinghen der kerken): end of the canonical hours to the seven sprinklings of the altar
note: Recto columns a and b, the last lines of verso column a and the upper strip of verso column b agree in wording and sequence with the Gulden legende as edited by W. Kuiper from Brussels KBR 15140 (ff. 398vb-399va), including 'Ten anderen sal men besien hoemense consacreert', the six acts of the altar consecration, the four kinds of charity with Genesis 28, and Christ's seven ways. A research reader compared the images with the edition's text of that one manuscript, not with manuscript images; the coordinator read recto column b lines 1-9 on the image. The leaf has Flemish spellings and a few single-word variants ('daermense met', 'bi huwelike', no 'eens', apparently no 'VII werven', 'lesen wi'). The catalogue's suggestion of Duranti's Rationale was tested on structure and by one Corpus Corporum search and is not supported; the Rationale was not collated at length. Most of the verso is too dark to read, and it is not established whether the leaf is already a recorded witness of the translation.

The catalogue already cites the edition, and its "Wybeert van Andernaken" is a label for an otherwise unattested Middle Dutch poem on figures of the Narbonne cycle, not an identified romance. note: The Handschriftencensus (no. 22744, work 6704) lists Houghton MS Typ 270 as part of the only known copy of this anonymous cycle, and Hamburger 2010 prints the leaf's 42 lines; the text names itself as the seventh sorrow. A research reader reread the recto and the last 13 verso lines on the image against Hamburger's print, which shows only that this is the leaf he edits. The print has small slips (siebenden, deynen, forscht, war gewar, Dor er, mit in, Do der, Yemer). The grouping with four sister leaves, the Augsburg 1470s localisation and the derivation from Speculum humanae salvationis ch. 44-45 are Hamburger's and the census's and were not tested. Jörg Zobel's 'Von den Schmerzen Mariae' in Cgm 568 was read on images at three places and is a different poem; no second copy is known.

identification: Caesarius of Arles, Sermo 144 (ed. Morin), In letaniis, De agenda paenitentia et Ninevitis, complete (inc. Evangelica lectio fratres carissimi dum legeretur); the sermon between the catalogue's Maximus and Gregory texts
note: The catalogue already identified the end of Maximus of Turin, Hom. XC, and the opening of Gregory's De mortalitate; the new part is the sermon between them, headed only 'Item unde supra', which is Caesarius, Sermo 144, complete from recto col. a line 15 to verso col. b line 21. A research reader compared the whole sermon with Morin's text in the OCR of the PL Supplementum 4 reprint (33 small variants, same order throughout) and read pp. 324-326 of Caillau's 1836 printing on page images; the coordinator read the opening on the image. The leaf's wording is that of the homiliary transmission (ut arbitror, purpuris deperire, short ending 'inculpabilis nemo est et immunis a reatu'), shared in part with Liverani's 1863 print from Roman and Florentine manuscripts, seen as snippets only. Morin held that Caesarius reworked an older unknown source; the leaf names no author. The homiliary type carrying this sequence is not established, Morin's own pages were not read as images, and recto col. b and verso col. a lines 1-33 rest on the first reading.

identification: Middle Dutch romance in couplets; not in the edited Geraert van Viane fragments or the Corpus Middelnederlands
note: The strip preserves four couplets from the heads of four columns of a Middle Dutch romance with a king and queen ("Sal ic bliuen ongehangen / Ende gine sult mi niet ontgangen"; "Des hadden si wonder groot / Ende die coninginne al bloot"). None of the lines is in the edited Geraert van Viane fragments or anywhere in the Corpus Middelnederlands. identification: Bible, Canticle of Moses (Audite caeli), Deuteronomy 32:1-27, Vulgate; book type (psalter with canticles, breviary or Bible) not established
note: The strip keeps 4-6 letters of each of 28 lines a face; about 40 of the 56 line fragments fall in Deut 32:1-27 in unbroken order at a steady interval of about 50 characters, and the four coloured initials stand at the openings of verses 8, 12, 23 and 26. A research reader reread every line on the native images and compared them with a Vulgate transcription, and with page images of the Clementine text in Dereser 1788 for verses 7-11, 16-18 and 22-25; the coordinator read a selection of lines on both faces. No difference of wording is visible, and the strip cannot show the form of the Vulgate text (at v.17 'is e', as read, agrees with daemoniis and not daemonibus; one reading of three letters). About fifteen lines are uncertain, the catalogue's verso is the textual recto, and the kind of book is not established.

identification: Moral-exegetical prose with a spiritual exposition of Joshua 11:10-11; work unidentified
note: Fragm. 95 b is a strip of moral-exegetical prose: one face urges contempt of something "harmful" with Job 20:27-28 and the rich men of Luke 12 and 16, the other expounds Joshua 11:10-11 spiritually (Joshua takes Asor and strikes souls with love). No printed text matched in Google Books, the Munich library, the Internet Archive or Hugh of St Cher's Postilla. The sibling Fragm. 95 a (F-gwts) is catalogued as Aquinas on the Sentences IV d. 44-45 and is a different, later text. Not identified; an unprinted Joshua commentary such as Langton's is the lead to test.

identification: Nicolaus de Byard, sermon for All Saints Congregate illi sanctos eius (Ps 49:5), opening and two later passages; piece A only; agrees with Paris BnF lat. 15951 ff. 336rb-336va
note: Piece A keeps the opening of the All Saints sermon Congregate illi sanctos eius and two later stretches of it, which agree in wording and order with Paris BnF lat. 15951 ff. 336rb-336va: the opening after the initial (Solent re[ligiosi] ... congregati ut orationes ... quasi impossibile erat), fourteen line-ends of verso col. a (quanto plures ... in omnibus populis ... nos laudabunt ... bien procu[rat] ... non est iustum quod p[ost]) and eleven line-beginnings of verso col. b (Esther 4:16, [man]davit ... [rep]eris in S[usis] ... ibi illi). A research reader compared them with page images of lat. 15951; an independent checker reread 21 of the weakest lines on the native images and found 17 in agreement and in order, corrected several readings of the witness, and confirmed the marginal note 'fr. N. de biart.' at the foot of f. 336r, which stands below the sermon's column but does not name it. The fragment differs at several points (the theme in short form, an extra clause 'sed vellera ovium', 'omnibus' for 'cunctis populis', two unmatched lines in the Esther passage), and the text before the sermon is not the end of the sermon preceding it in lat. 15951. The attribution rests on Schneyer (IV p. 244, Byard, Sermones de sanctis no. 194; V no. 2016, Robert of Sorbon), not rechecked, and on that note; a Fragmentarium editor judged Byard correct and the Sorbon listing one of Schneyer's over-ascriptions; piece B is unplaced and the collection the strips come from is not established. A Fragmentarium editor reviewed the identification and attribution (Nov. 2026), not the transcription.

identification: Aegidius de Fuscarariis, Ordo iudiciarius, cc. LXIX (Conclusio causae, second half) - LXX (Forma sententiae diffinitivae, opening); ed. Wahrmund pp. 124-126
note: Both pieces come from one two-column leaf and agree with Wahrmund's edition in wording and order over about 33 partial lines on each of two consecutive columns, including the author's opinion on the assessors' fee, the citations in sequence, the red chapter rubric and the model sentence of the archpriest of Bologna. A research reader reread every line on enlarged images and compared them with page images of pp. 124-126, text and apparatus; the coordinator checked passages on both faces of strip A against p. 125. Differences are few (rubric as in the edition's MS B, 'cuius malitie' as in M and V, 'et habebis', and as read 'dicte mulieris' as in P); they are recorded without a claim about the fragment's place in the tradition. Piece B supplies the other half of the first nine lines of strip A's columns, and the catalogue's recto/verso labels for B are opposite to those for A. Some rubbed lines were read only in part.

identification: Canonistic text on marriage, after 1215 (impediments, spiritual kinship, nuptial blessing); work unidentified
note: Fragm. 128 is a strip of a two-column leaf from a canonistic text on marriage of after 1215: one column on impediments ending with spiritual kinship ("actiones non passiones ... acquiritur uiro", citing C. 30 q. 4 and X 4.7), another on the nuptial blessing and priests at mass, citing De clandestina desponsatione, perhaps from a treatment of second marriages. Citations are underlined; no lemmata were seen. William of Rennes and Raymund, Tancred, Hostiensis's Summa, Goffredus, Innocent IV, Johannes Andreae, the Abbas antiquus and the ordinary gloss on C. 30 and on X 4.21 c. 1 were compared in OCR or by search and do not match. The faint, tiny script gave no secure run of words to search even after a second reading, so the work is unidentified.

note: Fifteen binding scraps from an unnoted office lectionary of about 1200, long lines, covering the Assumption octave to the Decollation of John the Baptist. Its lessons are Song of Songs 2-3 and 5, Paschasius Radbertus's Cogitis me, the Passio Bartholomaei (BHL 1002, abridged), Bede on Luke 22:28-29 and Petrus Chrysologus Sermo 127; the Fragmentarium description already had the Canticle, Paschasius and Chrysologus and assigned the Bede passage to Amalarius. Nine of the scraps join into three leaves of three cuttings per line. One Assumption lesson and five scraps remain unidentified; status partial because of those unplaced parts.

[2]r lines 6-12 and fol. [2]v lines 6-11. Differences are dialectal. Grote's psalms circulated in books of hours and complete psalters, and nothing on the leaf decides between them; BNM-I was unreachable (login). A Fragmentarium editor reviewed it in October 2026: text confirmed, one leaf; the join was then checked against the existing readings, not new images.

identification: Fifteenth-century scholastic text; too little legible to search
note: A narrow strip of a fifteenth-century cursive scholastic text, cut to ten to fifteen letters a line and imaged too coarsely to read connected words. Only isolated words (Dico, religione, officium, ubique) are legible. Unidentified; needs a better image before any search is worth running.

identification: Third-declension noun paradigms (mater, soror, homo, omnis) in the form of the elementary grammar Ianua; version not established
note: The strips hold third-declension noun paradigms in the form used by the Italian elementary grammar Ianua (Ps.-Donatus): mater, soror, homo, omnis and probably felix. Donatus's Ars minor is excluded. The series does not match the three printed Ianua editions compared (Rome c. 1475, Venice c. 1478 and 1491), which lack soror, so the result is partial: the type of text and its place are known, the exact recension is not.

content.title: Ianua (Ps.-Donatus), third-declension noun paradigms
content.description: Paradigms of mater, soror, homo, omnis and probably felix.
content.remarks: In the form of the Ianua; not the Ars minor of Donatus. The series differs from the printed Ianua editions of Rome c. 1475 and Venice c. 1478 and 1491, which lack soror; the version is not established.

dimensions: 171 mm x 50 mm, 55 mm x 35 mm, 58 mm x 30 mm
institution: Scherpenheuvel-Zichem, Abdij der Norbertijnen van Averbode, Archief
identification: Thirteenth-century text under tissue and a later breviary; no connected word legible
note: The 13th-century text stays unidentified: it is visible only under tissue, in a torn window about 3 cm wide and along one cut edge, and no connected word could be read. The legible writing in the images is the 15th-century breviary F-x3dh (Lenten chapters and collect, Palm Sunday antiphons). The split between the two records was fixed from their stated dimensions: the 171 x 50 mm piece is the covered spine strip in the larger hand. New imaging or separation of the layers is needed before any search.

institution: Leuven, Archief van de Abdij van Park
identification: Latin article on almsgiving (Elemosina) from a preaching aid, in paragraphs opening 'Elemosina debet ...'; work unidentified
note: Latin; an article on almsgiving in a preaching aid, in paragraphs each beginning "Elemosina debet ...", two of which survive in part ("fieri prouidenter", "dari [pauperibus]"). The paragraph on the poor runs parallel in matter and order to Bromyard, Summa praedicantium, Elemosina art. 7, but not in wording, and Byard, Peraldus and the Alphabetum narrationum were tested and rejected. The work is unidentified; the upper third of both faces is illegible in the published image.

content.title: Article on almsgiving (Elemosina) from a preaching aid
content.description: Paragraphs each beginning 'Elemosina debet ...', two surviving in part ('fieri prouidenter', 'dari [pauperibus]').
content.remarks: The paragraph on the poor follows Bromyard, Summa praedicantium, Elemosina art. 7, in matter and order but not in wording. The work is not identified.

catalogue_date: at earliest 1300 CE; at earliest 1349 CE
identification: German spiritual prose on compassion (2 Cor 11:29, 1 Cor 12:26); work unidentified
note: Not identified. Strip across a single-column bifolium of a small German prose book, first half of the 14th century, same binding campaign as F-28bq: a first-person passage on sharing a neighbour's trouble and weakness (2 Cor 11:29) and St Paul's saying that when one member suffers all suffer (1 Cor 12:26). The Handschriftencensus (no. 27263) lists it as an unidentified "Geistlicher Prosatext". No match in ReM, Google Books, Internet Archive or the sermon and mystical editions searched.

catalogue_date: at earliest 1300 CE; at earliest 1349 CE
identification: German spiritual prose: the Son's report to the Father and the Father's love for the Son; work unidentified
note: Not identified. Strip across a single-column bifolium of a small German prose book (first half of the 14th century, Central German spellings): the Son reports to the Father that he has fulfilled his commandment and redeemed mankind with his blood, and the Father is said to owe the Son the highest love because he is God. The Handschriftencensus (no. 27263) lists it with F-m05m as an unidentified "Geistlicher Prosatext". ReM, Google Books, Internet Archive and a dozen sermon and mystical editions gave no match.

shelfmark: Verzameling van literaire fragmenten, Album II, voorlopig nr. 14/7
identification: Commentary on the topics from conjugates and cases, probably on Peter of Spain, Tractatus V; commentary unidentified
note: The strip is from a commentary on the topics "from conjugates and cases", most probably on Peter of Spain's Tractatus V: the verso rejects "album est dulce, ergo albedo est dulcedo" and the recto reports what the "antiqui" say. Dorp's commentary on Buridan and Versor's on Peter of Spain were read on the page and are not the text, though they share its examples. Partial: the kind of work and its place are known, the commentary is not.

content.title: Commentary on the topics from conjugates and cases, probably on Peter of Spain, Tractatus V
content.description: The verso rejects the argument 'album est dulce, ergo albedo est dulcedo'; the recto reports what the 'antiqui' say.
content.remarks: Not the commentary of Dorp on Buridan or of Versor on Peter of Spain, which share its examples. The commentary is not identified.

identification: Strip on a binding with about ten rows of writing visible only as blurred bands; not legible in the published images
note: The strip on the spine of MdS 63 Ea 7 shows rows of writing only as blurred bands on all three published images, in every colour channel and after contrast processing. No letter was read and no search was possible. The catalogue's description as a glossed legal text could not be tested. New imaging is required before another attempt.

identification: Gregorian sacramentary, Advent orations: Suscipiamus, Excita ... saluari, the six 'Aliae orationes de adventu' (Excita ... operare, Conscientias, Prope esto, Concede ... ut magnae, Mentes nostras, Preces populi tui), Porrige nobis, Deus qui nos conspicis; kind of book open
note: A strip 4-6 letters wide: all 36 letter groups (20 lines on the recto, 16 on the verso) fall in order, one per line, in this series of Advent prayers, with 16-36 supplied letters between groups, and the text continues across the turn of the leaf. A research reader reread every line on the native images and compared them with page images of Wilson's Hadrianum (pp. 113, 116-117) and Mohlberg's St Gall 348 (p. 216); the coordinator reread recto lines 5-14 and verso lines 6-15. The strip has the Hadrianum order 'promisisti usque in finem saeculi'; the last two prayers are from the Gelasian Advent series, and the opening pair is not in the Hadrianum's mass order. It is not the same manuscript as Fragm. 3a of the same host volume (9 mm lines against 5-6 mm, different hand). Whether the book was a sacramentary, missal or collectar is open; the evidence is positional, on letter groups only.

fragmentarium.title: Gregorian Sacramentary, Advent orations

content.title: Advent orations
content.description: Suscipiamus; Excita ... salvari; the six Aliae orationes de adventu (Excita ... operare, Conscientias, Prope esto, Concede ... ut magnae, Mentes nostras, Preces populi tui); Porrige nobis; Deus qui nos conspicis. Four to six letters of each line survive.
content.remarks: Readings of the Hadrianum ('aeternae vitae', where St Gall 348 has 'vitae aeternae'); the last two prayers are from the Gelasian Advent series. The book may have been a sacramentary, missal or collectar. Not the same manuscript as Fragm. 3a (F-fjvt).

bibliography: H. A. Wilson, The Gregorian Sacramentary under Charles the Great (London 1915), pp. 113, 116-117
K. Mohlberg, Das fränkische Sacramentarium Gelasianum in alamannischer Überlieferung (Münster 1918), p. 216, nos. 1405, 1408

identification: Scholastic passage on the guilt of Christ's crucifiers (ending with 1 Cor 2:8) and a pastoral passage; work unidentified
note: Fol. [2]r has a passage on the guilt of Christ's crucifiers ending with 1 Cor 2:8 ("filium dei", "ac rebelles", "offenderunt", "populares", "maiores" legible), the matter of Aquinas ST III q. 47 a. 5-6 but not his wording; fol. [1]r is on another, pastoral subject ("nemo ambigit", "Abbas", "celebrare", "de clericis"). No connected phrase is secure enough to search and seven phrase searches found nothing. Stop: needs UV or infrared images of the line beginnings.

identification: Paper leaf in thin grey cursive; letter groups only, no searchable phrase
note: Both faces inspected at reading size; the thin grey ink gives only letter groups, with repeated line openings ("q'") suggesting a list, verses or notes. The hand looks like that of HS.2583/084 (F-vui8), which carries Ave verum corpus, but no text could be confirmed here and no search was possible. Stop: needs UV or infrared images.

identification: Elevation prayer Ave verum corpus natum in the last four lines of the written face; the lines above and the collection unidentified
note: The last four lines of the written face (canvas 0, native box 1350,2100-4200,2850) are the elevation prayer Ave verum corpus (AH 54 no. 167), read on the image over three continuous lines and compared with the standard text from printed prayer books (OCR and snippets). The lines above it and the left page are unread, so the collection the leaf comes from is not identified; the catalogue's "theological text" is better described as devotional notes. A better image of lines 1-12 would show whether an indulgence rubric precedes the prayer.

content.title: Ave verum corpus natum
content.description: Elevation prayer, in the last four lines of the written face.
content.remarks: The lines above and the other page are not identified.

bibliography: Analecta hymnica 54, no. 167

identification: Question commentary of the arts faculty: 'Consequenter queritur utrum multiplicatio individuorum sub eadem specie repugnet animabus separatis', preceded by a question on the first being; work unidentified
note: Four paper pieces from a late fourteenth-century scholastic question series. One question opening was read on the image: Consequenter queritur utrum multiplicatio individuorum sub eadem specie repugnet animabus(?) separatis, with an argument that the first being either willed and could not, or could and did not will, several individuals in one species. It follows a question on the first being under a metaphysical and a physical habit. There is no second heading and no lemma. A search index of Zimmermann's lists of Metaphysics commentaries and Siger's questions on the Liber de causis do not have the question in this wording, so the work stays unidentified.

content.title: Questions of the arts faculty
content.description: Opening of a question: Consequenter queritur utrum multiplicatio individuorum sub eadem specie repugnet animabus (?) separatis. It follows a question on the first being.
content.remarks: Work not identified.

identification: Scholastic questions on confession within an exposition of a base text; same book as MdS 45 Da 5 (F-3u3b, F-ho7z); work unidentified
note: The three linings of MdS 45 Da 6 belong with those of 45 Da 5 (F-3u3b, F-ho7z): first-person questions on confession inside an exposition of a base text, with a passage on an "edification" that falls if its foundation is moved. Phrase searches in Google Books, Internet Archive, Corpus Corporum and MDZ found nothing; the Astesana was read and rejected, the other confessors' summae rejected on form without collation. Reading is model-assisted; the large strip F2 is photographed too obliquely to read below line 7.

identification: Third-declension paradigms (mater, soror, homo, omnis, fortis, fortior) in the order of the elementary grammar Ianua, with a soror paradigm found in no Ianua text compared; one leaf with MdS 58 Ca 19/F1-2 (F-uvx5; reconstruction F-5oah)
note: Foot of a leaf with third-declension paradigms in the Ianua form: mater and soror on the recto, the end of fortis and fortior on the verso. It is one of three slices of the same leaf: MdS 58 Ca 19/F2 (plural of soror, then homo) is the head of the verso and F1 (omnis, start of fortis) its middle, so F-fuvo, F-uvx5 and F-5oah are one object, not independent witnesses. The series mater, homo, omnis, fortis, fortior is that of the pseudo-Donatan Ianua (Ciccolella 2008, snippets; mater also on the page image of the Rome c. 1475 print); soror is in no Ianua text reached. Not Donatus's Ars minor; a manuscript form of the Ianua with soror is likely but unproved.

content.title: Third-declension paradigms (mater, soror, homo, omnis, fortis, fortior), in the order of the Ianua
content.description: Recto: mater and soror. Verso: end of fortis and fortior.
content.remarks: The series is that of the pseudo-Donatan Ianua; the soror paradigm is in no Ianua text compared. Same leaf as MdS 58 Ca 19/F1-2 (F-uvx5; reconstruction F-5oah).

identification: Spine strips showing mid-line word fragments only; no searchable phrase
note: Only short mid-line fragments are exposed on two of the three strips, and the legible one (F1) is upside down in the images, which the first reading missed. An upright rereading gives a few words ("ymagini", "sua", a red-touched S) but no searchable phrase; one guess at Apocalypse 13 found no support.

identification: Justinian, Codex 7.62.31-32 (De appellationibus), with marginal gloss, on strip [1]; strip [2] from the same leaf, not placed
note: Strip [1] recto has five consecutive line ends of C. 7.62.31 pr. and the verso four of five line beginnings of C. 7.62.32.1-1a, one column later, read by a research reader on the images and compared with page images of Krueger 1877, the Leipzig 1831 edition and a glossed Paris 1559 edition; the coordinator read the key words on both faces. Only spelling differences were seen; verso line 3 could not be confirmed. Strip [2] comes from the same leaf, so the earlier placement of two pieces on its recto at C. 7.65.8, some six columns later, is withdrawn; they may be gloss. A Fragmentarium editor reviewed it in October 2026: strip [1] text confirmed; both strips one leaf; the reading took gloss for main text and missed citations interleaved with it. The gloss is too rubbed to identify; the Accursian gloss at this point is compatible with the one clear word, spectabil-.

fragmentarium.title: Justinian, Codex, with gloss

content.remarks: The gloss is not identified.

institution: Leuven, KU Leuven Bibliotheken Bijzondere Collecties
identification: Accursius, Glossa ordinaria on the Digestum vetus, gloss "illatae sunt" to D. 4.9.1.8 (strip 1)
note: Strip 1 "recto" carries five cut lines of the Accursian ordinary gloss on illatae sunt (D. 4.9.1.8): "est contrarium / -nque. §. quod si servus. et de hiis / vel al. ... l. i. et / ... / l. sequitur", agreeing in wording and order with the Paris 1566 print, col. 663 gloss h, which a research reader read on the page image; the coordinator read lines 1, 2, 3 and 5 on the manuscript crops. No "C." was seen before "de hiis", line 4 is unread under the liturgical offset, and line 5 is faint beyond "l. s.q.". This is the paragraph and gloss column of the sibling leaf Ms. 1032 (F-x60p), and the gloss column of that leaf's strip 5 keeps other words of the same gloss ("fug. qui-", "-is qui la-", weakly read) that appear complementary, so the strip very probably belongs to that leaf; the hands are compatible but no physical join was fitted. Strip 2 shows no legal text, the liturgical offset was not studied, and source-assisted image comparison also confirms the diagnostic citation sequence in Venice 1488, BSB scan 202, and Vatican Pal. lat. 731, fol. 86v (catalogued Bologna, 1290-1300). Both earlier witnesses have the second C. before de hiis; the fragment's apparent omission remains unresolved. No new letters were recovered and no textual-family relationship is claimed.

fragmentarium.subtitle: D. 4.9.1.8

content.remarks: Very probably from the same leaf as Ms. 1032 (F-x60p). Strip 2 has no legal text; the liturgical offset is not identified.

identification: Abridgement of William of Auxerre, Summa aurea III (faith, hope, charity); shares three compressions word for word with the abbreviation in Troyes, Médiathèque, Ms. 1966, which catalogues give to Herbert of Auxerre, but has passages that copy lacks
note: The strip is from an abbreviation of William of Auxerre's Summa aurea, book III (faith, hope, charity; Paris 1500 print fols. 136r-139r). It shares three compressed passages word for word with Troyes, Ms. 1966, ff. 108r-109r, catalogued as Herbert of Auxerre's Abbreviatio, and these are not William's wording as read on page images of the print. Two passages give abridged replies of William that the Troyes copy lacks, and no second Herbert manuscript could be read (Erfurt CA 8° 29 is behind an access challenge), so the result stays at medium confidence. The catalogue's verso precedes its recto.

content.title: Abridgement of William of Auxerre, Summa aurea, book III
content.description: On faith, hope and charity.
content.remarks: Three compressed passages agree word for word with the abbreviation in Troyes, Médiathèque, Ms. 1966, ff. 108r-109r, catalogued as Herbert of Auxerre's Abbreviatio; two passages give abridged replies of William that the Troyes copy lacks. Fol. [1]v precedes fol. [1]r in the text.

bibliography: William of Auxerre, Summa aurea (Paris 1500), fols. 136r-139r

identification: Six lines of cursive a face, illegible at the published size beyond 'ad sepulcra martirum'; work unidentified
note: The published images (about 2,400 px for the whole photograph) allow only isolated words: the recto is illegible, and the verso yields "ad sepulcra martirum" (probable) and possibly the names Cyprianus and Jeronimus opening rubricated items. Phrase searches in Corpus Corporum, Internet Archive, Google Books and MDZ found only the patristic sources of that phrase, and no candidate work was collated. A higher-resolution or UV capture is needed before another attempt.

identification: Two bifolia washed to a faint ghost; no connected line legible in the published images
note: Both bifolia are washed to a faint ghost on all four faces; contrast enhancement, background division and channel separation on the native images recover only the tall strokes of a small two-column cursive, and no connected line. Nothing was searched. UV or multispectral images are needed before another attempt.

catalogue_title: Unidentified Middle Dutch manuscript, possibly a religious text
identification: Middle Dutch saints' lives (Petronilla, probably Nicholas) divided by rubrics Prima, Secunda, Tercia [lectio?]; neither the Northern nor the Southern Dutch Legenda aurea; work unidentified
note: Six strips from a Middle Dutch book of saints' legends in numbered sections (red rubrics Prima / Secunda / [Ter]cia ...ctio, probably lectio; a red number lxxxx). One strip has the Petronilla legend and another probably the Nicholas story of the poor nobleman's daughters. Both passages were compared on page images with the Southern (Delft 1482 Passionael) and Northern (Gent UB HS.0123) translations of the Legenda aurea and match neither, so the text is another version, likely office lessons; the containing work was not found.

content.title: Legends of saints (Petronilla, probably Nicholas), in numbered lessons (?)
content.description: The legend of Petronilla and probably the story of Nicholas and the poor nobleman's daughters, divided by red rubrics Prima, Secunda, [Ter]cia ...ctio (probably lectio).
content.remarks: Neither the Southern (Passionael, Delft 1482) nor the Northern (Gent, UB, HS.0123) Middle Dutch translation of the Legenda aurea. The work is not identified.

identification: Small-format book arranged by Sundays after Pentecost ('Dominica xiiij, Mattheus', Mt 6:24; Dominica xi, Mc 7); sermons or postil, work unidentified
note: The four spine strips come from a small 14th-century book arranged by the Sundays after Pentecost: red rubrics "Do(minica) xj. M[ar.]" (F4) and "Do(minica) xiiij. Math." (F3) can be read, the latter followed by "[Nemo potest] duobus dominis servire" (Mt 6:24), which matches Roman/Franciscan pericope numbering and the catalogue's Mc 7:32 on F4. The suggested reading "dist. xiiij ... magister" (Sentences commentary) does not hold. The body text is out of focus in every photograph, so the work (sermons, postil or thematic outlines) is not identified; better photographs of F3 and F4 are needed.

content.title: Sermons or postil for the Sundays after Pentecost
content.description: Rubrics 'Do(minica) xj. M[ar.]' (F4) and 'Do(minica) xiiij. Math.' (F3), the latter followed by '[Nemo potest] duobus dominis servire' (Mt 6:24).
content.remarks: The work is not identified.

identification: Besides the catalogued Isidore, Etymologiae I: five lines before De soloecismo that end De barbarismo with matter on conlisio and hiatus not in Isidore's text; source unidentified
note: The unidentified text is five lines at the top of fol. 1r, the end of a chapter on barbarism that replaces or expands Isidore's Etym. 1.32.8-9: an L-alliteration example, conlisiones with Virgil (read as Aen. 5.866) and a second example, and the sentence "Hiatus vero et conlisiones per vocales et consonantes fiunt". It is not the standard Isidore text, not Julian of Toledo, and not in Zofingen Pa 32 or St. Gallen 237, which were read on the page; Spevak's 2017 study of additions to book I reports nothing at this point, and Pompeius offers parallels of content only. The leaf may come from a school copy of book I (Ars Isidori) with added Donatus-commentary material; that is a lead, not a finding.

content.title: Unidentified grammatical text on barbarism
content.description: Five lines at the top of fol. 1r, before De soloecismo, ending a chapter on barbarism with matter on conlisio and hiatus: an L-alliteration example, conlisiones with Virgil (Aen. 5.866?) and a second example, and 'Hiatus vero et conlisiones per vocales et consonantes fiunt'.
content.remarks: Replaces or expands Isidore, Etym. 1.32.8-9. Not the standard text of Isidore, not Julian of Toledo, and not in Zofingen, Pa 32 or St. Gallen 237.

identification: Trimmed leaf in a small faint hand; no secure word sequence at the published resolution
note: The strip occupies only about 650 x 1650 pixels of each published image, with lines 12-15 px high; contrast enhancement in three treatments on both faces gave letter groups but no readable word sequence, so no search was possible. The limit is image resolution as much as abrasion; a higher-resolution capture from the Erfgoedbibliotheek would reopen it.

shelfmark: Verzameling van literaire fragmenten, Album II, voorlopig nr. 17/7
identification: Rules of consequence on the integral whole; one rule ('a toto integrali distributo ad partem distributam') is closely parallel to Ockham, Summa logicae III-3 c. 3, the only text found with it; dependence not shown; work unidentified
note: The recto has the rule "Alia regula est a toto [integrali] distributo ad partem distributam est consequentia bona", a close parallel in shortened wording to Ockham, Summa logicae III-3, c. 3; the neighbouring lines do not follow Ockham's text. Albert of Saxony, Buridan with Dorp, the pseudo-Ockham Elementarium and Tractatus minor, Burley and Greve were compared and do not have the distributed rule; Marsilius and Strode were not reached. One shared rule with differing context and untested alternatives is a promising connection, not shown dependence; the work is not identified.

content.title: Rules of consequence on the integral whole
content.description: Includes the rule 'Alia regula est a toto [integrali] distributo ad partem distributam est consequentia bona'.
content.remarks: The rule is close, in shorter wording, to Ockham, Summa logicae III-3, c. 3; the neighbouring lines do not follow Ockham. Not Albert of Saxony, Buridan with Dorp, the pseudo-Ockham Elementarium and Tractatus minor, Burley or Greve. The work is not identified.

identification: Avicenna, Canon medicinae (Latin of Gerard of Cremona), III, fen 3, tract. 1, end of ch. 1 (De anatomia oculi) and rubric of ch. 2
note: Strip A keeps only the first or last few letters of the bottom 24 lines of two columns; 22 of 24 line ends on one side and all 24 line beginnings on the other, ending in the rubric [com]plexionum eius, stand in the order and spacing of Canon III.3.1.1-2 in the Padua 1479 print. A research reader compared them with the print's page images; the coordinator read the first eleven line beginnings of canvas 0 on the native image and lines 1-19 of that side on the print's pages. One doubtful reading (similiter for the print's simile) could not be decided; only one print was compared and the attribution of the translation to Gerard of Cremona is the conventional one, not checked. Strip B carries only a marginal scheme. The catalogue's 'probably a treatise on optics' is corrected to medical anatomy of the eye.

fragmentarium.subtitle: III, fen 3, tract. 1, cap. 1-2

content.title: Avicenna, Canon medicinae, III, fen 3, tract. 1, end of cap. 1 (De anatomia oculi) and rubric of cap. 2
content.description: Line beginnings and line ends of the last 24 lines of two columns, ending with the rubric of cap. 2 ([com]plexionum eius).
content.remarks: The text runs from fol. [1]v to fol. [1]r. Strip B (fol. [2]) has only a marginal scheme. Anatomy of the eye, not a treatise on optics.

bibliography: Avicenna, Canon medicinae, libri III et V (Padua: [Johannes Herbort], 1479)

catalogue_title: Mortuary roll asking for prayers for John, monk and cantor at an unidentified abbey
identification: Mortuary roll with the letter printed as Codex Dunensis no. 276 (already in the catalogue), here naming John, cantor, priest and professed monk; the sending house is named in neither witness and remains unidentified
note: The roll carries the same letter as Codex Dunensis no. 276, as the catalogue says, in a fuller form that names the deceased as John, cantor, priest and professed monk 'of our aforesaid monastery'; the line that named the monastery is lost and the dorse is blank. The printed letter has the sender removed as well, so no house is named in either witness. The encyclicals of St Bavo's Abbey, Ghent (roll of abbot Gerelmus, 1336, read on the image) share four or five formulae with it inside a different composition, and where the two differ the roll follows the Codex Dunensis wording, so St Bavo's is no stronger a candidate than another Flemish house. Nothing in the wording decides between Benedictines and Cistercians.

content.title: Encyclical letter of a mortuary roll
content.description: Letter asking prayers for John, cantor, priest and professed monk of the sending monastery, whose name is lost.
content.remarks: A fuller form of the letter printed in Codex Dunensis no. 276, which also omits the sender. Some formulae are shared with the encyclicals of St Bavo's Abbey, Ghent (roll of Abbot Gerelmus, 1336), in a different composition.

identification: Liturgical psalter (Gallican), Psalm 68:15-22 on 367a-1: 1v; the other three faces are not placed
note: On the face 367a-1: 1v ten line beginnings read in order as Psalm 68:15-22, with a two-line red initial at v. 17 where the Benedictine office divides the psalm for Wednesday Matins. A research reader reread the lines on the image and compared them with a transcription of the Stuttgart Gallican text; no page image of an edition or medieval psalter was used, and the monastic division was checked only in a modern table. Where it can be told the reading has the Clementine form 'respice in [me]'. The other three faces give word shapes only; Ps 67:20-24, the opening of Ps 59 under 'fer. iiij' (title too long for the lines, unresolved) and Ps 61:11 onward are leads, not placements. The identification is of the Psalm 68 face alone; book type is inferred and monastic use remains provisional.

content.title: Psalter, Psalm 68:15-22
content.description: Psalm 68:15-22 (Gallican), with a two-line initial at v. 17, Exaudi me Domine.
content.remarks: The division at v. 17 agrees with the Benedictine office for Wednesday Matins; monastic use is possible. The other three faces are not placed.

identification: Hostiensis (Henricus de Segusio), Lectura in Decretales Gregorii IX, on X 3.30.33-34 (De decimis: end of c. Cum non sit in homine, and c. Nuper abbates)
note: Twenty of the 21 surviving line ends and line beginnings on both faces agree in wording and order with Hostiensis's Lectura through nine successive lemmata. A research reader compared both faces on the published images with the page image of the Strasbourg 1512 edition (vol. 2, fol. 114r) and with text-recognition snippets of the Venice 1581 edition. Johannes Andreae's Novella rewords these comments and cites Hostiensis by name at the points the fragment preserves; it was excluded on the page image of the Venice 1581 edition (vol. 3, leaves 146v-147r) for the comments on Per censuram ecclesiasticam, De iure and Nisi cum ipsis. The ordinary gloss was excluded on a page image. No difference of wording in the surviving words; about one line's worth of text between lines 6 and 7 of the first face was probably absent from the manuscript (inferred from spacing), and the first line of the second face is cut through and unplaced. No manuscript of the Lectura was compared.

identification: Geert Grote, Getijdenboek (Middle Dutch hours), Hours of the Eternal Wisdom, Compline: end of hymn Ihesus regniert in den vreden and antiphon O gloriose coninc onder dinen heilighen (Van Wijk 1940, p. 111)

Differences are small (bis altoes without die, dinen for dine, waerdighe- for verwerdighen, weter for weder); verso line 8 and recto lines 1, 4-5 are rubbed and only compatible. Other Middle Dutch versions of Suso's Cursus were not compared, a prayer book with only the Wisdom Hours is not excluded, and the third strip (canvases 2-3) is illegible and unplaced.

It does not fit: the letter after long s is a minim with no descender, so the fragment cannot read 'sp'. No chant can be named; the fragment stays unidentified until the pastedown is lifted or imaged through.

note: The spine line reads 'item dauid rex apte dicitur', as the catalogue says; nothing else on the leaf could be read with confidence. That phrase was found only in Sedulius Scottus's commentary on Matthew at Mt 1:6 (ed. Loefstedt, p. 25, seen in snippets), so the leaf is probably from a commentary on the genealogy in Matthew. A test of the neighbouring letter groups against Sedulius's sentences gave no confirmation, his Hiberno-Latin sources could not be consulted, and one phrase does not identify the work.

identification: Missal, Holy Week: Tuesday, end of the Passion according to Mark (15:43-46); Wednesday, lesson Isaiah 63:5, 7 and gradual Ne avertas (Ps 68:18, 2). Use not determined
note: Sixteen line beginnings on the recto fall in order on Mark 15:43-46 and sixteen line ends on the verso on Isaiah 63:5 and 7 (without verse 6, as in missals) followed at once by the gradual Ne avertas with verse Salvum me fac. This is a substantial catalogue refinement: the catalogue already named Mark 15:43-46 and Psalm 68; the missal identification, the two days, the Isaiah lesson and the precise gradual are new. The complete book's plenary format is not established by the strip. A research reader reread every line on the native images and compared them with the OCR text of the Arbuthnott missal (1864), pp. 133-134, and with a Google Books snippet of a Lateran missal edition. The manuscript has omnibus que where Arbuthnott prints super omnia quae; Arbuthnott is a witness of the common formulary, not the fragment's use. The use is not determined, the rubric after the Passion is not securely read, and no manuscript missal was collated.
