identification: Strip with the first three to six letters of about thirty lines and four red paragraph marks; no complete word secure at the published size
note: Narrow binding strip with only the first few letters of each line on one face and an abraded other face. No complete word can be read at the published resolution, so no search was possible. Unidentified; would need an adjoining strip or better imaging.

identification: Cut edge of a marginal commentary in chancery cursive beside a pen-flourished initial; isolated letter groups only
note: Orientation settled: the opened strip (canvas 2) reads rotated 180 degrees and is direct Latin chancery cursive, not mirrored and not a right-to-left script. What is visible is the cut edge of the marginal commentary; the main text is under the residue band beside the pen-flourished initial. Only isolated letter groups can be read, so nothing was searchable and the text stays unidentified. A legal gloss is a guess, not a finding.

identification: Lenten sermons on the weekday Mass readings (Friday and Saturday after Ash Wednesday, Saturday of the second week), apparently for religious; collection unidentified
note: The four leaves are Lenten sermons on the daily Mass readings, not a theological treatise. They cover the Friday and Saturday after Ash Wednesday (Matt. 5:43ff., Mark 6:47ff.) and the Saturday of the second week (Gen. 27, Luke 15). The Saturday material reads religio as the ship and draws on Simon's tomb with its sculpted ships (1 Macc. 13). Jacobus de Voragine's quadragesimale and Hugo de Prato Florido's de tempore sermons were compared and do not match; the collection is unidentified.

content.title: Lenten sermons on the weekday Mass readings
content.description: Sermons for the Friday and Saturday after Ash Wednesday (Mt 5:43; Mc 6:47) and the Saturday of the second week of Lent (Gen 27; Lc 15).
content.remarks: Apparently for religious: the Saturday sermon reads the ship as religio. Not the quadragesimale of Jacobus de Voragine or the de tempore sermons of Hugo de Prato Florido; the collection is not identified.

identification: Moral compilation using medical similes (fasting, vanity of life, penance, confessor as physician); draws on Johannes de S. Geminiano, Summa de exemplis II, and shares text with Rainerius de Pisis, Pantheologia, Poenitentia c. XX; containing work unidentified
note: The five Gent leaves are a late fourteenth-century Latin moral compilation, not a medical treatise. Its chapters treat fasting, the vanity of human life, penance as the tending of a vine, and the confessor as a physician of souls. The river simile on fols. [1]v-[2]r reworks Johannes de Sancto Geminiano, Summa de exemplis II, closely. The physician-confessor chapters share long verbatim runs with Rainerius de Pisis, Pantheologia, s.v. Poenitentia c. XX, but are fuller and ordered differently. The containing work is unidentified.

content.locus: fol. [1]r; fol. [1]v; fol. [2]r; fol. [2]v; fol. [3]r; fol. [3]v; fol. [4]r; fol. [4]v; fol. [5]r; fol. [5]v
content.title: Moral compilation with medical similes
content.description: Chapters on fasting, the vanity of human life, penance as the tending of a vine, and the confessor as physician of souls.
content.remarks: Not a medical treatise. The river simile on fols. [1]v-[2]r reworks Johannes de Sancto Geminiano, Summa de exemplis II. The chapters on the confessor share long passages with Rainerius de Pisis, Pantheologia, s.v. Poenitentia, c. 20, but are fuller and ordered differently. The containing work is not identified.

identification: Ink too faint for connected text at the published size
note: These are two foxed paper leaves in a faint 15th-century cursiva, two columns, Latin theological prose. Only isolated words could be read (anima, gratia tripla, filius dei, misericordia, a possible "Beleth/Beda cap. xi" citation), which is not enough for a phrase search. The text is unidentified; better imaging is the precondition for further work.

identification: Scraped logic text legible only as isolated terms under UV
note: Scraped 14th-century two-column cover from Orselina, legible in UV only as isolated words: propositio, affirmativa/negativa, species, diffinitio, finita/infinita, and a red-paraphed "Contra". The genre looks like scholastic logic (Topics or Peri hermeneias material), but no connected phrase could be read, so nothing was searchable or comparable. Unidentified; it needs better imaging or reading at the object.

catalogue_title: Unidentified glosses on a legal text
identification: Legal text and gloss visible only as a few letters per line through a paper strip
note: Spine-reinforcement leaf of a 14th-century Italian glossed legal text, almost entirely covered by a paper strip. At the published resolution only 5-8 letters per line are exposed, and they could not be read to word level, even in blue-channel enhanced crops. The catalogue's own Wood's-lamp readings (Iur-, Mulieres) could not be checked on the images. No identification was attempted beyond listing the canon-law chapters that open with Mulieres; UV imaging or lifting the paper strip is needed.

identification: Questions on the origin and practice of confession; same object as part of F-ho7z; work unidentified
note: Not identified. These three linings are the 45 Da 5 half of the virtual reconstruction F-ho7z, so they belong with it by definition. Rereading the lower strip shows a sequence on how confession originates: from Christ's order at the raising of Lazarus, from a medical argument about disclosing a disease, and from James 5:16. Further searches, including inside Johannes Andreae's Novella on Omnis utriusque, found no text with this wording.

identification: Sermon or exposition material on Mary Magdalene and Jacob typology, probably de sanctis; not a psalter commentary
note: Not identified. One face treats Mary Magdalene through the topos of Christ defending the silent Mary against the murmuring Pharisee and the complaining Martha. The other face expounds Jacob (Esau the hunter as the devil, the stolen blessing, the wrestling with the angel) and probably applies it to the apostle James. The Psalm 9:30 verse is a cross-reference, not the base text. The Magdalene-then-James order suggests sermons or expositions de sanctis, but no text with this wording was found. Jacobus de Voragine's Sermones de sanctis and the Legenda aurea were read for both feasts and do not match.

identification: Six faded partial lines; nothing searchable at the published size
note: Not identified. Six faded partial lines in a small textualis currens with red capital strokes; the other face shows no legible text. The script, decoration and line spacing differ from Fragm. 331 a (F-2nxm), so the two strips come from different manuscripts despite the shared binding. Too little is legible for a phrase search; multispectral imaging would be needed.

identification: Scholastic question on whether complexio is the form of the body; work unidentified
note: The fragment is a 13th- or 15th-century scholastic question (the catalogue conflicts) on whether complexio is the form of the complexioned body ("forma complexionati corporis") or an accidental disposition. It has a Sed contra and replies Ad primum, Ad secundum, Ad tertium, and only one column block of the bifolium is legible at the published resolution. Phrase searches found only doctrinal parallels (Bonaventure, Albert, Aquinas SCG II.63, Taddeo Alderotti), no matching text. It stays unresolved pending better images.

content.title: Scholastic question on whether complexio is the form of the body
content.description: On whether complexio is the form of the complexioned body ('forma complexionati corporis') or an accidental disposition, with Sed contra and replies Ad primum, Ad secundum, Ad tertium.
content.remarks: The work is not identified.

catalogue_title: Subject index to unidentified theological texts on virtues and vices
identification: Subject index on virtues, vices and other topics referring to numbered items and to 'Godefridus' and 'Remundus'; indexed works unidentified
note: This is a 14th-century subject index (tabula) with "Q(ue)re n(umer)o" references to a numbered collection. It also sends readers to "Godefridus" (for the seven deadly sins and their contrary virtues, the ten commandments and penance) and to "Remundus" (penance, presumably Raymond of Peñafort). Its subjects range from theology and canon law to lapidary lore and the seven imperial electors, so the numbers probably denote items or volumes, not chapters of one work. Goffredus de Trano's Summa was checked in OCR and does not contain the vices septenary. Main work and Godefridus remain unidentified.

identification: Moral treatise on avarice quoting Seneca, Jerome Ep. 71 and Ambrose; containing work unidentified
note: The strip is a discursive Latin treatment of avarice that paraphrases and glosses its authorities: Jerome Ep. 71, Seneca NQ V.15, Epp. 94, 119 and 90, and Ambrose In Ps. 118 and De off. III.7. The catalogue's "Ep. 109" is Ep. 119.12. Manipulus florum and Trevet on Boethius II m.5 were checked and excluded. On OCR, Peraldus De avaritia shares the opening "ad pedes apostolorum" topos but with different authorities, Bromyard has Ep. 119 and the Ambrose line only in other articles and contexts, and the Communiloquium (poor OCR) has none of the quotations. The containing work is unidentified.

identification: Strips with two to four cut lines per column; too sparse to identify
note: The two 14th-century headband strips keep only 2-4 cut lines per column. A red rubric ending paula/pauli introducing a new item is the main lead. Legenda aurea De sancta Paula was tested and does not collate in the second column. Aquinas on 1 Timothy was also rejected. The strips are too sparse to identify without better imaging.

institution: Leuven, KU Leuven Bibliotheken Bijzondere Collecties
identification: Only ghosts of a large script on a stained paper leaf
note: A stained paper part-leaf with ghosts of a large textura. The only dark-ink group reads something like "...nnia et" and may be an offset. Nothing searchable in ordinary photographs; unidentified.

identification: One main-hand line end fits the Lauds antiphon Trium puerorum (Cantus 005191); not confirmed
note: The strip's one surviving line in the main hand ends ... benedicentes d(omi)n(u)m. This fits the Lauds antiphon Trium puerorum (CAO 5191), but the preceding and following words are too trimmed to confirm it. The two cursive lines below are unidentified.

content.title: Antiphon Trium puerorum (?)
content.description: The one line in the main hand ends 'benedicentes dominum', which fits the Lauds antiphon Trium puerorum.
content.remarks: The words before and after are trimmed, so the antiphon is not confirmed. The two cursive lines below are not identified.

bibliography: R.-J. Hesbert, Corpus antiphonalium officii, III, no. 5191

identification: No main text above the seam; marginal allegations suggest Gratian's Decretum, part II
note: Binding strip with only a blue/red running head ("...A . Q(?) . VII") and later marginal allegations in canon-law form (causa/quaestio references and chapter incipits). Its text block is trimmed off. The lower flap with large textura belongs to F-815q. Nothing searchable; unidentified.

identification: Two or three washed-out lines; nothing searchable
note: A narrow bifolium strip whose 2-3 surviving lines on one face are washed out. Only red paraphs, a red "...nio" and later pen trials are clear. Ordinary photographs give no searchable text; unidentified, and UV imaging would be needed.

catalogue_title: Law compilation | Unidentified legal text (fol. [1]r); Carta de foresta, art. 9-11 (fol. [1]v)
identification: Fol. [1]r is a canon-law list of penal cases citing the Liber Extra (X 5.38.13 Cum infirmitas, X 5.6, X 5.17), probably from an English pastoral manual of the Oculus sacerdotis / Pupilla oculi kind that pairs such lists with the Carta de foresta; the list itself is unidentified
note: Fol. [1]r is a canon-law list of penal cases, each with a Liber Extra citation; it is not a statute. One entry paraphrases X 5.38.13 Cum infirmitas ("Medicus nolens monere et inducere [infir]mum ... [ad]vocet medic[um anim]e ... ex. de [pen. et re. c. Cum in]firmitas"). Nearby are citations "ex. de iudeis ... postulasti" (probably X 5.6.14) and "ex. de raptoribus" (X 5.17). The compiling list is unidentified. The pairing of a case list with the Forest Charter matches English pastoral manuals: Pagula's Oculus sacerdotis (Penn Ms. Codex 721, ff. 50-55) and the Pupilla oculi both embed the Forest Charter among canon-law case lists. But the lists read in both (Penn 721 f. 54v, the satisfaction cases; the Pupilla interdict cases) do not contain the medicus entry.

content.title: List of penal cases citing the Liber Extra
content.description: Includes a paraphrase of X 5.38.13 (Cum infirmitas) and citations of X 5.6 (probably c. 14) and X 5.17.
content.remarks: Probably from an English pastoral manual of the Oculus sacerdotis or Pupilla oculi kind, which pair such lists with the Carta de foresta; the lists in Philadelphia, Penn, Ms. Codex 721, f. 54v, and in the Pupilla oculi lack the medicus entry. The list is not identified.

identification: Johannes Dacus, De gradibus formarum (sophisma), ed. Otto 1955, pp. 554-555 and 561
note: The corner of the front pastedown visible under the paper (canvas 0) agrees with Otto's edition p. 561, on the analogy of being and God as the measure of beings, in sequence over parts of ten consecutive lines (2-11), with variants; line 1 remains illegible; the joint line (canvas 11) agrees with pp. 554-555 ('primum substans est materia prima; nam quicquid substat'). A research reader reread all visible lines on the images; the coordinator read canvas 0 lines 8-11 against the edition. The source text is Google Books snippets of the edition that together cover the collated run; no page image was available. In line 7 the manuscript seems to have one word where the edition reads 'entis. Sed substantie' (unresolved), line 8 appears to read 'quia ens quod est sub[...]' rather than the edition's 'propter' (continuation unresolved), and the manuscript lacks the bracketed 'non' in the edition snippets (editorial convention unchecked). The catalogue's 'Commentary to Aristotle's Metaphysics (?)' was a genre guess; the fragment is not claimed as a new witness.

fragmentarium.title: Johannes Dacus, De gradibus formarum

content.title: Johannes Dacus, De gradibus formarum (sophisma)
content.description: Visible corner of the pastedown: the passage on the analogy of being and God as the measure of beings (ed. Otto p. 561). Joint: the passage on prime matter as the first subject (pp. 554-555).

bibliography: A. Otto (ed.), Johannis Daci Opera, Corpus Philosophorum Danicorum Medii Aevi I.2 (Copenhagen 1955), pp. 554-555, 561

identification: Quotes Regula Benedicti 6.1 under a heading on silence; containing work unidentified
note: The legible lines quote Regula Benedicti 6.1 ("Faciamus quod ait propheta: Dixi custodiam vias meas [ut non delinquam]"), introduced by "De silencio dicit vir sanctus in regula". The containing work, a later text citing the Rule under a heading on silence, is unidentified. A separate German piece on the same back pastedown is not part of this record's description.

content.title: Text quoting the Rule of Benedict on silence
content.description: De silencio dicit vir sanctus in regula: Faciamus quod ait propheta: Dixi custodiam vias meas [ut non delinquam] (Regula Benedicti 6.1).
content.remarks: Containing work not identified.

identification: Gilbert the Universal, Glossa ordinaria in Lamentationes, book I, on Lam. 1:16 and 1:17
note: Two in-situ spine tabs carry line ends from the Glossa ordinaria on Lamentations. Tab B is on 1:16 ('[docto]rum ecclesiam s(ibi) c[ommissam] ... fonte a[moris] ... [la]crimas p(ro)ducat') and tab A is on 1:17 Allegorice ('[q]ua p(ossi)t hostium / uince(re) & sua defende(re) / polluta fed[i]t[at]e car[nalium] ... hostes q(uibus)'). A research reader compared all seven visible lines with the Lyon 1545 Glossa page images (scans 392-393) and with snippets of Andree's edition (pp. 256, 260); the coordinator checked tab A lines 1-2 against scan 393. The wording follows the Glossa, not its source Paschasius ('hostes revincere, suaque defendere dogmata'). Martin of Leon, who reuses the 1:16 sentence, was not found to contain the 1:17 passage, a result that rests on MDZ OCR and the PL text only and weakens this alternative without conclusively excluding it. Andree's apparatus was not seen; the opening words of tab A l. 4 and tab B l. 2 are uncertain; F-dkld is a different volume.

identification: Imaged face carries only a painted initial
note: The only imaged face of the Cod. 3569 fragment is a 110 mm painted initial A with acanthus ornament and a later shelfmark; it carries no text. The adjacent text leaf belongs to the host. Unidentified; the hidden face, if any text survives, needs imaging.

identification: Abraded dorsal patch; no searchable text
note: The dorsal patch at the head of the wrapper's spine shows six or seven abraded lines on each side of a later spine strip. At the published resolution only isolated letters ("omne"?) can be made out, so nothing could be searched. The two-column Euphrosyne text in the first reading belongs to the wrapper bifolium, which is a sibling record, not to this one.

identification: Erased lower text unreadable in the published images; the legible table indexes the host volume
note: The legible red-and-black list on both pastedowns of Cod. 1695 is a table of contents to the host's own sermons (a1-e9, ending "In cena domini ... Finis tabule"), matching the host's lost opening, final sermon and 92 leaves; the catalogue already said so. The catalogued fragment is the erased German text beneath, which is not legible in the published visible-light images. Unidentified; UV imaging needed.

catalogue_title: Unidentified religious treatise in Anglo-Norman verse
identification: Marcus, Visio Tnugdali (Vision of Tundale), Anglo-Norman translation in octosyllabic couplets, Lucifer to the field of joy (ed. Wagner 1882, pp. 36-41)
note: The two leaves translate, in the Latin's order, the Visio Tnugdali from the description of Lucifer to the gate and field of joy with the fount of life, phrase by phrase and in sequence on all four faces. A research reader compared the reread columns with Wagner's 1882 edition, using page images for pp. 36, 38 and 41. The coordinator found phrase-by-phrase correspondence for canvas 3, col b, box 760,340-1420,1200, against p. 41 lines 2-8. The identification is of the work translated: no edition of this French text was found, so it was compared with the Latin. The translation is free and amplifying (especially on prelates), is in octosyllabic couplets, and differs in form from the edited Dublin TCD 312 alexandrine version. It is not recorded in the sources checked (ARLIMA, Easting 1997, Gardiner 1993, Picard 1989). Dean and Boulton 1999, Palmer 1982, Cavagna 2017 and Jonas were unavailable, and no novelty is claimed.

fragmentarium.title: Marcus, Visio Tnugdali (Anglo-Norman verse translation)

content.remarks: A free translation; not the alexandrine version of Dublin, Trinity College, MS 312.

bibliography: Visio Tnugdali, lateinisch und altdeutsch, ed. A. Wagner (Erlangen 1882), pp. 36-41

institution: Chicago, University of Chicago Hanna Holborn Gray Special Collections Research Center
identification: Commentary on the Apocalypse, Apoc 5:1-8 and 6:10-15, reading the seals as seven status of the Church; not Hugh of St Cher, Vitalis, Berengaudus, Olivi or Joachim; work unidentified
note: F-1tv3 is a continuous lemma commentary on Apoc 5:1-8 and 6:10-15 that reads the seals as seven status ecclesie, the sixth running from the coming of Antichrist to his death. The "top" and "bottom" strips are the middle and foot of the same two leaves, against the catalogue's suggestion of two bifolia. Hugh of St Cher, Vitalis/ps.-Albert, both Corpus Thomisticum commentaries, Joachim, Berengaudus (1554 print, page read), Olivi (OCR snippets of Lewis's transcription) and the PL Apocalypse commentaries (Richard, Haymo, Anselm of Laon, Alexander Minorita and others) were compared at Apoc 6:11-13 and do not match. Lyra and Gorran could not be checked. The work remains unidentified, probably an unedited school commentary.

content.title: Commentary on the Apocalypse, Apoc 5:1-8 and 6:10-15
content.description: Lemma commentary reading the seals as seven status of the Church, the sixth from the coming of Antichrist to his death.
content.remarks: The top and bottom strips are the middle and foot of the same two leaves. Not Hugh of St Cher, Vitalis (ps.-Albert), Berengaudus, Olivi or Joachim; the work is not identified.

identification: Literal exposition (divisio and lemma glosses) of Aristotle, De anima II.5-III.1 (417b5 to the opening of Book III at 424b22); not Thomas Aquinas or Giles of Rome; commentator unidentified
note: Literal exposition (divisio, "id est" glosses, "legatur littera sic", "Sciendum" notabilia, no quaestiones) of De anima II.5-6 (417b5-418a24) and II.11 to III.1 (423b29-424b22+). The catalogue's "427b22" is an error for 424b22, the opening of Book III. Compared with Aquinas's Sentencia (Corpus Thomisticum) at three loci and with Giles of Rome's Expositio (1500 print, page images, fol. 35r and 53v): neither matches. The question commentaries are excluded by genre, and the 1240s anonymous expositions (Bazán 1998, Gauthier 1985) were not accessible, so the commentator remains unidentified.

content.title: Literal exposition of Aristotle, De anima II.5-III.1
content.description: Divisio and lemma glosses on De anima II.5-6 (417b5-418a24) and II.11 to the opening of III.1 (423b29-424b22).
content.remarks: Not the commentary of Thomas Aquinas or of Giles of Rome; the commentator is not identified. The last lemma is at 424b22, not 427b22.

catalogue_title: Legendary | Miracles of St James and saints' lives of St Clement and St Eustace
identification: Anonymous preaching compilation of exempla in 20 chapters (prologue 'In hoc consequenti opusculo ordinantur in certis titulis'), section IV De sanctis, subchapters 1-6 and 34-39 (= Cambridge CCCC MS 327, ff. 175v-176r, 179v-180v)
note: The bifolium agrees in chapter sequence and in the compiler's own wording with section IV of the compilation in Cambridge, Corpus Christi College MS 327: the Gregory framings with the additions 'et estu immenso' and 'vir mirabili gratia dotatus', the false reference 'in xvi libro de sacramentis', and 'fructus vere patientie'. A research reader collated four passages from both faces with the Parker on the Web page images (ff. 175v, 176r, 180r) and checked the sequence through Becket and Giles on ff. 179v and 180v. The coordinator found line-by-line agreement for f. 25v col. b (canvas 1, box 1850,5100-4450,6150) against f. 176r, the rubric between the items differing ('vi cap.' against 'Similis precedenti'). The rubrication differs throughout (Gent numbers chapters within the section, Cambridge across the work, offset 89), and the wording differences are minor. The work is unedited and anonymous; the other recorded copies (Florence BNCF Conv. Soppr. D.8.1128, Les Enluminures TM 427, BL Sloane 4029) were not seen.

identification: Miscellany of excerpts and exempla, including ps.-Augustine, Dialogus quaestionum LXV qq. 15-20, Verba seniorum items and Jacques de Vitry exempla in other wording; collection unidentified
note: Partial (medium). ff. 2ra-rb are Ps.-Augustine, Dialogus quaestionum LXV qq. XV-XX (PL 40), compared in sequence. f. 4r has two Verba seniorum stories and the Ps.-Augustine/Hrabanus Sunday sermon "Sciendum est fratres karissimi". The florilegium on 1v-2v draws on Jerome Ep. 118, Augustine Enarrationes, Gregory Moralia and Cassian Inst. IV.43. The exempla from 4vb are retellings of Jacques de Vitry stock (Crane 114, 215, 256-257), not his wording, and no single known collection matched; the containing compilation is unidentified.

identification: Reworking of William Peraldus, Summa de virtutibus, De dono timoris (rubric 'De speciebus timoris. LXXXIII'); order differs from the print and from Clm 2654; containing work unidentified
note: The leaf carries Peraldus, Summa de virtutibus, De dono timoris: the end of the introduction on 1r, then the chapter De speciebus timoris (rubric "LXXXIII") through Cupiditatem nocendi per te habes on 1v. It agrees in sustained wording and sequence with the 1614 edition, pp. 330-331, and was checked on page images. The chapter is arranged differently from the printed text: there is no Bede/Bernard opening, Bernard's triplex timor comes after filial fear, and the chapter number does not fit Peraldus's divisions. A dated Peraldus manuscript of 1297 (Clm 2654) has the printed order, not the fragment's. So the leaf is recorded as partial: an abridgement or reworking of Peraldus whose own title is not yet identified. The catalogue's comparison with Ripelin's CTV V.39 is a parallel only.

content.title: William Peraldus, Summa de virtutibus, De dono timoris (reworked)
content.description: 1r: end of the introduction to De dono timoris. 1v: chapter De speciebus timoris (rubric LXXXIII), to 'Cupiditatem nocendi per te habes'.
content.remarks: Wording as in the 1614 edition, pp. 330-331, but the chapter is arranged differently from the print and from München, BSB, Clm 2654 (1297). The work containing this reworking is not identified.

bibliography: Guilielmus Peraldus, Summa virtutum ac vitiorum (1614), pp. 330-331

identification: Exposition of Hebrews 11:33-34, clause by clause with literal and moral senses (commentary or martyrs' sermon), not a Job commentary; not Thomas Aquinas or Hugh of St Cher; work unidentified
note: The text is a moral and literal exposition of Hebrews 11:33-34 ("operati sunt iustitiam" through "aciem gladii"), quoting Job 5:7, Heb 13:5 and 13:8, and Isa 54:7. It is not a commentary on Job. Thomas and Hugh of St Cher on the passage do not match, and no edition matched phrase searches. The text order suggests that canvas 1 precedes canvas 0.

content.title: Exposition of Hebrews 11:33-34
content.description: Clause-by-clause literal and moral exposition, from 'operati sunt iustitiam' to 'aciem gladii', quoting Job 5:7, Heb 13:5 and 13:8, and Isa 54:7.
content.remarks: Not a commentary on Job; a commentary or a sermon for martyrs. Not Thomas Aquinas or Hugh of St Cher. Not identified. fol. [1]v probably precedes fol. [1]r.

institution: Scherpenheuvel-Zichem, Abdij der Norbertijnen van Averbode, Archief
identification: Sunday-gospel homily or exposition on Mt 8:23-27 (4th Sunday after Epiphany), then Mt 13:24; cites Bede; collection unidentified
note: Sunday-gospel homily or exposition: the end of the fourth Sunday after Epiphany (Matthew 8:23-27, boat of the cross, ships of the devil, Apocalypse 8:9) and the opening of the fifth (Matthew 13:24) under a red initial. The catalogue's "Beda" is a cited source. The leaf paraphrases Bede, In Lucam/In Marcum on the disciples waking Christ, and shares imagery with Remigius, hom. 9. The containing collection is unidentified, and Voragine's sermons for the day do not match. Both faces were read by the research reader at native size.

content.title: Homily on the Sunday gospels: Mt 8:23-27 (Dominica IV post Epiphaniam) and Mt 13:24 (Dominica V)
content.description: End of the exposition for the fourth Sunday after Epiphany and opening of the fifth.
content.remarks: Bede is cited; the passage on the disciples waking Christ paraphrases Bede, In Lucam and In Marcum. The collection is not identified.

identification: Rhythmic poem on St Agnes, 'Mundi orbis gratuletur', followed by colophon verses naming Martinus de Grudencz; not in Analecta Hymnica, Chevalier or Cantus
note: The Agnes poem on 1v ("Mundi orbis gratuletur deum trinum veneretur Agnetis") was not found in AH 1-55 (full-text grep), Chevalier RH, Mone or Cantus; Walther's Initia could not be searched. Its signature verses ("Nomen autoris si tu scrutamine queris / Mar tibi sit primum ...") are a known colophon printed by Feller (1686, p. 448) from a Leipzig Paulina manuscript and discussed in Centralblatt für Bibliothekswesen 11 (1894), no. 36. Martinus de Grudencz is therefore attested as the name in a scribe's colophon, and his authorship of the poem is not established. Partial, low: the genre and subject are clear, but the text is unprinted as far as checked.

content.title: Rhymed poem on St Agnes, Mundi orbis gratuletur, with colophon verses
content.remarks: Not in Analecta Hymnica, Chevalier or Cantus. The verses naming Martinus de Grudencz (Nomen autoris si tu scrutamine queris) are a known colophon, printed by Feller from a manuscript of the Leipzig Paulina; his authorship of the poem is not established.

identification: Latin moral or homiletic prose on tears and lamentation (cites John 11, Apoc 8:13, Lam 1), not medical; work unidentified
note: The catalogue's "possibly medical" is wrong. The strips carry Latin homiletic or moral prose on weeping: Christ's tears at Lazarus (Jo. 11), the "Vae, vae, vae" of Apoc. 8:13 glossed as sins of heart, mouth and deed, the gift of tears, "rain scatters a great wind", Lam. 1:12. The topics overlap Fasciculus morum and the Legenda aurea, but no wording was matched. The work is unidentified; the genre is the only result.

content.title: Moral or homiletic text on tears and lamentation
content.description: On weeping: Christ's tears at Lazarus (Jo 11), the 'Vae, vae, vae' of Apoc 8:13 glossed as sins of heart, mouth and deed, the gift of tears, Lam 1:12.
content.remarks: Not medical. The work is not identified.

catalogue_title: Bible commentary | Possibly a commentary on John 12
identification: Sermon on the day's gospel, John 12:20-32, with Jer 46:12 ('fortis impegit in fortem'), probably Passiontide; not Voragine's Quadragesimale; collection unidentified
note: Face 1 is a homiletic exposition of John 12:20-32, described as "the gospel of the day" ("in euangelio hodierno"). It quotes 12:24, 12:26 and 12:32, and is preceded by a rubricated Jer 46:12 ("fortis impegit in fortem ... pariter conciderunt"). It looks like a Passiontide sermon, not a commentary. Jacobus de Voragine's Quadragesimale and Durand's Rationale were checked and do not match. Face 2 is too abraded to read.

content.title: Sermon on John 12:20-32
content.description: Exposition of the gospel of the day, John 12:20-32, after Jer 46:12 'Fortis impegit in fortem' in red. The other face is not read.
content.remarks: Probably for Passiontide. Not Jacobus de Voragine, Sermones quadragesimales; the collection is not identified.

shelfmark: Archief van Sint-Baafs en bisdom Gent, SN 196
identification: Compact commentary or summa on Gratian's Decretum (D.1, D.4, D.6, C.27 qq. 1-2); not Rufinus, Paucapalea, Rolandus or Bernard of Pavia; work unidentified
note: Two quire-guard strips carry a compact commentary or summa on Gratian's Decretum, not a theological treatise. The datable passages fall at D.1 (a "mos" diagram: scripta/constitutio, non scripta/consuetudo; "humanum genus duobus regitur"), D.4 ("quod principi placuit legis habet vigorem"), D.6 d.p.c.3 ("figurativa ... superficiem ... misterium") and C.27 qq.1-2 ("voto annexum", "licentiam transfretandi", "uxori suadeat"). Rufinus, Paucapalea, Rolandus and Bernard of Pavia do not contain the wording. Goffredus could not be searched, and the containing summa is unidentified. All exposed lines were read by the research reader; canvas 2's exposed strip is blank.

content.title: Commentary or summa on Gratian, Decretum (D. 1, D. 4, D. 6, C. 27 qq. 1-2)
content.description: Passages at D. 1 (with a diagram of mos: scripta, constitutio; non scripta, consuetudo), D. 4, D. 6 d.p.c. 3 and C. 27 qq. 1-2.
content.remarks: Not Rufinus, Paucapalea, Rolandus or Bernard of Pavia; the work is not identified. The exposed strip of the lower guard is blank.

catalogue_title: Commentarium super Petri Hispani summulas logicales
identification: Literal commentary on Peter of Spain, divisio textus on Tracts IX-XI (de Rijk 1972 numbering); front strip close to the anonymous Compilationes supra Summulas Petri Hispani ('Omnes homines') in Nuremberg GNM Hs 27773; the work is not established
note: The front strip follows the Compilationes' divisio of Tracts IX-X in Nuremberg GNM Hs 27773, fol. 128ra, clause by clause but not verbatim: it adds 'quia opposita iuxta se posita magis elucescunt' and reads 'explanat' for 'exponit'. The back strip shares only the structure of the Tract XI outline. Literal commentaries on the Summulae borrow from one another without acknowledgement, so this is a source connection, not an identification of the work. A Fragmentarium editor reviewed it in October 2026: front-strip parallels strong but imperfect, back strip without the same lemmata. Only one witness was compared; Vienna ÖNB Cod. 2389, reported by de Rijk as interpolated, could help settle the relation (manuscripta.at was down at the time of review). Stopped pending that witness.

content.title: Literal commentary on Petrus Hispanus, Tractatus IX-XI
content.description: Divisio textus of Tracts IX (De ampliationibus), X (De appellationibus) and XI (De restrictionibus).
content.remarks: The front strip follows the anonymous Compilationes supra Summulas Petri Hispani ('Omnes homines') as in Nuremberg, GNM, Hs 27773, fol. 128ra, clause by clause but with additions; the back strip agrees with it in structure only. The work is not established.

catalogue_title: Prophecy in Old French | for an unknown year
identification: Old French (Picard) version, for one year, of the Tuesday entry of the January kalends prognostic, Latin in ps.-Bede, Pronostica temporum (PL 90, 951-952); no French source text found
note: The slip is a Picard rendering, for a single year (awan, "this year"), of the Tuesday entry of the Latin Kalends-of-January prognostic (Si tertia feria [fuerint kal. Ian.], hiems umbrosa/imbrosa ... naves periclitabuntur et reges peribunt; Ps.-Bede, Pronostica temporum, PL 90, 951-952). All six clauses correspond in order. Nees perilleront means "ships will be imperilled", not "children will die". The French wording was not found in print, so this is a source identification (partial, medium).

content.title: Prognostic from the Kalends of January, Tuesday entry, in Old French
content.description: The six clauses of the Tuesday entry (Si tertia feria [fuerint kal. Ian.]) in order, for a single year ('awan').
content.remarks: Latin text in ps.-Bede, Pronostica temporum. 'Nees perilleront' means 'ships will be imperilled'. French source not identified.

bibliography: Patrologia Latina 90, cols. 951-952

identification: Prose abridgement of Priscian, Institutiones V (gender by final syllable, GL II 145-164); the abridgement is unidentified
note: The two text columns on 25r-v are a prose abridgement of Priscian, Institutiones V (noun genders by final syllable, GL II c. 145-164). Collation shows Priscian's rules, exception lists and connecting wording, with the citations stripped, recast as "Omnia nomina in -X desinentia..." regulae with "In AR./In AS./In ES./In US./In IS." cues. The specific abridgement is unidentified: it is not Papias, Alcuin or Petrus Helias as quoted by Vincent, and the Glosule and the Excerptiones de Prisciano remain untested. 26r has only a later pricing note; 26v is blank.

content.title: Abridgement of Priscian, Institutiones V
content.description: Rules for the gender of nouns by final syllable ('Omnia nomina in -X desinentia ...'), with Priscian's exception lists and without his citations.
content.remarks: The abridgement is not identified; it is not Papias, Alcuin or Petrus Helias as quoted by Vincent of Beauvais. 26r has a later price note; 26v is blank.

bibliography: Grammatici Latini, ed. H. Keil, II, pp. 145-164

catalogue_title: Unidentified text, possibly by Johannes Chrysostomos | Possibly De reparatione lapsi
identification: Rubric marks the end of John Chrysostom, De reparatione lapsi (Latin), and the start of a further Chrysostom work; main text too abraded to collate
note: The red rubric on canvas 1 reads "[Explicit ... Jo]hannis Crisostomi de reparacione [lapsi ... li]ber primus eiusdem de p[s]almo(?)". It marks the end of Chrysostom's Latin De reparatione lapsi and the start of another Chrysostom work, which supports the catalogue's guess. The brown text is blurred, and with both faces showing through each other none of it could be read or collated, so the identification of the body text is unconfirmed. Status partial, pending better imaging.

content.title: John Chrysostom, De reparatione lapsi (end) and a further work
content.description: Rubric: [Explicit ... Jo]hannis Crisostomi de reparacione [lapsi ... li]ber primus eiusdem de p[s]almo(?).
content.remarks: The rubric marks the end of the Latin De reparatione lapsi and the start of another work of Chrysostom. The main text is too abraded to read.

identification: Middle Dutch devotional prose, apparently a thanksgiving prayer echoing Anselm's 'gratias ago quia creasti in me imaginem tuam'; no source found
note: F-6zm1 (two narrow strips, about six lines) carries a Middle Dutch prayer-like text. It reads "...god na minen cleynen vermoch[...] / dattu my hebste ghemaket na d[inen beelde]...", a thanksgiving motif close to Anselm's gratias ago quia creasti in me imaginem tuam. Searches of CMNL, DBNL, Google Books and IA found no source with this wording. Busch's thanksgiving prayer and the Dutch Soliloquium were checked and rejected. Unidentified.

identification: Hippocrates, Regimen acutorum, book IV with Galen's commentary (Latin), Textus XIX-XX and XXIV-XXVII (Giunta 1527 numbering)
note: The red text is the Hippocratic lemma and the black is Galen's commentary. Face A carries the end of Textus XIX and the start of XX, and face B the end of the commentary on XXIV and Textus XXV-XXVII. A research reader compared XIX, XX, XXV and XXVII with page images of the Venice 1527 Giunta edition (MDZ bsb10139648, scans 709-712), and the coordinator found line-by-line agreement for Textus XXVII (canvas 1, box 600,2780-1480,3500, against scan 712). In XIX the manuscript reads 'sed ab assumpt[ione]' where the edition has 'sed ad defectionem'. The translator was not checked, no claim is made about the Latin version or print tradition, and the abraded mid-face commentary was not compared.

identification: Breviary chapter readings: Jer 23:6-7 with rubric 'Ad .ix. cap.' and Phil 1:7; office and use unidentified
note: Two strips of F-oc1a join vertically on both faces. They carry Jer 23:6 followed by the rubric "Ad .ix. cap." and a None chapter beginning "[P]ropter hoc" (probably Jer 23:7), and on the other face Phil 1:7. The leaf is therefore from an Office book (breviary or capitulary) with chapters, not a Bible. Day, use and book type remain open.

content.title: Office book (breviary or capitulary), chapters
content.description: Jer 23:6, the rubric 'Ad .ix. cap.' and a chapter for None, [P]ropter hoc (probably Jer 23:7); on the other face Phil 1:7.
content.remarks: Two strips that join vertically. Day and use not identified.

identification: Latin commentary strip with red-underlined lemmata; too faint at the available resolution to fix the lemma
note: Faint strip with native images of only about 15 px/mm. The red-underlined lemma may read "[ne] nos inducas" (Pater noster), but the reading is insecure and no source was compared. It stays unidentified pending better images.

identification: Offset of a two-column civil-law Codex lectura, probably on C. 6.43.3 (Communia de legatis, l. ult.) with the Authentica Res quae subiacent; not the Accursian gloss, Bartolus or the 1519 lectura printed as Bellapertica; commentator unidentified
note: Mirror-image offsets on both boards of a two-column 14th-century civil-law Codex commentary (ff./C. allegations only; first-person lectura style, not a glossed text). The lower board discusses fideicommissary restitution, alienation, usucapion and 30-year prescription, eviction in duplum, and pledging. This is the content of C. 6.43.3 and Auth. Res quae subiacent, which is therefore the probable locus. The same discussion is in the 1519 Bellapertica Codex lectura, but the fragment's wording did not match it, so the commentator remains unidentified.

content.locus: lower cover inside; upper cover inside
content.title: Lectura on the Codex, probably on C. 6.43.3 (Communia de legatis) and Auth. Res quae subiacent
content.description: Offsets of a two-column commentary. The lower board discusses fideicommissary restitution, alienation, usucapion and thirty-year prescription, eviction in duplum and pledging.
content.remarks: Not the Accursian gloss, Bartolus or the lectura printed under the name of Bellapertica (1519). Commentator not identified.

identification: The catalogued object, a 16th-century music fragment in white mensural notation, is not identified and was not attempted. The uncatalogued parchment cover leaf and strip of the same volume are a Mass book, probably a plenary missal: Feria II post Invocavit (Ez 34:11-14, Mt 25:31-35; turn-in Mt 25:46 and Is 55:6) and Feria II post Reminiscere (Jn 8:22-24)
note: The record was catalogued by a project that described only fragments with musical notation, so F-v7a4 is the music fragment; the missal leaf has no catalogue record, as a Fragmentarium editor confirmed in October 2026. The work on the missal leaf stands as a note on the host volume: a research reader collated 39 lines with page images of the 1519 Teutonic Order missal (fols. XXVII, XXXIIII), and the coordinator checked canvas 1 col. b lines 1-5 and the placement on scan 91. The music fragment is open.

identification: Chancery-style letter collection or formulary on six imaged guards ('marchioni montis ferrati', 'post labores studentibus conferuntur'); Petrus de Vinea, Thomas of Capua, Guido Faba, Rockinger's formularies tested without a match; 23 guards not imaged
note: Cod. 3664 guards: about 2-3 lines per strip in a two-column hybrid hand. They mix a Montferrat salutation, a petition formula and a royal "nostre maiestatis" passage on students with penitential and theological wording. Petrus de Vinea (1566 vulgate), Thomas of Capua (MGH 2011) and three Austrian/German formularies were checked and gave no match. Still unidentified; possibly a dictamen or letter collection, as the catalogue already suggested.

identification: Noted breviary, two consecutive Sundays after Pentecost (Iv-IIr strip): antiphon Erat quidam regulus (CAO 2661), collect Familiam tuam, chapters from Eph 6:10-16; then homily lessons from Jerome, In Matthaeum III on Mt 18:23-35, chapter Phil 1:6 and antiphon Dixit autem dominus servo (CAO 2274). IIv homily on Mt 22:15-22 (unscanned) and the unnotated Jn 17 strip remain unidentified
note: Lead from a CoMMA manuscript-text search (tools/comma.py), checked on page images. A research reader (Claude) read the lower strip of both images at native resolution; the two images show one continuous band of the opened bifolium, the right text block split across them. The IIr lines (cuius uxorem et filios uenundatos perseuerante illo in malitia ... nec ecclesiastice interpretationis est nec a prudentibus uiris rec[ipiend..]) were collated on the page image of BnF lat. 17991 (breviary, 12th c.), f. 147v col. b, and with Jerome's text in PL 26 via Corpus Corporum. They agree with both, sharing with lat. 17991 the readings uenundatos and sic et uxorem against PL uenundandos; lat. 17991 puts a lesson break after intelligi uolunt and runs the lesson to non dimittentur, while here the lesson ends at recipiend[..] and the chapter follows on the next line. Chants were checked in Cantus Index; the regulus and Dixit autem antiphons belong to consecutive Sundays, and lat. 17991 f. 148r has Dixit autem as the gospel antiphon after the same homily. The collect and the Eph 6 chapters sit with the regulus antiphon, not with Mt 18 as in the Roman Missal; this hints at the use but was not tested against other books. The Lille 814 and Cambrai 528 HTR hits were not checked on images. The status stays partial: the IIv homily is known only from the catalogue transcription (it follows Jerome and argues like the Heiric-attributed PL 95 homily, Hom. CXCIV, but not in its wording), and the unnotated strip at the top seam (Jn 17:7-8, red rubric [..]e ascensione domini) still points only to a Mass book of the Ascension season.

content.remarks: Text as in Paris, BnF, lat. 17991, f. 147v-148r.

identification: Offset on a spine of Latin scholastic prose in Italian textualis; the 1642 px photograph gives only scattered words, no connected run to search
note: The fragments are offsets from four parchment spine linings, upside-down mirror images that read correctly after a vertical flip. They show a few words per line of 14th-c. Italian Latin prose, probably scholastic: repellit, intrinseco, existit, veniat, praeter, quod possit, solo alio, immediate, ut tho.. No connected phrase could be read from the single low-resolution photograph, and searches on the surviving words found nothing. The text remains unidentified pending higher-resolution imaging.

identification: Same photograph as F-x33a (Cod. 3588 back board); its German tab has about fifteen cut words, too few to search; the Latin tab is the Rule of Benedict 6.1 passage already recorded under F-x33a
note: F-isvn and F-x33a publish the same photograph of the back-board spine linings of Cod. 3588. F-isvn's catalogued German fragment is the tab below the third cord, partly under the turn-in. Its five cut lines ("Item frem[d..] / das man k.. / vnd das er da.. / vnd darumb ..") are too short to identify. The Latin tab quoting Regula Benedicti 6.1 belongs to F-x33a, and nothing visible shows whether the two tabs come from one manuscript.

institution: Scherpenheuvel-Zichem, Abdij der Norbertijnen van Averbode, Archief
identification: Recto too faint for connected text; what is legible looks like further pen trials and notes (a repeated heading 'De bea[ta] ma[ria]?'), not book text
note: The recto of F-722c could not be read connectedly even with contrast enhancement. No candidate was tested. The heading formula "De bea[ta] ma[ria]? / et q(ui) l..." occurs twice (top right, and lower left at y≈1530), and short entries "Me bene ..." repeat in a ruled box. So the recto too looks like notes or pen trials rather than the end of a theological text.

note: F-3d30's strip F2 keeps only the ends of 10-11 lines of column A and the first letters of column B (ff/fo/s/te/r/a). F1 is not readable in any image. The other strips in the photographs are F3/F4 of sibling record F-0df1 (F4 = Psalm 63, the red-Q textualis). Proximity searches on the few secure words (aliquando, vacat qualiter, pro principi, celebri) gave no usable lead.

identification: Office lectionary strips (later marginal 'l. i, iii, iiii'), 1-2 words a line; ordered line-end searches against the Vulgate found nothing; homiliary texts untested
note: Two 12th-century gutter strips keep only one to eight letters a line. Later marginal l(ectio) i / iii / iiii notes show that the text was read in Office lessons. Ordered line-end and line-beginning chains against the Vulgate, and proximity searches in Corpus Corporum, gave no candidate. The fragment is left unidentified; homiliary and legendary corpora remain untested.

identification: Copy sheet of three documents of the 1446-1451 Tyrolean settlement: Frederick III's pardon of the Tyrolean estates (Vienna, 2 April 1446), Albrecht VI's parallel pardon (1446, dating clause lost), and Duke Sigmund's confirmation of the Tyrolean liberties (Innsbruck, 17 August 1451)
note: Regests read on the image (01v); document 1 agrees with Chmel, Regesta Friderici III, Anhang 65, and document 3 with Chmel, Materialien I/2 no. CLXXIV, pp. 354-355; document 2 matches Schober no. 17 and RI XIV/4 on issuer and action. Supplied from Chmel: document 1's feast, year and mediator, and document 3's year; document 2's issuer's name (under tape) and its dating clause are lost.

note: Beneficiary, the abbot clause, the blazon and the 26th Roman regnal year are read; the year 1601 is probable. The outside record is the Vienna chancery file of this grant (ÖStA, AVA Adel RAA 208.47): its catalogue entry names Georg Jäger, his son Melchior, abbot of Stams, and the arms with the Lehenartikel, dated Prague, 18 June 1601, and its painted arms (fol. 4) match the blazon, which this sheet leaves unpainted. The blazon and parties agree with F-fc4z.

identification: Jacobus de Voragine, Legenda aurea (bifolium Frg. 217_1 only): end of Martin, Brice, opening of Elizabeth (Graesse caps. 166-168, pp. 750-753) and part of Clement (cap. 170, pp. 783-786); strip Frg. 217_2 not identified
note: Five passages on all four pages of the bifolium Frg. 217_1 were reread on the native images and agree in wording and sequence with Graesse 1850 (pp. 751 and 784 on page images, other pages on OCR) and with Maggioni's text in Corpus Corporum; the November order Martin-Brice-Elizabeth-(Cecilia)-Clement and the rubricated 'De nomine' prologue, with readings absent from Juan Gil de Zamora's reworking, show it is the Legenda aurea itself. A research reader (Claude) collated four passages; an independent research reader read a fifth (canvas 1 right, Clement, region 4620,2980,2080,580) before seeing the comparison and matched it against Graesse p. 784 and Maggioni. Variants are minor (particles, omissions such as 'visu', corruptions such as 'latiorem et affluentiorem'), and the copy often sides with Maggioni against Graesse ('emulus', 'regionum', 'amen', 'eicite'). The identification covers item 217_1 only: the strip Frg. 217_2 is read only in scraps, not identified, and not shown to come from the same book. Lines outside the five passages rest on the first reading.

identification: Jacobus de Voragine, Legenda aurea, four bifolia with chapters for Dominic, Donatus, Cyriacus, Laurence, Cosmas and Damian, Michael, Francis, Dionysius, Eustace, All Saints and Martin (Graesse caps. 113-166)
note: Five passages, at least one on each bifolium, agree in wording and chapter structure with Graesse 1850: Cosmas and Damian (pp. 636-637, page images), Michael (OCR), Laurence (p. 489, page image, and Maggioni's text in Corpus Corporum), and the opening of All Saints and Francis's stigmata (OCR). A research reader (Claude) collated Cosmas and Damian, Michael and the opening of Laurence; an independent research reader read the continuation of Laurence on canvas 6 left (regions 1450,1560,2150,640 and 1450,2880,2150,540) before seeing that comparison and matched it against Graesse p. 489 and Maggioni, and added the canvas 5 and canvas 2 passages. The Philip and Decius passage in Laurence is present; 'Nec te moueat ... dispensauit' is transposed before 'Iste phylippus', 'ut ait Sicardus in chronica sua' and 'Vel forte ideo ...' are absent there, and the copy reads 'phylippus iunior uehementer' with Maggioni; with other small variants ('gemini', 'theodora') these are variants within the work, and the redaction is not determined. About half the text rests on the first reading or is unread. A fifth bifolium of the same manuscript is F-c7me (Frg. 242), confirmed by a Fragmentarium editor.

identification: Noted monastic antiphoner, Matins of the Third Sunday of Lent (Oculi): responsories Memento mei (end) to Dixit Joseph (incipit), with the nocturn-III antiphon Cum immundus spiritus
note: One leaf (old foliation LVI) carrying seven chants of Matins of Oculi (Cantus 007144, 007769, 006999, 006479, 002009, 007146, 006476), read on both faces; text runs from the image labelled 01v to 01r. Chants, verses, cues and the rubric 'Ad cc.' agree with the Morimondo antiphoner, BnF NAL 1411, ff. 71v-72v, on its page images; an independent research reader compared R. Iste est frater (canvas 1) word for word with f. 71v-72r. The leaf lacks Morimondo's versicle 'Scapulis suis' before Merito and shares its 'Tollite de frugibus'. The chant order matches Cistercian inventories (Morimondo, Rein, Lubiąż, Salzinnes) and Köln 1161, supporting Cistercian use as an inference only; date and place of origin are not tested.

note: One leaf read on both faces, text order from the image labelled 01v to 01r with one line lost at the trimmed top; chants identified with Cantus IDs. The texts agree on page images with the Zwiefalten antiphoner, BLB Aug. LX, ff. 112r-v and 166v-167r; an independent research reader compared the antiphons Domine si in tempore to Cum venerit (canvas 0) with f. 112v. Differences: the leaf lacks Zwiefalten's hour versicles and three Exaltare responsories, and reads 'ad dextris', 'domino cooperante', 'Cum venerit' and Annuntiaverunt as sixth apostles' antiphon. The Ascension order matches Zwiefalten and A-Wn 1890 and is not Cistercian, a South German monastic placement inferred from chant order only; the Common of Apostles directly after the Sunday after Ascension and the short last line of canvas 1 are unexplained. Date and house of use not tested.

A research reader (Claude) reread 39 lines on the images and collated them with Borgnet's page images; an independent research reader read the upper part of 76v column a blind on the image and found it agreeing with Borgnet p. 263 across the chapter 16/17 boundary. identification: Revers of 1545 by a married couple, Bernhar[d] and his wife (surname lost), to Stams abbey for goods held in Erb- und Baurecht, one acre 'in Tarmu[...]' (probably Dormitz by Nassereith), sealed by [.]örburger, Pfleger and judge of Imst (probably Christoph Hörburger)
note: Lower half of an original counter-letter (Revers) dated 1545 in words, day and month cut away, by 'beder Eeleut, Bernhar[.] vn[d ...]' for goods of Stams abbey in Erb- und Baurecht at 1 lb Berner yearly. One acre lies 'in Tarmu[...]', probably Dormitz by Nassereith (old forms Tarmuncz, Tarmiz in the Imst district archive inventory), and the bounds name a sawmill, Lienntz(?) Rueppen(?) Erben (a blind reader: 'Knappen(?) Erben') and Martin Teutschman, whom a Stams Revers of 22 July 1549 places by the sawmill at Nassereith. Sealed by '[.]örburgers Phleger vnd Richters zu Ymbsst', probably Christoph Hörburger, who with the court clerk Georg Engelschalk seals an Imst tenant's Revers in 1555 (Brixen, Domkapitelarchiv, Urk. 2486). Partial because the issuers' surname is lost and no record of the act was found in the Stams charter regests on monasterium.net; the sheet was later the wrapper of a Stams Kelleramt register for 1570 (Hs. 129).

content.title: Revers of a married couple to Stams Abbey for goods in Erb- und Baurecht
content.description: Lower half of the document. A married couple, Bernhar[d] and his wife (surname lost), acknowledge goods of Stams Abbey held in Erb- und Baurecht at 1 lb Berner yearly, among them an acre 'in Tarmu[...]' (probably Dormitz by Nassereith) and land below a sawmill next to Martin Teutschman. Sealed by [.]örburger, Pfleger and judge of Imst, probably Christoph Hörburger. 1545, day and month lost.

identification: Lehenbrief: Abbot Paul and the convent of Stams grant the Walthauserin, Johann's son and daughter (Johannes and Petronella) and other Stiftsfreie at Tartsch fields and a meadow at Mals in Erblehen; [15]43 (century supplied), place, day and month lost
note: The regest is read on the image: issuer Abbot Paul and the convent of Stams, beneficiaries, grant in Erb- und Baurecht, plots at Mals near St Martin's church, rent of rye and barley to the Zinskasten at Mals and 1 lb Berner; the endorsement names Johannes, Petronella and Wilhalm. Only 'Unnd Im Dreiundvierzigisten Jare' survives of the date (the preserved readings have 'Dreiunddreissigisten'); the century is supplied: only Paul I Käsinger can issue in a forty-third year, and the Stams archive's regests have Abbot Paul granting in 1541 and 1543 and Abbot Simon from April 1544 (Kaisheim history: 1540-1544; Siebmacher's 1542 is contradicted), giving 1543. The host volume, Hs. 119, is titled for 1578. The 'n.' placeholder leaves open original, engrossment or copy; no outside record found.

identification: Enea Silvio Piccolomini: orations Quamvis omnibus (Regensburg 1454; Wolkan III Nr. 291, pp. 542-546) and Constantinopolitana clades (Frankfurt 1454; Müller, Reichstags-Theatrum I, pp. 479-480); De liberorum educatione, grammar section to the opening of the defence of poets (Wolkan II Nr. 40, pp. 129-140)
note: Two paper bifolia in one fifteenth-century hand, taken from the binding of Stams Hs 308 in 1964: bifolium 1 has the Regensburg oration on one leaf and the Frankfurt oration on the other, bifolium 2 has De liberorum educatione from the end of the analogy and derivation section through barbarism and solecism to the opening of the defence of poets. A research reader reread selected lines on all leaves except the right page of canvas 1 and compared them with Wolkan III and Wolkan II on Internet Archive OCR and with Müller 1713 on the MDZ page image (p. 480) and OCR (p. 479). An independent research reader read seven lines of canvas 3 right (box 4350,2180-6650,2620) on the image and found them in agreement with Wolkan II p. 131 on the page image, and checked the locus of canvas 3 at pp. 129, 130, 138 and 140. Variants are minor (e.g. vitanda? / vindicanda, nostro / vestro, Viscella / vistula, omission of nobilissimum Ladislaum, dicemus / dicamus). The right page of canvas 1 and most of the left pages of canvases 2 and 3 rest on the image-only first reading, which was exposed to a pencil note naming Aeneas Piccolomini and the Regensburg diet on canvases 0-1.

note: A research reader collated passages from all four columns line by line against Steele's page images (pp. 109, 114-120), finding sustained agreement in wording and sequence with Philip of Tripoli's Latin base text, not Bacon's glosses. A second research reader independently read canvas 0 col. a lines 13-25 (the red and white stones) and found agreement with Steele p. 118 over 13 lines, with 'pondus derham' for 'pondus denarii'. Other version differences: 'planetarum' for 'plantarum' repeatedly, 'philosophando' for 'prophetando', 'luna accrescente' for 'decrescens', the Pliny note on the Moon carried in the text (Steele reports it only as a footnote; compared on OCR), and several eye-skip omissions. A later vertical inscription, 'Vrbarium / Mitlkhellner Ambts, auf das Sechzehen- / hundert dreyzehent Jar', shows the leaf was the cover of the 1613 Urbar of the Mittelkellner office. identification: Galen, Ad Glauconem de medendi methodo, old Latin translation, book II: end of the chapter on soft swellings and the chapter on scirrhus, with the subsection 'de uirtutibus adipum' (Greek II.5-6, Kühn XI 101-105; Venice 1522, tract. II cap. x-xi; Vendôme, BM, Ms. 109, f. 28v-29r)
note: A research reader reread verso lines 2-12 and 14-24 and the foot of the recto on the native images and compared them with the page image of the Venice 1522 Latin Galen (tract. II cap. x-xi) and, for the verso, with Vendôme, BM, Ms. 109, f. 28v-29r: the wording and order agree from 'Fit autem sirosis id est durus tu[mor] ex glutinoso quodam' through the remedies called malactica to the ranking of fats ('ualde melius est leopardinum quam leoninum & melius est ursinum quam taurinum'), and the leaf sides with the Vendôme manuscript against the print in several readings. Gariopontus's Passionarius, which takes over the chapter, is not the text of the leaf: the Basel 1531 edition and Paris, BnF, NAL 695 lack the ranking of fats and word three sentences differently. The red chapter number xxxiiii beside 'Incipit ... uirtutibus adipum' is unexplained, since Vendôme 109 numbers the section xiii and Paris, BnF, lat. 6837 numbers it xv. Most of the abraded recto was not compared, three recto lines were read only with the source as a guide, and no critical edition of the translation was used. The verso lay face to face with a seventeenth-century German account leaf, Stams, Frg. 175, leaf 9r (F-pmci): each carries the other's offset.

content.description: 01r: end of the chapter on soft swellings, with a plaster recipe. De adipibus uer[o opti]mum est leoninum inter quadrupedes ... Expl.: [De uola]tilibus autem obtimum est adipe anserin[um].
content.remarks: Agrees with the Venice 1522 edition (tract. II cap. x-xi) and with Vendôme, Bibliothèque municipale, Ms. 109, f. 28v-29r, where the section on fats is chapter xiii of book II. The number xxxiiii on this leaf is unexplained. Not the reworking in Gariopontus, Passionarius, which lacks the ranking of fats. 01r is abraded and only partly read. The verso carries the offset of the German account entries of Stams, Frg. 175, leaf 9r (F-pmci), which carries this verso's offset.

note: Two consecutive paper leaves of an office book without lessons, text order 107-2v, 2r, 1v, 1r (the pencilled r/v labels are reversed on both leaves; the join was confirmed by two readers). A research reader compared the Henry chants, chapter, hymn cue and collect with the Bamberg breviary of 1575 and the Kunigunde chants with Analecta Hymnica 26 on page images, finding sustained agreement in wording and order; a second research reader read the Lauds antiphons and the 1v join before seeing a source and confirmed it. The psalm scheme is secular, not monastic or Cistercian; the diocese of use (Bamberg-like, but the office was also used in Augsburg, Salzburg and Austria) is not established, and date and origin were not assessed.

note: One parchment leaf of a monastic breviary, later a binding wrapper. A research reader compared the chants with the Cantus Database transcription of the Cistercian antiphoner of Rein (A-Wn Cod. 1799**, ff. 228r-231r), the only inventory with the whole run of fifteen chants in this order, and the chants, rubrics and lessons with the Historia de spinea corona (Dillingen 1584) on page images; a second research reader read canvas 0 column b lines 11-22 before opening the print and confirmed sustained agreement. The leaf matches neither witness exactly: its nocturn II psalm cues for antiphons 5-6 (Domine Deus salutis, Dominus regnavit) differ from both Rein and the print (Te decet, Domine Deus salutis), its nocturn III versicle agrees with the print against Rein, and its lesson division differs from the print's (split at Propterea and Tu vero, print Lectio IIII Si contumeliam absent, two lessons not in the print). Cistercian use is an inference only; date, origin and the source of lesson viii are not established.

Jerusalem luge); rubrics agree with the Ordinal of Innocent III (Van Dijk 1975, pp. 244, 259-260)
note: The run of lessons, chants and rubrics was read on all four pages and agrees in content and order with the papal-court Ordinal of Innocent III (Van Dijk and Walker 1975, pp. 244, 259-260), compared in Google Books snippets only; the nine-responsory structure is that of the secular cursus, but monastic books also used it on these days, so the use is not established. An independent research reader read Lam 4:4-14 (canvas 1 col 1) on the image against the Vulgate. The leaf has 'sine capitulo' (with a Franciscan breviary rubric) for the Ordinal's 'sine lectione', and omits filiae, mulierum and sacerdotum in Lam 4. Which book of the curial/Franciscan/Roman-use family it came from, its date and origin, and the extent of the Good Friday nocturn III lessons are not established.

content.title: Breviary, Good Friday and Holy Saturday

content.remarks: The rubrics agree with the Ordinal of the papal court of Innocent III; the use is not established. Text order: 01v right, 01r left, 01r right, 01v left.

bibliography: S. J. P. van Dijk and J. Hazelden Walker, The Ordinal of the Papal Court from Innocent III to Boniface VIII and Related Documents, Spicilegium Friburgense 22 (Fribourg 1975), pp. 244, 259-260

identification: Noted hymnal, probably Cistercian: Common of Saints (end of Deus tuorum militum, Iesu corona virginum, Christe cunctorum) and hymns of an Office of the Passion, probably of the Crown of Thorns (end of Bonaventure's Christum ducem; Beata Christi passio with Qui pressura in the arrangement of Mone's MS K; Iesu velatus facie at Terce); Mone I nos. 85-87
note: The hymns were read on all four pages and compared with Mone, Lateinische Hymnen I nos. 84-91 (archive.org OCR text) and with Waddell's Primitive Cistercian Breviary (Google Books snippets); an independent research reader read canvas 1 left against Waddell and Cantus and found agreement apart from 'adque' and 'mentibus' (Waddell 'atque', 'sensibus') and 'pariterque' (Cantus 'pariter et'). Qui pressura agrees with every feature Mone reports for his Karlsruhe MS K, headed for the feast of the Crown of Thorns, and Iesu velatus facie is listed under De corona spinea in Clm 2541 (at Terce) and Heidelberg Cod. Sal. X,7 (Salem) in MMMO; the leaf itself has no feast heading, so the occasion is probable. The Deus tuorum militum ending, the division of Iesu corona virginum and the Gloria tibi domine doxology make Cistercian use probable. The marginal rubric on canvas 1 right is unread, the leaf order is not settled, and the date and origin were not examined.

identification: Deed of sale: Abbot Pelagius of Stams, with the consent of King Ferdinand I, sells Ludwig von Brunnenstain a redeemable yearly rent on pledged abbey woods, tithes and rights (redemption 300 gulden); Michaelmas (29 September), probably [1539] (1538 not excluded), place lost
note: The regest is read on the image: issuer Abbot P(?)elagius of Stams (first letters uncertain, ending -agius clear), the Roman king's consent, buyer Ludwig von Brunnenstain, sale of a redeemable rent on pledged abbey property, redemption at 300 gulden with return of the letter, and the dating clause 'sannt Michels des heiligen Ertzenngels tag' (29 September). The year is lost at the cut right edge and is supplied as [1539]: the text names 1539 in line 7, and Pelagius Baur resigned on 18 April 1540 (Monasticon metropolis Salzburgensis, 1908, snippet); if line 7's 1539 is a future payment date, 1538 is possible. A fresh reader given neutral crops confirmed the year words of line 7, the Michaelmas clause, 'Ludwigen von Brunnenstain' and the back title 'Ad Annum 15.77'; it saw only '?reagius' for the abbot, which the coordinator reread as Pelagius. The capital, the yearly rent, the place and the buyer's identity are not established; no outside record of the act was found (monasterium.net Stams regests, ÖStA, Regesta Imperii, Google Books searched).

fragmentarium.title: Deed of sale of Stams Abbey

content.title: Abbot Pelagius of Stams sells a redeemable yearly rent to Ludwig von Brunnenstain
content.persons: Pelagius, abbot of Stams; Ludwig von Brunnenstain; Ferdinand I
content.description: Pelagius, abbot of Stams, with the consent of the Roman king Ferdinand I, sells Ludwig von Brunnenstain a yearly rent with right of redemption, secured on woods, tithes and rights of the abbey; redemption at 300 gulden, with return of the letter. Michaelmas (29 September), probably [1539]; the place is lost.
content.remarks: The year is lost at the cut edge; 1539 is named in the text, and 1538 is not excluded.

identification: Lehenbrief of King Ferdinand I as count of Tyrol: Hans Veit von Annenberg, for himself and as Lehenträger for Anthoni, Sigmund and Jacob, after the death of [...]ristan von Annenberg, receives the Tyrolean fiefs (castle at Latsch with orchard, sawmill, tithes, meadows, farms), with confirmation of a grace of King Henry; [1527-1564] by title, dating clause lost
note: The regest is read on the image: the royal style ('...Hungern, Behaim, Dalmatien, Croatien etc. Künig, Infant', which in a grant of Tyrolean fiefs fits only Ferdinand I), Hans Veit von Annenberg as petitioner for himself and as Lehenträger for Anthoni, Sigmund and Jacob, the grant of the fiefs of the County of Tyrol after the death of '[...]ristan von Annenberg', the confirmation of King Henry's grace, and the fief list beginning with the castle at Latsch. The left part of every line and the dating clause are cut away; the date is [1527-1564] from the title alone. A fresh reader given neutral crops confirmed the style, the names, 'Künig Hainrichs', 'Burg zu L(a/o)tsch' and the back title '15 Stambs 64', and with the coordinator read '[...]ristan' in line 4. The surname's minims allow Ammenberg; Annenberg rests on the fief group, which matches the 1510 Annenberg Lehensrevers quoted in the Hofnamen im Landgericht Schlanders (snippets) in items, order and wording. No record of this act was found; sealing cannot be checked.

fragmentarium.title: Fief grant of King Ferdinand I to Hans Veit von Annenberg

content.title: Ferdinand I grants the Tyrolean fiefs of the Annenberg family to Hans Veit von Annenberg
content.persons: Ferdinand I; Hans Veit von Annenberg
content.description: King Ferdinand I, as count of Tyrol, grants Hans Veit von Annenberg, for himself and as Lehenträger for Anthoni, Sigmund and Jacob, after the death of [...]ristan von Annenberg, the fiefs held of the County of Tyrol, and confirms a grace of King Henry. The fiefs begin with the castle at Latsch and an orchard, a sawmill, tithes, meadows and farms. The dating clause is lost; [1527-1564] from the royal title.
content.remarks: The fief list agrees in items and order with the 1510 Lehensrevers of Siegmund von Annenberg quoted in Die Hofnamen im Landgericht Schlanders (1927).

identification: Two documents of Bishop Georg of Austria of Brixen (1525-1539) to the parish clergy of his city and diocese: (A) annual circular on the cathedraticum, examination of curates, alms collectors and reserved and marriage cases, with the calendar of movable feasts for 1530; (B) faculty for Lenten confessions with reserved cases; issued [1529], no dating clause, copy on paper
note: The leaf holds two documents, each opening 'Georgius dei gratia Episcopus Brixinensis'; issuer, addressees and substance of both are read on the image. Neither keeps a dating clause: the circular's calendar is for 'Anno Tricesimo proximo venturo', and its figures (letter B, Septuagesima 13 February, Easter 17 April, Pentecost 5 June, Corpus Christi 16 June) fit 1530 (Julian), so it was issued in [1529]; Georg was bishop 1525-1538/39 (snippets). A fresh reader given neutral crops confirmed both openings, letter B, the Septuagesima and Easter dates and 'Quade[ragesima]'; it read 'Tricesimo primo', which the coordinator reread as 'Tricesimo proximo uenturo' (x clear), and the calendar fits 1530, not 1531. The unsealed paper leaf is a copy or chancery exemplar, later the cover of Stams item II/633 (1535); place and day of issue are lost. No outside record of either circular was found.

identification: Deed of sale: Abbot [Bernhard] and the convent of Stams sell Hans V[eh]lin and Anton Welser of [Memmingen] a redeemable yearly rent of 50 Malter rye from the abbey's great corn tithe at Kettershausen (Augsburg diocese) for 1100 Rhenish gulden; Friday after St George, probably [14]92 (27 April 1492); cancelled original in two strips
note: The two strips are one charter, each line running from item 1 on into item 2. Issuer, buyers, object, place, 50 Malter (25 each), price 'ailffhundert' gulden, payment between Martinmas and Christmas, redemption, sealing and the dating clause 'In dem Zwa[y]vnd ne[w]ntzigisten Jare An freytag nach sant Jörgen' are read; the abbot's name and the hundreds of the year are lost at the left edge and supplied, and the unit 'Zwa[y]' is uncertain. Hans Vöhlin died on 18 March 1496 (snippets), which excludes 1496 and fixes 27 April 1492; Abbot Bernhard of Stams is attested in 1492 (monasterium.net regest). A fresh reader given neutral crops confirmed the issuer, Anton Welser, 50 Malter, Augsburg diocese on the Günz, Kettershausen, the seal clause, the St George clause and the endorsement; it lost the year's tens under holes, could not read the sums and read the first buyer's faded surname otherwise; the coordinator reread the year as above, the sums as 'ailffhundert' and the surname as V[eh]lin, and the third person's forename, [Er?]hard or Bernhard Vöhlin of Memmingen, keeps its first letters lost. No outside record of the sale was found.

fragmentarium.title: Sale of a rent by Stams Abbey

content.title: Deed of sale of a yearly rent by the abbot and convent of Stams
content.persons: Bernhard, abbot of Stams; Hans Vöhlin; Anton Welser
content.description: Abbot [Bernhard] and the convent of Stams sell to Hans V[eh]lin and Anton Welser of [Memmingen] a redeemable yearly rent of 50 Malter rye from the abbey's great corn tithe at Kettershausen (diocese of Augsburg), for 1100 Rhenish gulden. Friday after St George, probably [14]92 (27 April 1492).
content.remarks: Cancelled original; the two strips are parts of one charter.

identification: Corrected deed of sale, probably a draft: vendors (with Agnes [K/A]i(r)cherin(?), Cristan Holtzmai[..](?) and their wives) sell [object lost]; in the sealing clause 'Richter vnnd Ambtman' 'zu Welthau' (Wilten; probable reading) is struck and replaced by the abbot and convent of Wilten; Hanns W[e]isen(?) of Natters probably receives the seal request; witnesses of Natters; Landgericht Sonnenburg, Conversion of St Paul (25 January, probable), year 'Tausennt Funffhundert vnd In dem Achtund[..]', decade not preserved
note: The lower part of a corrected German deed of sale, probably a draft, is read on the image: the vendors' warranty, Agnes [K/A]i(r)cherin(?) (named twice, probably one woman; two blind readers read 'kircherin'), Cristan Holtzmai[..](?) (blind: 'haltmair(?)') and 'vnsere hausfrawen', witnesses Oswald Spirgl and Pölt Cammerlannder of Natters, 'im Lanndgericht Sonnenburg', 'an Sanndt Pauls Bekerr[..]' (25 January, probable). In the sealing clause the words first written, 'Richter(s) vnnd Ambtman(s)' (confirmed by a blind reader) 'zu W[i/e]ltha[u/n]' (probably Wilten), are struck in two places and replaced by '[..] Herrn Abbt(s)' and 'Convent'; 'Hanns W[e]isen(?) zu Naters' probably received the vendors' seal request and is not shown as buyer. The year ends 'Achtund' with a mark that is possibly a carry-over sign, and every line start is cut away, so the decade may have stood on a lost line start; the back reads 'Raitt(?) Stambs 15[..]5[2 or 3]', probably the title of an account the sheet later covered, which would put the deed before about 1552/53. No record of the act was found by site search of monasterium.net (Wilten and Stams charters) or in Google Books and Internet Archive full text; Wilten charter 106 E of 5 May 1539 (https://www.monasterium.net/mom/AT-StiAWilten/Urkunden/106_E/charter, image read) names the Aicher family of the Aichhof at Natters, held of Wilten, and a witness Cristan Holtzmaister of Fulpmes; it is another act, and a lead only if the surnames are 'Aicherin' and 'Holtzmaister'. The object, price and buyer are lost, Wilten's lordship over the property is not established, and the surnames, the place word and the back have not had a secure independent reading; no human review.

fragmentarium.title: Deed of sale with corrections, Landgericht Sonnenburg

content.title: Corrected deed of sale, probably a draft, with the abbot of Wilten substituted as sealer
content.persons: Agnes Aicherin (?); Cristan Holtzmais[..]; Hanns W[e]isen (?); Oswald Spirgl; Pölt Cammerlannder
content.description: Lower part of a deed of sale, probably a draft: the vendors, with Agnes Aicherin (?), Cristan Holtzmais[..] and their wives, give warranty for a property now lost. In the sealing clause the words first written, probably 'Richter vnnd Ambtman zu Welthau' (Wilten), are struck and the abbot and convent of Wilten written above. Hanns W[e]isen (?) of Natters probably received the seal request; witnesses Oswald Spirgl and Pölt Cammerlannder of Natters. Done in the Landgericht Sonnenburg on the Conversion of St Paul (25 January, probable); the year reads 'Tausennt Funffhundert vnd In dem Achtund[..]', its decade not preserved.
content.remarks: The object sold, the price and the buyer are lost at the cut left edge. On the back 'Raitt (?) Stambs 15[..]5[2 or 3]', probably the title of an account the sheet later covered. An Aicher family held the Aichhof at Natters of Wilten, and a Cristan Holtzmaister of Fulpmes witnessed for its heirs in 1539 (Stiftsarchiv Wilten, Urkunden 106 E); a connection with that farm is possible, not shown.

identification: Breviary, Proprium de sanctis, 6 Sept-16 Oct (Magnus to Gallus, with a lacuna after 8 Sept), plus a bifolium with May saints and the Ascension; lessons from Vita S. Magni BHL 5162d, Stephen of Liège's Vita S. Lamberti, Eucherius's Passio Acaunensium martyrum and Hincmar's Vita Remigii
note: The leaves are a breviary sanctorale with nine-lesson secular Matins; rubrics and pencil calendar dates place leaves 1-12 in calendar order from St Magnus (6 Sept) to St Gallus (16 Oct), with at least one leaf lost between leaves 2 and 3. A research reader collated four lessons: Eucherius's Passio Acaunensium c. 3 (6r) on page images of MGH SRM III pp. 33-34, Stephen of Liège's Vita S. Lamberti §5 (3r) on PL 132 col. 645, and the Magnus death narrative (1v) on AASS Sept. II p. 755; the Magnus lessons on 1r follow BHL 5162d, but Coens' edition (Anal. Boll. 81, 1963) was seen only in Google Books snippets. A second research reader placed the Remigius lesson on 9r as Hincmar, Vita Remigii c. 1, on the page image of MGH SRM III p. 260. The lessons abridge and reword their sources (e.g. 'et fide nobiliores' for 'sed nobiliores fide', 'dispensatione' for 'dispositione', 'ista conferentibus' for 'ita serentibus'). Leaf 13 is a bifolium with May saints, a common of Eastertide and the Vigil and feast of the Ascension; its layout, line spacing and script match leaves 1-12, so it is probably from the same book, but its section is open, and the diocesan use is not determined.

identification: Office lectionary or breviary, summer temporale: Dominica IV (end), V and [IX] post Pentecosten, with homily lessons from Bede, In Lucam II (Lc 5:1-3) and Jerome, Ep. 121.6-7 (Lc 16:1-3), full gospels Lc 5:1-6 and Lc 16:1-9, collects Protector in te sperantium and Largire nobis, Benedictus antiphons; use not identified (monastic by inference only)
note: The rubrics (Dominica v. secundum Lucam, Ad Benedictus antiphona), the collects and three antiphons confirmed in Cantus Index place the texts on the fourth, fifth and ninth Sundays after Pentecost in the common medieval numbering; the book is an Office book, not a missal. A research reader collated the Bede lessons with Giles's edition (vol. 10 p. 391) and the Jerome lessons with CSEL 56 p. 22, both on page images. The lessons are abridged: Jerome's sections 2-5 are skipped, his Greek gloss is recast, Luke 15:2 is given in Vulgate wording, and 'fodere non valeo, mendicare erubesco' is omitted; Bede reads concursus for conventus and adds Christi. A second research reader read leaf 2v (Luke 16:3-9, collect Largire, antiphon Dixit dominus villico) and found it agreeing with the Sarum Missal and Breviary for the ninth Sunday after Trinity on page images; Sarum, a secular use, has a Bede homily there and no full gospel after the lessons. The full gospel read after each homily here suggests monastic Matins, but the use is inference only, and the red marginal lesson numerals and several faded rubrics were not read. The bifolium is conjugate but not central: the sixth to eighth Sundays are lost between its leaves.
