identification: Rufinus of Aquileia, Latin translation of Eusebius, Historia ecclesiastica II 6,6-10,2 (Mommsen, GCS Eusebius II.1, pp. 123,4-127,14); identified by P. Bruno Griesser in 1928
note: The leaf was identified and collated against Mommsen's edition by P. Bruno Griesser in January 1928; his notes and letters are photographed on this record (canvases 2-5), though the catalogue title is 'x'. A research reader reread 37 lines on both faces on the native images and compared them with page images of Mommsen pp. 123, 125 and 127, confirming the text and Griesser's readings. Differences from Mommsen include 'conferti' and 'cum fames' (both with manuscript N), 'admissa', 'sic' for 'sicut', omitted 'sanctis', 'obtulit', 'hac', 'uox', 'dederat' and the false divisions 'dum nouissem p(er) reb(us)' and 'consonant iam'. The stained verso lines 10-16 rest on the first reading; date and textual affiliation were not examined.
known_from: P. Bruno Griesser (Mehrerau), handwritten description and collation against Mommsen's edition, with letters of 8 and 15 January 1928, photographed on the Fragmentarium record F-fpb6 (images Stams_STA_Frg_184_Adl_01r to Adl_02v04v)

identification: Matins lessons of a twelve-lesson office: for St Barnabas, Gregory the Great, Homiliae in Evangelia 27, 1-3 (PL 76, 1205-1206), then the Gospel John 15:12-16 and the Barnabas collect; for Sts Peter and Paul, Ps.-Augustine, Sermo Caillau-Saint-Yves I, 58 (end; PLS 2, 1009-1010) and Maximus of Turin (attrib.), Homilia 70 'Beatissimorum apostolorum' (PL 57, 399-402).
note: A research reader reread lines on all four faces and compared them with page images of PLS 2, col. 1010, PL 57, cols. 399-402 and PL 76, cols. 1205-1206. There is sustained agreement in wording and order with all three: a full column of the Ps.-Augustine sermon, about twenty lines of the Maximus homily and sixteen lines of Gregory. The leaves have some better readings than PLS (Habet profecto mysterium nobilitas ista penarum; probabatur) and liturgical adaptations of the sermon's ending, and they differ from PL in small points (magisterium tam, Quanti, cum diligendo). The rubric for lesson xi is visible but that for lesson xii is not seen, so lesson xii is inferred. The Barnabas collect was matched only to later printed missals. The two lines after the heading for the Nativity of John the Baptist are not identified. Twelve lessons with the Gospel written out after them fit monastic, probably Cistercian, use; that is inference, not tested against a Cistercian book.

identification: Three acts of one appeal before the governor of Brescia, Luis d'Icart (Spanish-imperial regime), Brescia, 4, 13 and 23 February 1514: the vicar Hieronymus de Pischariis confirms the Martinengo podestà's sentence for Giovannino de Barberiis against Antonia, widow of Antonio de Casariis, over a will whose witnesses were not 'rogati'; the governor refers appealability to his judge Pino Numai; then declares the case unappealable on two conforming sentences
note: The regests are read on the image: court and officers (vicar and auditor Hieronymus de Pischariis, judge of malefices Pino de Numais, 'Nos Ludovicus Ycart ... Brixie Bergomique ... Castellanus Locumtenens & Gubernator generalis'), parties (Antonia widow of Antonio de Casariis of Martinengo and Bartolomeo de Casariis against Filippo and Giovanni Maria, sons of the late Giovannino de Barberiis), the ground (witnesses to the will not proved 'rogati') and three dating clauses, two with the year in words and indiction 2 (4 Feb. 1514; 13 Feb. 1514; 23 Feb. 1514, with the month torn after 'fe-'). A fresh reader given neutral crops confirmed the dates, year words and indiction, Brescia (Broletto, citadella nova), 'Ludovicus Ycart locumtenens & gubernator', Pino Numai, Martinengo, Antonia q. Antonii de Casariis and the vicar's surname, which it read 'piscatrijs' (a Fragmentarium editor gives Pischariis; the image has 'pisch(a)rijs', h not t); it read the Barberiis forename as 'Joannis', which the research reader reread at 2x as 'Joannini', and it could not read Icart's title, which is left unread. Icart as governor of Brescia and Pino Numai's office at Brescia are corroborated in printed histories (Google Books snippets only); no record of the suit itself was found, and the Brescia and Bergamo state archives were not checked. The sheet is an unsealed extract of the case record; no human review.

fragmentarium.title: Appeal before the governor of Brescia

content.title: Three acts of an appeal before Luis d'Icart, governor of Brescia
content.persons: Luis d'Icart; Hieronymus de Pischariis; Pino Numai; Antonia de Casariis; Giovannino de Barberiis
content.description: 4 February 1514: Hieronymus de Pischariis, vicar of the governor, confirms the sentence of the podestà of Martinengo for Giovannino de Barberiis against Antonia, widow of Antonio de Casariis, over a will whose witnesses were not proved 'rogati'. 13 February 1514: the governor refers the question of appeal to his judge Pino Numai. 23 February 1514: the case is declared unappealable on two conforming sentences.

identification: Deed of sale: [name lost] of Ögsten, son of the late Thoman Sch[..], and his wife Katherina sell to [name not read] and '[..]alenen' his wife the Baurecht of a holding at Ögsten (Östen, Umhausen) in the Ötztal, Gericht St. Petersberg, held of an abbey ('Gotzhauss vnd Closter'; Chiemsee, that is Frauenchiemsee, on the archivist's typed slip); St Genevieve's day (3 January) 152[.], last digit of the year not read
note: The text face, photographed upside down, was read rotated, with a twentieth-century typed slip and pencilled transcription in view, so none of the names has had an independent reading: the sellers ('Ogsten weylenden Thoman sch[..]', '[..]ppen Im gericht sanndtpetersperg(?)', 'Vnd Ich Katherina weylenden [..] sein eliche Hausfraue'), the sale ('hergeben vnd verkaufft'), the buyers ('dem(?) Erbern E[..]', name not read, and '[..]alenen seiner hausfrauen als kauffern'), the object ('Baurecht Der zway(?) Stu[..]', 'daselbs zu ogsten gelegen', 'von dem Gotzhauss vnd Closter'), neighbours ('margrethen witschyn(?)', '[..] Frischma[..](?)', 'Clementen walsers') and the date ('Beschehen an sand Gen[..]', '[..]aintzigisten Jare'). The abbey's name, Chiemsee, is the typed slip's and was not read on the leaf; the last digit of the year is not read and the pencilled 152(5?) is modern. The modern label's 'B VI' and 'L V' are probably drawers of the Stams charter archive, whose deeds L V 2 (1467) and L V 3 (1505) concern the tithe at Umhausen and Östen held by the Frischmann family. No record of this act was found in the Stams charters 1517-1535 or the Frauenchiemsee charters 1519-1535 as listed on monasterium.net, by site search there for Östen, Umhausen and Roppen, or by snippet search in Die Gemeindearchive des Bezirkes Imst (1995); no human review.

content.title: Sale of the Baurecht of a holding at Ögsten
content.description: [Name lost] of Ögsten, son of the late Thoman Sch[..], and his wife Katherina sell to a man whose name is not read and '[..]alenen' his wife the Baurecht of a holding at Ögsten (Östen, Umhausen) in the Ötztal, Gericht St. Petersberg, held of an abbey that the archivist's typed slip names as Chiemsee (Frauenchiemsee). Neighbours named include Clement Walser and, with a query, a Frischmann. Dated St Genevieve's day (3 January) 152[.].
content.remarks: The last digit of the year is not read; the pencilled 152(5?) is modern. A modern label says the sheet was until 1966 the cover of P. Paul Gay, Explicatio in Danielem Prophetam.

identification: Breviary, eight-lesson nocturns: Kings lessons for Sundays after Pentecost (1 Sam 1:10-17; 3 Kings 1; 'Dominica viii', 3 Kings 8:1-7); Decollation of John the Baptist, lesson ii from Peter Chrysologus, Sermo 127 (PL 52, 549), Gospel Mark 6 and Lauds and hours antiphons; Nativity of the Virgin, lessons v-viii from Ps.-Augustine, Sermo 194 (PL 39, 2105-2106), and on the conjugate leaf lessons i-vii from Paschasius Radbertus, Cogitis me §16 (Ps.-Jerome Ep. 9, PL 30, 139-140).
note: A research reader reread the lessons on the page images and compared them with page images of PL 52, cols. 549-550, PL 39, cols. 2105-2106 and PL 30, cols. 139-140. The reader also looked up the chants (Herodes enim tenuit, Misso Herodes, Puellae saltanti, Gloriosae virginis Mariae ortum, Corde et animo, Regali ex progenie, Montes Gelboe) in Cantus Index. Agreement is sustained. Sermon 194 is abridged for the Office: lesson vii leaves out about twenty printed lines. The Cogitis me lessons adapt the letter's address and run through §16 from recto to verso; a second research reader read the verso before opening PL 30 and matched it in sequence. They read que quasi for PL in qua velut. Several faded, stripped or overwritten pages were not read, and the Kings lessons were not collated against an edition. Eight lessons in the first two nocturns and the Gospel written out after Matins fit monastic, probably Cistercian, use; that is inference, not tested against a Cistercian breviary.

identification: Guillelmus Durantis, Repertorium aureum iuris canonici (Breviarium aureum), book I: end of De electione, De translatione, De auctoritate et usu pallii, De renunciatione, De supplenda negligentia prelatorum, opening of De temporibus ordinationum (X 1.6-1.11); Paris 1513 edition, fol. xvi verso - xix recto
note: A research reader reread the recto's right column and the top of the verso's left column on the native images and compared five passages with page images of the Paris 1513 edition (Munich, BSB): they agree in wording and order, among them 'An soli pape liceat compellere aliquem dimittere', 'vide in nostro speculo' and the opening 'An restituendus sit qui dolo aduersarii renunciat'. The five red title headings and the initial under each agree with the edition, including its combined heading 'De temporibus ordinationum et de etate et qualitate'. The leaf is badly abraded: the recto's left column, the lower third of both sides and the body of the verso's right column were not compared, and most words were read with the edition open. Only one printed edition was used; an abridged form of the work is not excluded.

identification: Abridged German (Bavarian-Austrian) excerpts from the sermons printed as Berthold von Regensburg's in Pfeiffer-Strobl vol. 2 (1880): strip 2 has LX (229,20-231,31, running 2v then 2r); leaf 1 has LIX (shame in confession, 223,35-224,6) followed after a red rule by LXI 'Von den siben planeten' (234,26 to the close, 237,16), running 1v then 1r. The abridgement and the book it comes from are not identified.
note: Both pieces were read at native size and compared with Strobl's text (archive.org OCR): line ends and beginnings of the strip follow LX through the three torments and the six murderers, and leaf 1 follows LIX and LXI in sustained wording, with heavy cuts. The fragment has four passages or readings that Strobl records only from Karlsruhe, Cod. Donaueschingen 292 (two confirmed on that manuscript's page images, fol. 14r and 17r; one of them, on Mary forgiving, stands in Latin on the fragment), but in the Saturn section it twice has the edition's wording where that manuscript differs. LX does not stand between LIX and LXI as it does in the full collection, and the strip's LX piece is followed by a piece beginning 'Es sind etliche', not placed. No other copy of the abridgement was found: Innsbruck ULB Frg. 32 and Cod. 380 fol. 138r are other sermons; Admont Cod. 784 (a 'Siben stern' piece at fol. 28rb, known from a 1927 incipit list) and Klosterneuburg Cod. 886 could not be read because manuscripta.at was unavailable, and Richter 1969 was not consulted.

content.remarks: Several additions otherwise recorded only from Karlsruhe, Cod. Donaueschingen 292 are present, one of them in Latin (quia beata virgo Iudeis indulsit ...); in other places the wording is that of the edition against that manuscript. The abridgement and its parent collection are not identified.

identification: Notarial instrument: Martin Eisengrein, papal protonotary and count palatine, legitimates Johannes Vel(t)mair, son of the unmarried Wolfgang Vel(t)mair, under an inserted legatine faculty (probably the nuncio Zaccaria Delfino's, Pius IV year 6?); Ingolstadt, notary Johannes Elsner; year lost, probably 1565
note: The regest is read on the image: issuer Martin Eisengrein (display capitals EISENGREI[N]), protonotary of the Holy See and count palatine; beneficiary [Jo]hannes Velmair (second occurrence possibly Veltmair), son of 'Wolffgango ... soluto'; legitimation for inheritance and offices by a faculty addressed 'dilecto nobis in Christo Martino E[...]' by an envoy 'cum potestate Legati de latere' at the court of 'Maximilianum Romanorum'; given at Ingolstadt in Eisengrein's residence in the afternoon; witnesses Eustachius St[...] and Michael Aurbach, clerics; notary Johannes Elsner of Silesia, Wroclaw diocese, with his sign. The instrument's own year, day and month are lost at the cut right edge; the inserted faculty is dated at a damaged fold, read with doubt as Pius IV 'anno sexto' (1565), so 1565 is likely but supplied, and the grantor is probably Zaccaria Delfino (word 'Ph[arensis]'), though Pastor dates Delfino's appointment of Eisengrein as protonotary to 1563. A fresh reader given neutral crops confirmed the issuer, the place and hour, Maximilian, the legatine clause, the address to Martin E., 'Wolffgango ... soluto', the notary's name and sign and the witness Michael Aurbach; it read the surname as 'Velmair' and the second witness as 'Sta[...]', and could not read the fold line. No record of the legitimation was found (Google Books, MDZ, Internet Archive searched); no human review.

content.title: Notarial instrument of legitimation
content.persons: Martin Eisengrein; Johannes Velmair; Wolfgang Velmair; Zaccaria Delfino (?); Johannes Elsner
content.description: Martin Eisengrein, protonotary of the Holy See and count palatine, legitimates Johannes Vel(t)mair, son of the unmarried Wolfgang Vel(t)mair, under an inserted legatine faculty, probably of the nuncio Zaccaria Delfino (Pius IV, year 6?). Ingolstadt, in Eisengrein's residence; notary Johannes Elsner of Silesia. Year lost, probably 1565.

identification: Jacobus de Voragine, Legenda aurea, one bifolium: opening of Francis (cap. 149) and end of Dionysius, Calixtus, opening of Leonard (caps. 153-155), Graesse 1850 pp. 662-665, 685-688; pasted over with printed waste of Peter Lombard's Sentences with Henricus de Gorinchem's conclusions (Basel: Nicolaus Kesler, 19 February 1492)
note: A research reader reread about 50 lines on both leaves and compared them with Graesse on page images (pp. 662-663, 687-688) and OCR (pp. 664-665, 685-686): sustained agreement, with two eye-skips supplied in the margin by a corrector, five reasons for Francis's name in the main text where Graesse has seven (the corrector adds the other two in the margin), and readings such as 'cum multis' for 'cum militibus'. From the same manuscript as F-n2rx (Frg. 219), confirmed by a Fragmentarium editor: same line spacing (about 7.2 mm), text block, script, rubrication and sewing stations, and its text falls before and after F-n2rx's Francis/Dionysius bifolium. A second research reader confirmed lines 12-27 of the Francis page against Graesse p. 663 on the page image. The printed sheets are Lombard's Sentences with Gorinchem's conclusions from Kesler's edition of 19 February 1492 (GW M32486), named by a Fragmentarium editor and confirmed on the Lisbon copy (BNP inc. 56): the distinction 1 piece agrees line for line, including the readings that set aside the 1489 printing; the turned-in strips are Legenda aurea caps. 125 and 131, possibly from another copy. The version of the Legenda aurea remains open.

identification: Latin preaching compilation (unidentified): sermon 'de animabus' on 2 Macc 12:46 and notabilia; sources a distinction on sinners as in Nicolaus de Gorran on Eph 2:2 ('Quidam stant qui a futuris abstinent'), Honorius Augustodunensis, Speculum ecclesiae, Dominica II in Quadragesima (panther moralisation, PL 172, 887) and the seven words from the cross as in Hugh Ripelin, Compendium theologicae veritatis IV.21 (ascribed in the MS to Bernard)
note: Face 1 opens with 'quidam stant qui a futuris abstinent sed de preteritis non satisfaciunt', with Matt 20:6 and Ps 37:12 as proof-texts, as printed in Nicolaus de Gorran's postil on Eph 2:2 (page image of the 1692 edition, p. 459); the same distinction is reused by Nicolaus de Plove, so the compiler's direct source is open. The rubricated Sermo de animabus that follows ('Sancta ergo et salubris est cogitatio') divides its text as useful 'nobis ad tria et animabus ad tria', the first point being that the souls make complaint before Christ against heirs who do not help them; no search (Schneyer, MDZ, Google Books, Internet Archive, CoMMA, German manuscript catalogues) found it. Face 2 paraphrases Honorius' moralised panther (page image of PL 172, col. 887) and gives the seven words from the cross with seven lessons in the order of the Compendium theologicae veritatis IV.21, ascribed to Bernard. Pieces 102-3 and 102-4 of Stams Frg. 102 (F-vujo) are in a similar hand, scale and column width and may come from the same manuscript; this is a candidate from photographs, not an established join.

content.title: Sermo de animabus on 2 Macc 12:46, with notabilia

Inc.: Sancta ergo et salubris est cogitatio ... His verbis ... Nota quod nobis et animabus illud est utile et salubre. Nobis quia ad tria et animabus quia ad tria. Other face: the moralised panther after Honorius Augustodunensis, Speculum ecclesiae, Dominica II in Quadragesima, and the seven words from the cross with their seven lessons as in Hugh Ripelin, Compendium theologicae veritatis IV.21, here ascribed to Bernard.
content.remarks: The sermon and the compilation are not identified. Possibly from the same manuscript as Stams, Frg. 102, pieces 3 and 4 (similar hand and column width; not verified on the originals).

identification: Deed of exchange: Cristan Platter auf dem Haunoldt gives his share of the Haunoldt farm, inherited from his late father Thoman Platter and owing ground rent to Stams abbey, to the married couple Sebastian Kurtz and A[...] for their holding and a balancing sum, with Stams consenting as ground lord; 17 June, year lost (probably sixteenth century), place and court district lost
note: The regest is read on the image: issuer Cristan Platter 'Auf dem Haunoldt', the married couple ('Eewirtleut') Sebastian Kurtz and A[...], the exchange of Platter's share of the Haunoldt farm inherited from Thoman Platter, the reserved ground rents and consent of Stams abbey, a balancing sum in gulden 'zu Dreyssig kreitzer' of Tyrolean currency, and the dating clause 'den Sibenzehenden tag Monats Junij' (17 June). The year, the amount, the court district, the wife's name and the sealer's name are lost at the cut right edge. The hand and the gulden-kreuzer reckoning fit the sixteenth century; the sheet was later reused as the cover of a Stams office register labelled 'Ao 92', probably 1592, but the date of that binding is unknown, so it does not date the deed. A fresh reader given neutral crops confirmed Cristan Platter, 'Auf dem Haunoldt', Thoman Platter, 'Gotshaus [St]ambs' with 'Grundtzinsen', Sebastian Kurtz, the currency phrase, the day and month; a research reader reread the back heading as '[Ke]llerambts Vrbar Ao 92'. A Cristan and a Thoman Platter, smiths at Ötz, and a Sebastian Kurz, headman of Mötz, appear in printed sources (snippets only) and may be the parties; no record of the act was found (monasterium.net Stams regests, Google Books, Internet Archive searched); no human review.

content.title: Deed of exchange of Cristan Platter auf dem Haunoldt

content.description: Cristan Platter auf dem Haunoldt exchanges his share of the Haunoldt farm, inherited from his late father Thoman Platter, with the married couple Sebastian Kurtz and A[...] for their holding and a balancing sum in gulden. The ground rents of Stams Abbey are reserved and the abbey consents as ground lord. Dated 17 June; the year, the place and the court district are lost.

identification: Jacobus de Voragine, Legenda aurea, cap. 159 (Simon and Jude, end) and cap. 162 (All Saints, rubric and opening), Graesse 1850 pp. 709-711, 718
note: Four strips of one two-column leaf. A research reader compared the recto's first column (Simon to the advocates and the sign of the cross) with the page image of Graesse p. 709, and the verso's second column (the closing notice on Simon citing Eusebius, Bede and Beleth) with the page image of p. 711; the other two columns and the All Saints opening (p. 718) were compared with OCR text only. The typed archival slip on canvas 0 had already named the feast (ss. Simon and Jude) and transcribed the verso's second column, without naming the work. The copy goes straight from Simon and Jude to All Saints without Quintin and Eustace, ends Simon and Jude with a short '[..]artiu[m]? adeptus est' in place of the Trajan/Atticus and 'Nonnulli' passages, largely omits the apostles' reply to the angel at Samir, and reads 'cum beatus Symon apostolus', 'fuisse no[..]' and 'potestis'; the version is not determined. The catalogue's r/v labels are reversed, the narrow crumpled strips are largely unread, and the leaf is not from the same manuscript as F-n2rx (one column, Eustace before All Saints) or F-c7me (one column at about 7.2 mm line pitch against two columns at about 4.8 mm). An independent check read the recto's second-column line-beginnings and the verso's first-column line-ends against page images of Graesse pp. 709-710 and confirmed the identification and leaf order.

identification: Missal, sanctorale from Barbara (4 December) to Placidus (5 October), Masses placed by feast; Augsburg saints and Benedictine features, use by inference only; ownership note of Benediktbeuern
note: The pieces give the Mass propers of a fifteenth-century manuscript missal sanctorale in calendar order, ending after Placidus with 'Reliqua vide in fine libri'. A blank page carries the note 'Presens Missale pertinet ad Monasterium Benedict(en)pewren' (Benediktbeuern, diocese of Augsburg). A research reader compared the Ulrich, Afra and Hilaria Masses with the Missale Augustanum of 1491 on page images: the Ulrich collect (apart from 'atque pontificis' for 'gloriosi') and the Hilaria secret agree, and the words struck through after that secret open the 1491 postcommunion. Most other chants, readings and prayers differ. A second research reader found all three Petronilla prayers different from the 1491 print (the leaf uses common-of-a-virgin prayers). So the leaves are not a copy of the Augsburg diocesan missal. The Augsburg saints (Ulrich, Afra, Hilaria, Magnus, Willibald, Emmeram, Castulus) and the monastic items (Maurus, Romanus, Placidus, commemorations of St Benedict after 11 July) point to a book of the Augsburg region with Benedictine features, but the use is inference only. Pages 6-19 rest mostly on the image-only reading, and the binding strips 98_1 and 98_2 are illegible.

content.title: Missal, sanctorale
content.description: Masses from Barbara (4 December) to Placidus (5 October), ending 'Reliqua vide in fine libri'.

Not the Missale Augustanum of 1491, with which the Ulrich collect and the Hilaria secret agree. Strips 98_1 and 98_2 illegible.

identification: Office lessons from the Vulgate, 1 Samuel (1 Kings) 7:9-15 (lessons ii-iii of one day) and 8:14-9:1 (with 'Feria quarta L. I' at 8:22)
note: A research reader read all 33 lines of both faces on the native images and compared them with page images of the Rome critical Vulgate, vol. V, pp. 102-106, with its apparatus; the text agrees word for word apart from attested variants ('bellum', 'filii Israel', 'samuelis', 'liberavitque'), two unrecorded ones (7:9 omits 'integrum'; 8:16 'optimos iuvenes') and the lesson opening at 8:22 adapted to 'Dixit ergo Dominus ad Samuelem: Audi vocem populi'. The text missing between the faces fills about two columns, so the strip is probably the gutter column of a two-column leaf and the r/v labels run against the text order. Placement in an early week of the post-Pentecost Kings series (Tuesday-Wednesday) and a secular rather than monastic office are inferences only; no lectionary of known use was compared, and no person has reviewed the reading.

identification: Breviary (secular cursus), sanctorale: offices for 1-14 (probably 15) September (Verena, Giles (abridged Vita S. Aegidii, BHL 93, as lessons), octave of Augustine, Nativity of Mary, Protus and Hyacinthus, Exaltation of the Cross, Cornelius and Cyprian) and 1-8 November (All Saints with Augustine, De sermone Domini in monte I.1, as Matins homily; All Souls; Eustachius; Leonhard; Willibrord; Quattuor Coronati); use undetermined
note: Six laid-paper binding pieces from a 1625 urbar carry Office chants, chapters, collects, Matins lessons and rubrics for September and November saints' days. A research reader reread every face on the native images. The All Saints third nocturn (antiphons Cantus 5151, 2390, 1594, Gospel Matt 5:1-3, Augustine homily) was checked against Cantus and against a page image of PL 34, col. 1229; the homily omits 'sicut in Evangelio secundum Matthaeum legimus'. An independent checker collated the Giles lessons (4r lines 1-17) with the Vita S. Aegidii (BHL 93) §§3-4 on the page image of Jones 1914, p. 100: they are abridged, read 'oratione sua' for 'fusa', and begin lesson ii at 'Die vero dominica'. The collects were checked against the Gregorian sacramentary in transcription and an Acta Sanctorum snippet; the Leonhard collect 'Deus qui largiflua', one Exaltation prayer, the 5v Nativity homily, the 3r lesson and piece 6 are unlocated, and 15 September is probable only. The use is not determined: three-lesson nocturns point to a secular breviary, and the octave of Augustine and Verena suggest a south German or Alpine, possibly Augustinian-canon book, which is untested.

identification: Noted breviary, probably of secular cursus (Office with neumes; probably the central bifolium of a gathering): 1 January (Matins end with Bede, Hom. evang. I.11 = PL 94 col. 54; Lauds, Hours, Vespers), ferial chapters before the Epiphany, Epiphany first Vespers, Compline and Matins nocturn I (Isa 55:1-2+55:12-56:2, 60:8-15, 61:10)
note: A research reader reread all eight columns on the native images. The 1 January lessons agree word for word with Bede, Hom. I.11, in PL 94 col. 54B-D (page image), over two passages in different columns. The Isaiah lessons were compared with the Vulgate in archive.org OCR text; a second research reader independently collated Isa 60:8-15 on a page image of the Clementine Vulgate (Hetzenauer 1914) and found 60:12 'quod servierit tibi peribit' without 'non' and 60:15 'qui te pertransiret' (word order), both confirmed on the image. The chants were compared with Cantus Index standard texts and inventories. The three-antiphon first nocturn (19 Cantus inventories go straight to the versicle, 52 add a fourth antiphon) suggests a secular cursus; the rare None antiphon Circumcisus est dominus (Cantus 001807, 11 south German, Swiss, Austrian and Bohemian entries, ten at Matins) has its one secular witness, an Augsburg Cathedral antiphoner-breviary of c. 1580, at None as here. Use, region and the central-bifolium leaf order are inferences; the Hereford Breviary comparison was OCR only, no person has reviewed the reading, and the catalogue date 1000-1099 was not tested.

identification: Unidentified German sermons: an exposition of Proverbs 6:16-19 ending on detraction, the Pater noster as a ladder of seven rungs, the Purification, and Beelzebub as 'vir muscarum'
note: Two paper leaves of a 15th-century German sermon collection in two columns, East Swabian / West Bavarian, Latin quotations underlined. 163-1 holds the end of an exposition of Proverbs 6:16-19 closing on detraction ('Et notandum quod detractio fit quadrupliciter'), then a Pater noster sermon in which the ladder's two poles carry seven rungs, the seven petitions; 163-2 holds a Purification sermon and a piece on Beelzebub that quotes the Glossa ordinaria on Luke 11:15 and moralises the fly as the proud, the greedy and the unclean. Searches of Schönbach's Altdeutsche Predigten I-III, Grieshaber, Roth, Jeitteles, Wackernagel, Berthold von Regensburg and Kelle's Speculum ecclesiae (in-volume OCR search), and of Google Books, Internet Archive, MDZ, Corpus Corporum and the Handschriftenportal, found no source. The Pater noster exposition as a ladder of seven rungs in Berlin, Staatsbibliothek, Ms. germ. oct. 449, ff. 84r-115r (about 1400, Bavarian) is untested because no digitisation is listed.

content.description: 163-2v: the offering of two turtle doves, the dove's two properties, Simeon 'an disem tage', 'Fasciculus mirre dilectus meus'. 163-2r: the idol's temple and the flies on its altar, 'Judei autem vnius dei cultores in derisionem gentilium belzebub appellabant ... vir muscarum sive habens muscas', and the fly's three properties.

identification: Matthias Burgklehner, Die Fürstliche Grafschafft Tirol, 12-sheet wall map, copperplate engraved by Andreas Spängler: three pieces from at least two impressions of the east-central sheet (Lienz, Puster valley, Cadore, 'Inhalt der Tirolischen Landtafel'), from the plate of 1629, impression date unknown; offset on the backs unidentified
note: The engraved lettering, symbols and hatching agree with the same sheet of BSB Mapp. IX,205 e (image 22) in ten areas compared side by side on page images: five by a research reader (the table, Lienz, Rosenberger, St Mark lion and Venedig cartouche, Ritterpurg cartouche) and five by an independent checker who read them on the Stams images before opening the copy (Puster valley west and east, Ampezzo and Cadore, the graduated border with the plate's 'XXXXVI', the Drau and Gail edge). Pieces 2 and 3 repeat areas of piece 1, so at least two impressions are present; the village figure is 894. The date 1629 is the copperplate edition's, per the BSB catalogue and Brunner (2002); no date is on the pieces, and with the plates surviving and one exemplar compared, the impression date and state are untested. The pencil notes on the backs (dates read 1633 and possibly 1744) and 'aus Hs 287' / 'Hs 308' point to reuse as binding waste at a date that is open; the mirror offset of a two-column Latin gothic text on the backs is unidentified. No human review.

identification: Missal (probably Cistercian): proper prefaces and Communicantes of Christmas and Epiphany; end of the Ordo missae (Corpus/Sanguis custodiat me, Placeat, Meritis et precibus); Sanctus end and Agnus Dei
note: A research reader read every page on the images and collated the prefaces, Communicantes and post-communion section with page images of the Cistercian missal Fribourg BCU L 305 (ff. 138r-v, 144v) and the Missale Romanum, Milan 1474 (pp. 202, 210-211); an independent checker reread the Sanctus/Agnus page and compared the Agnus Dei with L 305 f. 144r on its page image. The leaf runs from Corpus and Sanguis 'custodiat me' straight to the Placeat and 'Meritis et precibus', as L 305 does and the Roman print does not, but it differs from L 305 in small readings ('genitricis eiusdem dei', 'nostre' omitted). The use is probably Cistercian (medium): a 'Meritis et intercessionibus' blessing and 'custodiat me' also occur in Salzburg-province and other German diocesan books (Seckau, Brenner's codex), so the features pointing to Cistercian use, not shown to be exclusive, are the 'precibus' wording and the absence of ablution prayers; the printed Augsburg order of 1510/1555 (Hoeynck) differs, but no medieval Augsburg missal and no Brixen, Salzburg, Freising or Benedictine missal was checked and the Carthusian use is untested. The second Sanctus and Agnus after the Meritis blessing are unexplained, the order of the two leaves is inference, and the faint prayer after the Agnus is unidentified.

The face pencilled 1v carries the red folio number cxvij, so it was the original recto, and 'Ad Romanos' follows Eph 2:22 directly, so Eph 4:7-13 is absent on direct reading. The use is not identified: it is not the Roman use of the 1474 print ('concede propicius' for 'presta quesumus', a different epistle series and different one-apostle orations), and the Cistercian missal of Kaisheim (Clm 7901, 1531) differs in its readings for apostles. note: The catalogue's 'Bill's notes' already named the feast (Visitation) and the antiphons Transivit in itinere (204950) and Longam viam (202933) on one face; the research identified the office and the other faces. A research reader read every inked line on the images and collated it with the page image of the Breviarium Romanum c. 1481 (BSB bsb00048874, scan 114) and the chants with the Cantus inventory of Utrecht 406; an independent checker read the faded lesson on slips 1r and 2v on the image and found it the same as the print, apart from the apparent omission of 'collaudabat Ierusalem' and 'cupiebat · Noluit' running on. The lesson text differs from the 1481 Roman breviary, where 'Abiit igitur' and 'Noluit' open lessons v and vi and Maria parens follows lesson iv, Cum igitur angelus. The readings 'prospere' and 'temptavit' agree with the catalogue note and so are not independent of it. Cistercian use is only consistent with the evidence: Analecta hymnica 24 lists a Cistercian breviary, Prague XIII A 5 b, to which the office was added, but its lessons were not compared.

identification: Bavarian-Austrian German feast-day sermons, unidentified: an Ascension sermon with a Latin protheme and three reasons for the Ascension (piece 1), and a Marian sermon, most likely for the Assumption (pieces 3 and 2), which quotes in German, probably, Anselm of Canterbury's prayer to Mary ('angelos vincis puritate'), and certainly Bernard of Clairvaux, In assumptione B. V. Mariae ('Quantum enim gratiae in terris') and Ps.-Augustine ('Si coelum te vocem, altior es')
note: Five paper pieces of a fifteenth-century sermon book. Piece 1 (running 1v then 1r) has an Ascension Day sermon: a Latin protheme ending in the Ave Maria, the thema given in German as 'Jhesus Christus ist auff gevaren in die hoch', three reasons for the Ascension (Jn 14:6, 14:2, 16:7 and 13) and a scheme of three kinds of truth; the preacher says he has already spoken before 'mein herren' and now speaks 'ze tewsch' to 'lieben brueder'. Piece 3 opens a Marian sermon under a Latin heading ending '... ne B. Marie' and names Anselm; piece 2 renders three authorities in sequence, matched against Corpus Corporum transcriptions (Bernard and Ps.-Augustine secure, Anselm likely, one word unread). These are quoted sources, not the sermons: the German Assumption sermon of Munich, BSB, Cgm 230, fol. 174r-183v, was read in full on page images and is a different text, and searches of the German wording and of the Latin protheme found nothing. Latin sermon books of Stams origin now at Innsbruck (ULB Tirol, Cod. 739, 613, 602, 443) were not opened, and manuscripta.at was unavailable.

identification: Two manuscripts. Items 81_1-2 (hand 1): anonymous Tractatus passionis 'Scitis quia post biduum' (ed. Ferber 1935), on the arrest, the bloody sweat, the crucifixion outside the gate, Christ's age and the vinegar and gall. Hand 2: Antonius Rampegolus, Figurae Bibliae, in 81_7r (Humilitas, figura of A), 81_8r (Fides, end of A, B Docet manus meas ad prelium, opening of C), 81_9 (Religiosi, end of A and B, Expoliavi me tunica mea), 81_10r (Perseverantia, B, figura of Apoc. 1, to Exibit homo) and 81_11v (Diabolus, D, Sinite parvulos); items 81_3 and 81_4-6 and the faces 81_7v, 81_10v and 81_11r not identified
note: Hand 1: five passages on both faces of items 81_1 and 81_2 agree in argument, order and authorities with the commentary in Clm 2941 on page images, four collated by a research reader and 81_2r col. B by an independent checker who read it on the image before opening the source; the Stams copy has wording variants and two places of different content (a Bernard quotation on 81_2v, a note on 'Quem queritis' on 81_2r), a different redaction or copy, and Ferber's edition was not seen. Hand 2: 81_9v was collated by a research reader with the Paris 1510 print (scans 345-346, Religiosi), and an independent checker collated on page images 81_10r with scan 326 (Perseverantia), 81_8r with scans 160-161 (Fides B-C, where 'Docet manus meas ad prelium' is a lemma at scan 160 col. a) and Clm 14376 images 91-92, 81_11v with scan 129 (Diabolus D) and Clm 14376 image 72 col. b, and 81_7r with scan 189 (Humilitas). A complete CoMMA search (one batched pass, 1 November 2026) found Clm 14376 and BnF NAL 337 for 81_8r and nothing above chance for the short passages of 81_4 and 81_6. The fragment agrees with Clm 14376 against the print in some readings (insuetus, artis bellice, dum leduntur ... totus perditur fructus) and with the print against Clm in others (in pugna, Jo(b). In arte, eos vias), so its text follows neither throughout. Items 81_4-6, 81_7v, 81_10v and 81_11r are in the same hand but unplaced (81_5 too fragmentary to search), item 81_3 is unread, NAL 337 was not seen on images, the material (paper per the catalogue) was not checked, and there is no human review.

Other differences include 'spiritus' and 'rana et' omitted, 'mors pecori', and the clause 'quando tabernaculum ... colebatur; cum' left out, probably by eye-skip; about 17-25 lines are lost per column at head and foot. The modern blue marginal note ('Manuale' struck out, 'Officia propria Brixinensis, Brixen 1673') names the printed host volume, not the text; the host copy was not checked. Date, origin and textual affiliation were not examined, and Dombart-Kalb (CCSL 47-48) was not consulted.

identification: Peter Comestor, Sermones: end of Sermo XIV, In dominica Laetare (PL 198:1763-1764), and the Palm Sunday sermon Apprehendent septem mulieres (Comestor's Sermo XV in PL 198; printed among Hildebert's works, PL 171:475-476), under the rubric 'Sermo Manduc(atoris)'
note: A research reader collated four columns on two faces with page images of PL 198, cols. 1761-1764, and PL 171, cols. 475-476: the fourth and sixth temptations and the explicit of Sermo XIV, then the theme and an early passage of the Palm Sunday sermon, in the printed order; PL 198 lists that sermon as Comestor's Sermo XV directly after XIV, Soissons BM 131 (Comestor, Sermones) has the same sequence, and Schneyer (seen only as OCR text) cross-refers it to Comestor. An independent checker read the rubric at x4 as 'Sermo Manduc'' (expansion editorial) and confirmed on page images that face B middle column lines 6-7, 'Ebdomade(s) veteris t(estamenti) octava(m) app(re)hend(en)t noui' ('noui' moderate confidence) before 'uigilanter dic(it)', is in Soissons 131 f. 8v col. a (ending 'apprehendunt unam') and absent from PL 171 col. 476, where the fragment's 'Unum sane' also stands against PL's 'Unde [f. quod] sane'; four other manuscripts read 'novi' in CoMMA's machine transcription only. Soissons 131 runs parallel to PL 198:1764 and fills the fragment's columns evenly, so the spacing needs no fuller text; the copy also adds a doxology to Sermo XIV and extends the Palm Sunday theme. The two outer blocks of line-ends and line-beginnings match neither PL nor a complete CoMMA search, but have too few searchable words for the misses to mean anything. The catalogue joins this strip with Frg. 142 (F-vjii) in reconstruction F-dr4l, which is not public; same scale, line pitch, column width, hand and rubric style make one manuscript plausible, not proven; no human review.

identification: Gallican psalter (Psalterium Gallicanum), Psalms 36:40-37:9 (recto) and 37:12-20 (verso), two horizontal strips from one leaf; the strip-2 recto/verso labels are the reverse of the leaf's
note: A research reader reread all 28 lines and compared them with the Stuttgart Vulgate's Gallican text (online transcription) and the Roman psalter of the Eadwine Psalter (OCR): the strips agree with the Gallican wherever it differs from the Roman ('supergresse', 'Putruerunt', 'lumbi mei impleti sunt', 'redargutiones', 'nequando', 'in flagella'), and the Ambrosian psalter is excluded at 37:8. An independent checker reread the 14 lines of canvas 1 (boxes 3100,1350,1600,670 and 3100,2580,1650,660) before opening a source and compared them with the Gallican and Roman psalters of PL 28 cols. 183-186 on page images, confirming the Gallican text and finding that 37:7 omits 'sum' after 'Miser factus' on an undamaged line. Words broken across the cut ('super|gresse', 'exau|dies'), the tail of a red Q cut through between the strips, and marginal writing that runs on from one face to the other show that the faces labelled 1r and 2v make one side of the leaf, the recto, and 1v and 2r the verso, so strip 2's labels are the reverse of the leaf's. The faded marginal writing is unread, Jerome's Hebrew psalter was not checked, and whether the book was a psalter or an office book, its date and its origin are not established.

identification: Nikolaus Herman, Haußhaltung (verse rendering of Johannes Mathesius, Oeconomia; printed as 'Haußhaltung Johannis Mathesij', Nürnberg 1561), from 'Haußsorg das ist ein schwere last' to 'Versamlet vnd bstetigt zur erd', abridged; preceded by an unidentified German verse paraphrase of Psalm 128
note: Section 2 agrees in sustained wording and sequence with the 1561 Nürnberg print (VD16 M 1419), collated by a research reader on BSB page images (bsb10203350, scans 11-15) over more than twenty-five verses and by a second research reader over fifteen further manuscript lines, read before opening the print at those places. The copy is abridged (by the copyist or in an exemplar, not known): 10 verses on servants, 32 widower verses and 10 deathbed verses are omitted, and the 8 verses on making a will are replaced by a text not found in the editions searched in the MDZ full text, with 'Gotes gnad'; 'Saul war' is 'Sanct Mar[tins]' and 'er thuen doch als' is '[vns]er thuen doch als', both print verses. Herman's authorship rests on Mathesius's 1564 preface, seen in the 1796 reprint (bsb11260410, scan 8); the exemplar edition is unknown. Section 1, a Psalm 128 paraphrase ending '... Amen' then 'denn es war[..]', shares two verses with Luther's 'Wol dem der in Gottes furcht steht' but is not placed (Vehe 1537 excluded; Hans Sachs and Ulenberg untested). The back has modern notes 'Urbari Wessobrunn 1594' and '1595'; no human review.

note: A research reader collated three passages (35_2v, 35_1v, 35_1r) on the images with page images of Paris, BnF, lat. 14174, fol. 22r, where the same tables stand unattributed: they agree in wording, sequence and table layout. identification: Missal (probably Cistercian): end of the Ordo missae from the Libera nos embolism to Meritis et precibus; a Mass of the Visitation(?) added in a later hand
note: The catalogue's r/v labels are reversed: the face pencilled 69v is the recto. A research reader read the main text on the images and collated it with page images of the Cistercian missal Fribourg BCU L 305 (ff. 144r-v) and the Missale Romanum, Milan 1474 (pp. 210-211): the commixtio after the Agnus in the 'promerendam et capessendam' form, 'libera me queso', 'custodiat me' straight to the Placeat, and 'Meritis et precibus' agree with L 305 and not with the Roman print, with small differences ('Et cum spiritu tuo', 'dominus'). The use is probably Cistercian (medium): a 'Meritis et intercessionibus' blessing and 'custodiat me' also occur in Salzburg-province and other German diocesan books (Seckau, Brenner's codex), so the features pointing to Cistercian use, not shown to be exclusive, are the 'precibus' wording, Corpus/Sanguis straight to the Placeat, and the commixtio after the Agnus; the printed Augsburg order of 1510/1555 (Hoeynck) differs, but no medieval Augsburg missal and no Brixen, Salzburg, Freising or Benedictine missal was checked and the Carthusian use is untested. An independent checker read the added small-hand Mass on the image and compared it with the Visitation Mass of the 1474 print (vol. 2, p. 208) on its page image: the collect ('elizabet inspirasti', probable reading) and the Song of Songs lesson fit, so a Visitation Mass added in a later hand is likely, but the feast word is illegible.

identification: Grant of a heritable holding, issued at Stams under the issuer's own seal (issuer's name lost; probably the abbot of Stams): [property lost] to [tenant lost] and his heirs, with compensation for improvements, the issuer's right of first purchase, and rent and rights reserved; St Bartholomew's day (24 August), year lost
note: The lower part of a German deed (item 166_1) is read on the image: the grant 'den wir(?) im(?) vnd allen seinen erben geben', improvements ('mit pessrung'), the right of first purchase, 'zins vnd recht allwegen vorbehalten', sealing with 'aigen anhangendem insigel', and the dating clause 'Geben zu Stams in dem Jar als man zalt nach Cristi vnser[...] [..]are(?) an sant Bartholmes des hailigen zwelfpoten tag'. The year, the issuer's name, the tenant and the property are lost, so the result is partial. The sealing and dating formula matches that of an original grant by abbot Georg of Stams dated St Bartholomew's day 1467 (Stiftsarchiv Stams, Urkunden L V 2), and the clauses follow those of three leases of the same abbot of 1467 copied in Urkunden O XIX 17 (both compared on the images); these are different acts, and they suggest, without dating the fragment, the lease formulary of the Stams abbots of the later fifteenth century and a loss of perhaps a third to two fifths of each line at the right. Item 166_2 is a blank parchment strip; no outside record of the act was found among the Stams regests dated on or near 24 August between 1342 and 1540 on monasterium.net.

content.title: Grant of a heritable holding, Stams, St Bartholomew's day
content.description: The issuer (name lost, probably the abbot of Stams) grants a holding to a tenant and his heirs, with compensation for improvements, the issuer's right of first purchase, and rent and rights reserved, and seals with his own pendant seal. Given at Stams on St Bartholomew's day (24 August); the year is lost.
content.remarks: The names of the issuer and tenant and the property are lost with the upper and right-hand parts. The clauses and the sealing and dating formula follow those of leases and grants of abbot Georg of Stams of 1467 (Stiftsarchiv Stams, Urkunden L V 2 and O XIX 17), which are different acts.

Lehen', with the duty to escort the abbot from Finstermünz with six or eight horses; 29th day, month and year lost [1546 or later, probably 1546-1558]
note: The regest is read on the image: the action (fief reverse), the abbot of Stams as lord, the Schrofenstein children (Magdalena, Vo?l/t?iri(?), Margretha) through their named guardians and a Lehenträger, the farm zum Steg at Oberlana, the escort 'Von der Vinstern Müntz vntz auff den Ve/orren(?)' on pain of forfeiture, and 'Beschehen am Neunvnndzwaintzigisten tag'. Two fresh readers, given 21 shuffled neutral crops of this document and of Frg. 166 with no transcription, confirmed Brandis zu Leonburg, Cristoff and Georg Philipp von Schrofenstein, the children's names, Montanj, Fueger and the horses; the coordinator reread every disagreement on the image, leaving the abbot's name unread, the first father's second name as 'Cr[..]ssen(?)', 'Rechtem Lehen' and 'Jaufenburg' probable, and confirming the 29th. The month and year are lost; the window (1546 or later, most likely 1546-1558; 1562-1564 under Maximilian II not excluded, since the wards may still have been minors) is supplied from the royal title and, for its lower bound, from a Google Books snippet on the 1546 extinction of the Schrofenstein male line. No outside record of the act was found (monasterium.net Stams regests, Google Books, MDZ); no human review.

identification: Easter table of 28-year lines beginning in 1353 (solar-cycle rows xxij-xxviij), with its canon: Peter Philomena of Dacia, Canon supra kalendarium ('Quere inter numeros in superiori parte istius tabule'), adapted to the Easter table (example 1380, letter e); with a golden-number rota whose year line reads 1357 (or 1354) and a Tabula paschalis
note: The ten canon lines agree in wording and order with Peter of Dacia's canon on the page image of Clm 3512, fol. 289ra, adapted to this table: the example is 1380 with letter e (Clm: 1311, t), 'littera primacionis' probably becomes 'littera annualis/annalis', and Clm's sentence on second-tier years is absent. The grid is identified by its numbers: in line k, row r the year is 1352 + 28(k-1) + r and the letter codes that year's Julian Easter (a-v from 21 March, punctus right; a-q from 10 April, punctus left); about 90% of some 110 legible cells agree, and line 1, row 28 'e' is Easter 1380, the canon's example. An independent checker read canon lines 5-10 on the image before reopening Clm 3512 (not blind, having read the canon transcription) and read the grid blind before testing it against computed Easter dates. Pedersen's edition was seen only in snippets and no other copy of this adapted canon or table was found; no human review.

identification: Terence, Andria III.5-IV.2 (lines 607-686), manuscript copy of the play text (pieces 3-4)
note: Pieces 3-4 are two nested paper bifolia with a continuous copy of Terence, Andria 607 to about 686, with scene headings and pen initials but no commentary. A research reader collated six pages with page images of Melanchthon's edition (Strasbourg: Knobloch, 1527). An independent reader collated a further page (lines 647-657) against the same print and found no substantive difference. The text has the 16th-century humanist readings (subducere, Factum est hoc, tu aliud reperi, aliquid iam inuenturum, C. scio) and differs from the 1527 print only in small points (no 'etiam' at 644, 'prosim', 'ancila', possibly 'cognoueris'). No single printed exemplar is claimed, and the copy is not dated: the pencil year 1534 refers to the host volume II/6 36. Pieces 1-2 carry German letter-draft pen trials, and pieces 5-9 a Latin-German proverb exercise with letter drafts; these are unidentified.

identification: Unidentified Latin legal commentary citing civil and canon law (14th century?), possibly on a provincial canon on castle chaplains
note: Two strips from a densely abbreviated legal commentary in long lines (14th century?) that alleges civil and canon law ('ff.', 'C.', and 'xviii. di.' twice, Decretum D. 18 on synods) and underlines words of the text it comments on. The words 'ad sinodos ueniant' on one face, with the ordinary, the archdeacon and obedience ('ordinarium archidiaconum(?)', 'obediencie(?)') on the other, possibly point to a commentary on the provincial canon on the chaplains of nobles' castles, 'nisi ante episcopo vel loci archidiacono obedientiam faciant manualem, et ad synodos veniant' (for example in the Mainz provincial statutes of 1310, De maioritate et obedientia, Schannat-Hartzheim, Concilia Germaniae IV; OCR text only). This rests on three words and the subject; the other possible lemma words are uncertain and do not stand in the canon's order, and no commentary on the canon was found to compare. Faded ink at the published resolution allows no connected reading longer than about five words; phrase searches (Google Books, Corpus Corporum) and a batched CoMMA search gave no lead above noise, and better imaging of the underlined lemmata is needed.

content.title: Unidentified legal commentary

content.remarks: 'ad sinodos ueniant' possibly points to a commentary on a provincial canon on castle chaplains (as in the Mainz provincial statutes of 1310, De maioritate et obedientia). Not identified.

identification: Treatise on letter-writing (ars dictandi): kinds of conclusio and the parts a letter may consist of, parallel to Tommasino di Armannino, Microcosmus (ed. Bertoni 1921, pp. 26-27); containing treatise unresolved
note: A paper leaf with a stub, about 148 x 124 mm, with some 24 long lines a face in a faint Gothic cursive. Face v gives kinds of conclusio (Rogativa, Condicionalis, probably Causativa) and then the letters made of two or three parts, with the model petition 'Rogo te quatinus pretermissis omnibus Bononiam ...' and 'non credo epistolam', in the order of Tommasino di Armannino's Microcosmus, in every passage read (or of the fuller work he says he abridged); a research reader compared nine passages with the page images of Bertoni's edition. The wording differs in places (word order, the conditional example, the five parts listed by name), several lines are unread, and face r, which has enlarged words such as 'Per xpm', was not matched to that text. The treatise the leaf comes from is therefore not established.

identification: Two units. Pieces 102-3 and 102-4 (one leaf of a pastoral book, unidentified): Lateran IV c. 21 Omnis utriusque sexus and the monastic chapter De negligentiis on accidents with the chalice and host, as transmitted with Cistercian statutes. Pieces 102-1 and 102-2: rubricated moral texts (rubrics 'De modo vivendi', 'Profundum triplex', 'De tribus dietis') sharing passages with Konrad von Brundelsheim (Soccus), Sermones de tempore, Sermo 33, and with an anonymous sermon for the 12th Sunday after Pentecost in BnF lat. 455, f. 44; containing works unidentified
note: Pieces 102-3 and 102-4, in a Gothic bookhand, are parts of one leaf: one side runs continuously through Lateran IV c. 21 from 'Omnis utriusque sexus' to 'vulneribus sauciati'; the other has 'Istud tamen quod intus cecidit ... et illam ablucionem sacerdos sumat. Quod si de corpore domini in palla ... Quod si infirmo datum reicitur ... eo quod alterius ore', the chapter De negligentiis, compared on the page image of Charleville-Mezieres, BM, Ms. 64, f. 144v-145r, where it stands among Cistercian statutes. The same chapter circulates in Premonstratensian statutes, Benedictine customaries and synodal books, so the fragment's direct source and the book it comes from are not fixed. Pieces 102-1 and 102-2, in a small cursive, share the passage under 'De modo vivendi' with Soccus, Sermo 33 (1484 print, page image), and about ten lines under 'Profundum triplex' with the sermon 'Exiens Iesus ... Si quis beneficia Domini diligenter attendit' in BnF lat. 455 (page image), in each case shorter and with differences; their other faces (few are chosen and the capital sins, ill-gotten goods and heirs, Reuben, Dathan and Abiron, avarice as an incurable sickness) have no source found. Pieces 102-3 and 102-4 resemble Stams Frg. 25 (F-joy1) in hand, scale and column width and may come from the same manuscript; this is a candidate from photographs, not an established join.

content.title: Concilium Lateranense IV, c. 21 Omnis utriusque sexus; De negligentiis (accidents with the chalice and host)
content.description: One leaf in two pieces, Gothic bookhand. One side (102-4r, continued on 102-3v): Omnis utriusque sexus ... vulneribus sauciati. Other side (102-3r): Istud tamen quod intus cecidit prius debet in calice ... Quod si infirmo datum reicitur ... eo quod alterius ore.
content.remarks: The chapter De negligentiis is transmitted with Cistercian statutes (for example Charleville-Mezieres, BM, Ms. 64, f. 144v-145r) and in other monastic and synodal collections. The book these pieces come from is not identified. Possibly from the same manuscript as Stams, Frg. 25 (similar hand and column width; not verified on the originals).

content.title: Moral texts with rubrics, possibly a compilation
content.description: Small cursive. Passages under the rubrics De modo vivendi, Profundum triplex and De tribus dietis, with others on the few who are chosen, the capital sins, ill-gotten goods and heirs, Reuben, Dathan and Abiron, and avarice.
content.remarks: Piece 102-2r shares a passage with Konrad von Brundelsheim (Soccus), Sermones de tempore, sermo 33; piece 102-1r shares a passage with an anonymous sermon for the 12th Sunday after Pentecost, Exiens Iesus, in Paris, BnF, lat. 455, f. 44. In both places the text is shorter and differs in wording. The containing work is not identified.

identification: Nicholas of Lyra, Responsio ad quendam Iudaeum ex verbis Evangelii secundum Matthaeum: end of the reply on Mt 5:44, the objection on the leper (Mt 8) with the start of its reply; other side, end of that reply, the objection on Mt 11:25 (Confiteor) and the sabbath objection and reply (Mt 12)
note: Two joined strips of one two-column leaf. About 48 lines of the first side agree in wording and sequence with Lyra's Responsio, collated by a research reader on the page image of the Venice (Giunta) 1603 glossed Bible, t. 6, cols. 1725-1726. An independent research reader compared a passage not used for the identification, the lower main column and line-ends of the second side, with cols. 1727-1728 of the same edition and found the sixth (Confiteor) and seventh (sabbath) objections in order. The fragment follows Lyra's order and readings ('meruerant', 'dixit curato a demone') where the printed Fortalitium fidei of Alfonso de Spina, which reuses the text, differs; no Fortalitium manuscript was compared. The copy introduces the fifth and sixth objections with an unnumbered 'Item accipit' where the prints have 'Quinto' and 'Sexto', and it has minor wording differences. No manuscript of the Responsio was compared, the second side is matched by anchors only, and the copy's date and origin are not established; no human review.

note: Two pieces of one leaf (a strip and a larger piece on each face, the strips photographed upside down) carry the commentary on Ps 129:3-4 and 6-8 with red-underlined lemmata and red source signs, ending with the red initial of Ps 130. A research reader compared the verse 4 and verse 6 passages with the PL 191 page images (archive.org, cols. 1169-1170) and found agreement in extracts, order and Lombard's own linking phrases. An independent checker compared the lower lines of the canvas 1 piece (Ps 129:7-8 into Ps 130) with the PL page image and confirmed it, adding the word order 'totius peccata [mundi]' and a red 'c' at 'sanguis pretiosus'. Differences include 'Qua spe clamas', 'Unde subdit', 'offerebantur' (all three also in the Glossa ordinaria), 'usquequo moriamur' without 'non', and an ending of verse 8 shorter than PL, where two rubbed lines leave it open whether a closing Cassiodorus sentence was shortened or missing. Compared with the printed edition only. Gilbert of Poitiers' unprinted commentary was not compared, and there is no human review.

note: Strip 257-2 and pieces 3, 4 and 6 are one leaf of a notated antiphoner (piece 4v continues lines of strip 2r: the chant text runs across the junction, though the torn edges do not fit letter to letter). It runs from the end of O crux splendidior and In ferventis olei to the Ascension Magnificat antiphon Pater manifestavi, invitatory and nocturn I, then R. Post passionem (V. Et convescens) and R. Omnis pulchritudo (V. A summo caelo). This is the order of the Klosterneuburg CCl 1018 inventory in the Cantus Database. A research reader compared the readings with Cantus Index texts and that inventory. An independent reader reread strip 2v and found the Post passionem and Omnis pulchritudo text in order on page images of Munich Clm 4306. The ink set off on the wooden board probably reads the same run as strip 2v. Two items after the Magnificat and the invitatory text are unidentified. identification: Commentary on the preposition examples of Donatus, Ars minor ('Ad patrem, apud villam'): senses of 'ad', pater/patro, 'apud', villa/villicus/rusticus; a fuller version of the tract printed with the Nuernberg 1500 Donatus (Hain 6363) and as 'Ad patrem pro iuvenibus' (Leipzig 1516); exact version and author not found
note: A 15th-century cursive paper strip with red-underlined lemmata: the earlier face (catalogued as verso) numbers the senses of 'ad' with examples ('amice ad quid venisti', 'passiones huius temporis ad futuram', 'ad aquilonem') and treats the verb 'patro' ('Patro luxurior'); the later face treats 'apud', then villa, villicus (German 'mayr', 'hoffmaister') and rusticus, ending with the verses 'Rusticus a rure quoniam ...' and 'Dicitur agrestis'. The printed tract on Donatus's examples 'Ad patrem. Apud villam' has the same order of topics, the same examples and the same verses, read on the page images of the Nuernberg 1500 Donatus (scans 65-66) and of 'Ad patrem pro iuvenibus', Leipzig 1516 (scans 3-5); some of the strip's readings ('patro as are', 'Patro luxurior', 'quoniam') were settled with the print in hand. The strip is longer and differently worded (other examples for time and number, a passage on rustic manners with the German words 'pawrn' and 'torpl'(?), Luke 16:1 'qui habebat villicum' quoted as an example for villicus), so its own version is not identified; a CoMMA search found nothing above noise.

content.title: Commentary on the preposition examples of Donatus, Ars minor: 'Ad patrem', 'Apud villam'

Later face: 'apud', then villa, villicus and rusticus, with the German glosses 'mayr', 'hoffmaister', 'pawrn' and the verses 'Rusticus a rure ...', 'Dicitur agrestis ...'.
content.remarks: A fuller and differently worded version of the anonymous tract printed with Donatus, Ars minor (Nuernberg: Hieronymus Hoelzel, 1500; Hain 6363) and as 'Ad patrem pro iuvenibus' (Leipzig 1516). The version on the strip is not identified. Luke 16:1 is quoted as an example for 'villicus'.

note: On the inner side of a paper binding leaf, four verse lines and the commentary of two text blocks follow the Mainz c. 1493 print of Nomina et verba defectiva (GW M13741) in sequence, argument and examples. A research reader compared the first block with the page images of scan 35 (and the Hagenau 1491 print, scan 27) and the lower second block with scan 45. An independent checker compared the upper lines of the second block (impersonal verbs) with the page image of scan 45 and found the same points and examples in the same order, with additional material in the manuscript. The commentary is worded differently throughout and adds a first notandum and examples of impersonals ('interest penitet pudet', 'amatur docetur'), so it is closely related to the printed commentary, not the same text; which way the relation runs is not shown. The first verse line is also Doctrinale v. 339, but the other verses are not in the Doctrinale. Canvas 0, the edge strip and the turn-ins are unread, the Isaiah flap (Is 9:6, 62:3) is identified only as Bible text, and there is no human review.

note: The secret and complenda of SS. Ingenuin and Albuin, patrons of Brixen, agree with the Brixen Mass printed by Resch (1760) from the 14th- and 15th-century Brixen books, read on page images; this probably places the book in the diocese of Brixen, where Stams lay (the formulary was not tested against other dioceses' books), without deciding between diocesan and Cistercian use. A research reader read the larger leaf and the strip and compared the prayers with Resch and the readings with the Vulgate; a second reader compared strip lines (Col 1:9-14, Mt 9:18-22) with the Milan missal of 1474 on page images and found small variants (deo patri, & impone without tuam, duodecim annis, dixit illi). The larger leaf is written on one side only and refers to other folios by Arabic number, so it may be an added leaf of supplementary Masses; the rubric over 1 Cor 10 / Jn 6 is read only probably as Dominica infra octavas corporis Christi. Dorothy texts were seen only as printed-missal snippets, and the cross-reference block is partly unread.

identification: End of a German deed with a convent's seal ('Conuennt Innsigel hierangehanngen'; the words before are lost), possibly of Stams abbey, probably 1538: [parties and object lost] ... a clause on a rent ('Das(?) der Zeinnß absein(?)'); 'Beschehen an [day lost] ... [hund]ert. Vnnd im Achtunddreyssigisten Jare'
note: The lower right corner of a German parchment deed reads '...behalt(e)n ist. Das(?) der Zeinnß absein(?). Vnnd wann(?) diser brief / Conuennt Innsigel hierangehanngen, Beschehen an / [...]ert. Vnnd im Achtunddreyssigisten Jare'; the seal word has C, o, four minims, e, four minims, t, so a convent's seal was attached (a blind reader read 'Co[n]uennt Inn S[g]al'). Script and flourishes resemble an original of Abbot Pelagius of Stams of 25 May 1538 (Stams, Urkunden L_LXXII_7 on monasterium.net, ending '...Funffzehenhundert Vnnd im Achtunddreissigisten Jare'), and a tenant's Revers of 4 June 1538 (Stams, L_XIX_7) has the same hand style and the fragment's own 'hieran gehanngen, Beschehen am'; so the hand gives the date and region, not the issuer (every comparator is from the Stams fonds), and the fragment is probably of 1538 and possibly a Stams deed. The hundreds, the day, the parties and the object are lost and no record of the act was found. Faint lines of an earlier Latin book text (one word read, 'dirige') cross the same face at right angles, so the parchment appears to be reused; the endorsement on the back is not read.

identification: Grant of a peasant fief (Lehenbrief) by the prince-provost of Ellwangen, 'Johann C[...] ... Probst, vnd Herr zu [El]lwangen' (Johann Christoph II von Freyberg-Eisenberg, surname supplied), to [start of name lost] Lutz, probably at Stimpfach near Ellwangen (leaf: 'Lutzen zu Stimpfach(?)'): the whole fief there with house and barn under one roof, meadows and fields, next to land of Wolf Wilhelm von Knöringen zu Rechenberg(?); Ellwangen, 19(?) February 1618
note: The first line reads 'W[ir] Johann C[...] ... Probst, vnd Herr zu [El]lwangen, Bekhennen offentlich mit disem b[rief]', the recipient is '[...] Lutzen zu Stimpfach(?)', who bought 'das ganze Lehen' there from a predecessor's widow ('seeligen hinderlassnen weib ... erkaufft hatt'), a neighbour is 'Wolf Wilhelmbs von Knöringen zu Rechenberg(?)' (a blind reader: 'Wolf Wilhelmb von Rä[..]iger zu Re[..]enberg'), and the deed closes '[...]hangendem(?) Secret besiglet ... Statt Ellwangen, den [Neün?]zehenden tag deß Monats Februarij, Jm Sechzehen[hundert] Achtzehenden Jar'. The provost's surname is supplied from the Ellwangen fief charters in Staatsarchiv Ludwigsburg (B 425), where an original of the same provost for the mill at Stimpfach of 6 August 1618 (U 54, image online) has the same opening line and date style. No record of this grant itself was found by Archivportal-D search, the start of the recipient's name is lost with the torn corner and the centre of the leaf is unread, so the result is partial. Cut down as a book cover (cover shelfmark 'BB d 4').

identification: Sermon text on St Elisabeth: the end of one sermon and the opening of a second on Qui invenit mulierem bonam (Prov 18,22), whose incipit agrees closely with the anonymous sermon Schneyer, Repertorium IX, p. 897, no. 159 (Wolfenbüttel, Cod. Guelf. 23.26 Aug. 4°; compared in repertory snippets only); shortened and rearranged Legenda aurea c. 168-170 text (Elisabeth, Caecilia, Clement), possibly the bodies of that collection's sermons 159-161; with Collectio epithetorum lists and unidentified model letters
note: Piece 101-3v has the end of a sermon on St Elisabeth, the red rubric 'S(ermo) s(ancte) elizabeth' and the opening of a second sermon on Qui invenit mulierem bonam (Prov 18,22); its first twenty or so words ('ista verba optime [conve]niunt beate elysabeth ... sunt valde commendabilia in muliere ... inveniuntur in ea') agree closely with the incipit Schneyer gives for an anonymous sermon in Wolfenbüttel, Cod. Guelf. 23.26 Aug. 4° (Repertorium IX, p. 897, no. 159), read in snippets of the repertory and not in the manuscript. Four other faces (101-10r, 101-10v, 101-5r, 101-5v) carry shortened and rearranged text of Legenda aurea c. 168, 169 and 170, collated with Graesse, including on 101-10r two sentences from the closing exposition of c. 168 moved into the narrative; they are possibly the bodies of that collection's sermons 159-161 (Elisabeth, Caecilia, Clement, each ending in a Legenda aurea sentence), but no copy of those sermons was available to compare. Other pieces carry Collectio epithetorum lists whose epithets for women agree item for item with München UB 4 Cod. ms. 812, fol. 7r, and model letters between a father, a son and his schoolmaster (rubrics such as 'Magister ad patrem ut mittat sibi li[bros]', 'Responsio filii ad patrem'), source not found. One book is probable (same hand and rubrication) but no join was found; the author of the sermon collection is not established; no human review.

identification: Unidentified concerted Mass, one alto-clef part on two paper leaves, probably complete (Sinfonia, Kyrie, Gloria, Credo, Sanctus with Osanna, Agnus Dei; no Benedictus), headed 'M. 4'(?); no composer named
note: Two paper leaves from one part of a concerted Mass, in alto clef with one flat and probably in G. Leaf 1r has a written-out 'Sinfonia', then Kyrie and Gloria; 1v runs through the Credo to 'iudicare uiuos' and ends with rests, a new time sign and a custos that agrees with the first note of 2r, so the leaves are probably consecutive; 2r runs from 'Et in spiritum sanctum' through Sanctus, Osanna and Agnus Dei with no Benedictus; 2v is ruled but blank. The part's Sinfonia and Kyrie openings were not found by interval search in RISM Online, a weak negative for an inner part, and the pitch readings are unchecked. The two Stams Masses of about 1670 in RISM that also survive as binding waste (Mus.ms. 1550 by Paul Kienhaimer and the anonymous Mus.ms. 2589) have no key signature and a Sonata before every movement, so the fragment belongs to neither.

identification: Jacobus de Voragine, Sermones quadragesimales (Lent weeks 2-4, Easter Sunday Sermo II, Easter Monday Sermo I); 47_1r: prayers of the Mass pro praedicatoribus; 47_2-3 Marian sermon and 47_1r note on the seven grades unidentified

Eight pieces were compared with the Venice 1582 edition on its page images and agree clause by clause: 47_4r/4v (Friday of week 4, Sermones I-II), 47_5v (Easter Sunday, Sermo II), 47_7r (Wednesday of week 3, Sermo II), 47_8r (Easter Sunday, Sermo II), 47_10r (Wednesday of week 2), 47_14r (Saturday of week 4), and 47_15r/15v (Saturday of week 3, Sermo I). One research reader made five of these comparisons. A second reader read four further passages blind before opening the source and corrected three machine-assigned loci. The differences from the print are of wording, omission and order. Pieces 6, 9 and 11-13, 10v and 14v are matched only by machine against the OCR and are provisional. On 47_4, 47_5, 47_8 and 47_15 the face catalogued 'v' is the original recto. 47_1r carries the secret Famulis tuis and the complenda Conserva domine of the Mass for preachers recorded by Gerard de Frachet (compared through snippets). The Marian sermon on 47_2-3 and the seven-grades note on 47_1r are unidentified. No human review.

identification: Latin lecture notes on Aristotle's De caelo, lib. II (Quaestiones with Conclusiones, 17th-century cursive), agreeing closely, in places word for word, and in order but for one sentence, with Georg Klainer SJ, Theses philosophicae de quinta substantia Peripateticorum sive de coelo (Dillingen 1608), theses XXII, XXIV-XXVII and XXXV; probably notes from a Jesuit philosophy course closely related to the one behind those theses and, like the leaf, drawing on the Coimbra Commentarii in De coelo; the course manuscript is not identified
note: A paper bifolium reused in a binding, with conclusions on the spherical figure of the heavens, the Empyrean, the order and nobility of the heavens, the light of the stars, and the figure and motion of the stars. Read against page images of Klainer's Dillingen theses of 1608, the notes follow theses XXII, XXIV-XXVII and XXXV, often in the same words and in the same order except for one sentence placed as in the Coimbra commentary, including lines not found in the Coimbra commentary by a text search of its OCR ('quin seipsos caeli frangerent ac perrumperent', 'infimum et nobis proximum', the exception of the Sun's heaven). The notes are fuller than the print and keep Coimbra matter that it lacks (the waters above the heavens, Pliny and Scaliger on stars seen from a well), so they are probably notes from a lecture course closely related to the one behind the theses, not a copy of them; notes made from the printed theses together with Coimbra cannot be excluded, and nothing shows the course was given at Dillingen. The lecturer and the year are not fixed by the leaf.

identification: German prose with Latin authorities on seeing God and Christ, probably a sermon (two paper pieces, 15th-century Bavarian-Austrian cursive); probably paraphrases Bernard of Clairvaux, Sermones super Cantica 2.1, and quotes his 'videre hominem hominis conditorem'; containing work not found
note: Two paper pieces in one hand, reread at native size; the stained lower third of 1r and the Latin lines on 1v remain weakly read, and the strip's verso is blank. The strip probably paraphrases Bernard, Sermones super Cantica 2.1 ('ich bedenk die grosse ... alt veter vnd propheten ... so träg dergegen pin'), and goes on to divine love as a fire ('gotlich lieb ist ain feur'). The leaf argues from 2 Cor 3:18 and an ostrich exemplum ('der strauss von der kraft seins gesichts vnd von der hitz der sune') that the sight of God makes man like God, applies the mirror, string-music and flower topos (as in Compendium theologicae veritatis VII.31) to 'die aller schönst menschait Christi', and ends with Bernard's sentence in German ('sehen den menschen der des menschen schepfer ist'; Sermones super Cantica 20.3, read on the page). Both Bernard passages circulate as sermon authorities, so the German writer perhaps took them from an intermediate source. The containing German work was not found by Google Books, Corpus Corporum or Internet Archive searches, nor by search in Schnell's edition of Peuntner's Liebhabung Gottes; that strip and leaf are one text is likely but not proved.

content.title: German prose on seeing God and Christ, probably a sermon

Expl. (160-1v): das wir aber sehen den menschen der des menschen schepfer ist.
content.remarks: The work is not identified. The senses topos is that of Compendium theologicae veritatis VII.31, applied here to Christ's humanity. 160-2v is blank.

identification: Thomas Aquinas, Expositio libri Posteriorum Analyticorum, lib. I, lect. 8, nn. 1-5 (recto) and 8-9 (verso)
note: A narrow strip from one wide column: the recto keeps line-ends of lect. 8 nn. 1-5, the verso line-beginnings of nn. 8-9, both agreeing in wording and sequence with the Leonine text (about forty partial lines). Research readers compared both faces with page images of Leonine vol. I (1882), pp. 166-170, one of them reading the stained recto lines 6-11 and abraded verso lines 1-7 before opening the source. The scribe's 'sic demonstratio fieret' (recto line 14) carries interlinear b/a transposition marks restoring the edition's order. The verso reads 'et ex duabus' and 'et ex praemissa', readings the Leonine apparatus gives from manuscript groups ACDELQST and BCDEO respectively; these are noted, not used to place the strip. The last recto line is cut through the letters and unread. No date, origin or textual affiliation is claimed; no human review.

identification: Commentary, probably on Prudentius, Dittochaeon (Tituli historiarum), Old Testament stanzas (12, 16 and probably 19); the commentary itself unidentified
note: Nine abraded paper pieces in a small abbreviated cursive, with words in a larger book hand inside red frames. Three framed phrases are words of Prudentius, Dittochaeon: 'Fer|uebat via' (stanza 12, 'Fervebat via sicca eremi'), read the same by four readers, 'yericho' (stanza 16, 'Procubuit Iericho'), read by three readers who had no candidate text, and, less securely, 'Dauid' (probably stanza 19, 'David parvus erat'), read by one of them. 'Fervebat via' carries most of the weight; David and Jericho alone are common biblical names. The matches were found by Corpus Corporum search in a transcribed text; no page of the poem or of a commentary on it was compared, the other frames are not placed, and the cursive is unread.
